title: Targeting Parental Risk Factors for Children's Anxiety: A Factorial Randomized Trial with Three Intervention Components
journal: J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Parent-focused interventions have the potential to reduce parental risk factors for children's anxiety. We tested three theoretically distinct intervention components, targeting distinct parental risk factors, to improve understanding of the role of these factors in children's anxiety, and to guide intervention program development.

METHOD: We used a 12-week factorial experiment with random allocation to any possible combination and order of three single-session online components: (1) reducing family accommodation, (2) increasing parental empathetic responses, and (3) cognitive restructuring for parental maladaptive cognitions. Assessments took place at baseline (T 0 ), after the first component (T 2 ), after all components (T 6 ), and at follow-up (T 12 ). Our primary outcome was parent-reported child anxiety at T 2 . We used intention-to-treat regression-based ANCOVA models.

RESULTS: The components did not reduce parent-reported anxiety at T 2 , but the empathetic responding component improved parental empathic responding at all timepoints and parent-reported anxiety at T 6  and T 12 . The family accommodation component improved family accommodation at T 2 , but this effect disappeared once parents received additional components. The cognitive restructuring component did not produce any effects.

CONCLUSION: Online, single-session components did not reduce parent-reported anxiety at the primary timepoint, and most outcomes did not change. Nevertheless, components targeting parental empathic responding and family accommodation can meaningfully change parental risk factors for children's anxiety. Targeting empathetic responses seems most promising for reducing children's anxiety. These findings may contribute to the development of more precise parent-focused interventions for children's anxiety.

title: Does later chronotype cause poorer adolescent mental health? An adolescent brain cognitive development study
abstract:
BACKGROUND: This study investigated whether chronotype (biobehavioral preference for sleep and wake timing) across early adolescence impacts mental health symptoms at age 13-14. This is a relationship with growing correlational evidence but limited causal exploration.

METHODS: Participants were 7,489 adolescents (aged 9-10 at baseline; 13-14 at the fifth assessment wave) from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study (ABCD). Marginal structural models with machine learning-based weight estimation were used to assess the causal impact of chronotype at ages 11-12 and 12-13, as measured by the youth-reported Munich Chronotype Questionnaire, on several dimensions of mental health symptoms at age 13-14 (parent-reported Child Behavioral Checklist internalizing and externalizing values, n = 2,668; child-reported Prodromal Psychosis Scale, n = 2,698).

RESULTS: There was no effect of chronotype at age 11-12 on any outcome. However, later chronotype at age 12-13 was associated with slightly more severe externalizing symptoms (b = .29, p = .04) and more psychotic-like experiences at age 13-14 (b = .05, p = .02), but not with more severe internalizing symptoms. Post hoc analyses indicated the lack of relationship with internalizing held for both anxiety and depression symptoms and in both sexes.

CONCLUSIONS: There are likely causal effects of adolescent chronotype on mental health symptoms, but these are dependent on the dimension of mental health and period of adolescence. The typically reported association between later chronotype and more severe internalizing symptoms may not manifest until later adolescence (such as with the common postpubertal shift in chronotype).

title: Promoting healthy families: a three-arm randomized controlled trial of Triple P and Circle of Security-Parenting versus treatment-as-usual for families with young children (2-6 years)
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Parenting programs grounded in social learning (SL) and attachment theory are widely implemented, yet few trials have directly compared their effects across multiple parenting domains in community contexts. This study examined the relative effectiveness of an SL-based program (Triple P - Level 4 Group) and an attachment-based program (Circle of Security - Parenting, COS-P) against treatment-as-usual (TAU) when delivered online through community agencies.

METHODS: A three-arm randomized controlled trial was conducted across four community organizations in Ontario, Canada. Caregivers of children aged 2-6 years (N = 502) were randomized (1:1:1) to Triple P, COS-P, or TAU. Primary outcomes were child behavioral difficulties (SDQ-Total) and parental overreactivity with post-intervention, 6-, and 12-month follow-up. Secondary outcomes included parental attributions, parenting stress, and caregiver mental health. Analyses followed an intention-to-treat framework using mixed-effects models (ClinicalTrials.gov #NCT04702191).

RESULTS: Relative to TAU, Triple P demonstrated significant short-term reductions in emotional symptoms and conduct problems, and immediate improvements in hostile and helpless parenting and anxiety; however, most between-group effects did not persist beyond post-intervention. Effects on total child behavior problems at 12 months were no longer significant after correction for multiple testing. Improvements in parental attributions were sustained at 12 months. COS-P differed from TAU on only one outcome, at one time point. Within-group improvements in child behavior, dysfunctional parenting, and caregiver mood were observed in TAU, with COS-P and Triple P showing similar trends. Exploratory analyses suggested broader benefits for Triple P relative to COS-P.

CONCLUSIONS: Triple P demonstrated selective short-term benefits relative to TAU across child behavioral and parenting outcomes, with sustained effects limited to parental attributions. COS-P showed no measurable effects relative to TAU. These findings highlight the importance of behavioral management and self-regulation components and point to the need for further research examining contextual moderators, maintenance strategies, and sustainable delivery approaches, including digital formats.

title: Developmental trajectories of tonic and phasic irritability from ages 12 to 21: early predictors, co-development, and psychiatric outcomes in young adulthood
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Irritability is a common and impairing, transdiagnostic feature of youth psychopathology. Theory distinguishes tonic irritability (persistent irritable mood) from phasic irritability (episodic temper outbursts), yet little is known about how these dimensions co-develop across adolescence into young adulthood and relate to later psychiatric outcomes.

METHODS: Participants were drawn from a longitudinal community cohort assessed at ages 12, 15, 18, and 21 (N = 532 with data at one or more waves). Tonic and phasic irritability were derived from youth-report items spanning multiple measures. We tested the factor structure and longitudinal measurement invariance of tonic and phasic irritability, then modeled co-development using parallel-process latent growth curve models. Sociodemographic factors and parental lifetime psychopathology (assessed at age 9) were examined as predictors of growth factors. Growth factors were used to estimate associations with age-21 psychiatric diagnoses and self-injurious thoughts and behaviors.

RESULTS: A two-factor model distinguishing tonic and phasic irritability fit better than a one-factor model at each wave, and configural, metric, and scalar invariance were supported from ages 12 to 21. On average, tonic irritability increased modestly whereas phasic irritability declined. Despite divergent mean trajectories, tonic and phasic slopes were positively correlated, indicating coordinated change. Baseline tonic irritability predicted steeper declines in phasic irritability, whereas baseline phasic irritability did not predict change in tonic irritability. Higher tonic intercept and steeper tonic increases were associated with higher odds of depressive and anxiety disorders and suicidal ideation at age 21; tonic intercept also predicted suicidal acts, and tonic change additionally predicted non-suicidal self-injury. In contrast, higher phasic intercept predicted greater odds of disruptive behavior disorders but lower odds of depression, and steeper phasic decline was associated with greater odds of depression.

CONCLUSIONS: Tonic and phasic irritability are separable yet developmentally linked across adolescence into young adulthood and show distinct clinical correlates. Distinguishing persistent mood-based irritability from outburst-based irritability may refine developmental models of risk and intervention targets.

title: Estimating direct and indirect genetic effects on emerging variation in depressive symptoms in early adolescence: a trio polygenic score analysis in the MoBa cohort : Author list
abstract: Early adolescence is a common period of onset for depressive symptoms. In part, this may reflect a developmental expression of individuals' genetic propensities as they undergo physiological and hormonal changes and interact with new environments. Many commonly proposed mechanisms assume direct effects of an individual's own genes on emerging variation in their depressive symptomatology. However, estimates of genetic influence based on analyses in unrelated individuals capture not only direct genetic effects but also genetic effects from parents and other biologically related family members. In data from the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort (MoBa), we used linear mixed models to distinguish developmentally-stable and adolescence-specific direct and parental indirect genetic effects. In within-family models, we examined effects of polygenic scores for major depressive disorder (MDD), ADHD, anxiety disorders, and educational attainment (EA) on depressive symptoms measured at ages 8 and 14. Children's own MDD polygenic scores showed adolescence-specific effects on depressive symptoms (β PGS*wave =0.041, [95% CI: 0.017, 0.065]). Developmentally-stable direct effects from children's polygenic scores for MDD (β = 0.016, [0.006, 0.039]), ADHD (β = 0.024, [0.008, 0.041]) and EA (β=-0.02, [ -0.038, -0.002]) were also evident. The only evidence of indirect genetic effects was a stable effect of maternal EA polygenic scores (β = 0.04, [0.024, 0.054]). Direct genetic effects linked to genetic liability to MDD accounted for emerging variation in depressive symptoms in adolescence. These results imply that specific etiological mechanisms related to MDD may become particularly relevant for depressive symptoms during early adolescence compared to at earlier ages.

title: Co-developmental trajectories of emotional symptoms and peer problems from childhood to adolescence: associations with positive and negative mental health outcomes
abstract: This study used data from the Millennium Cohort Study (MCS) to examine the co-developmental trajectories of emotional symptoms and peer problems from ages 3 to 17. A sample of 16,983 children (48.8% female, 82.4% White ethnicity) was analyzed using parallel-process latent class growth models (PP-LCGMs) to explore how emotional symptoms and peer problems evolve over time and their associations with positive and negative mental health outcomes at age 17. Five trajectory classes were identified: "Primary peer problems" class (12.2%), "Co-increasing high risk" class (4.0%), "Co-decreasing medium risk" class (7.1%), "Primary emotional symptoms" class (10.3%), and "Persistent low risk" class (66.6%). The "Persistent low risk" and "Co-decreasing medium risk" classes reported the highest levels of mental wellbeing and self-esteem, relatively high levels of self-control, and the lowest levels of psychological distress, self-harm, and suicide attempt at age 17. The "Co-increasing high risk" and "Primary emotional symptoms" classes reported the poorest outcomes. The "Primary peer problems" class fell between these classes. Findings highlight the importance of identifying heterogeneous co-developmental patterns of emotional symptoms and peer problems from childhood to adolescence and call for tailored intervention programs to reduce risk and promote long-term well-being.

title: Mortgage Lending Risk Maps From the 1930s Influence the Prevalence of Youth Mental Health Problems in the Modern Era
journal: J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Historical mortgage lending policies and practices serve as a key foundation of modern-day socioeconomic systems. Few of these structural legacies have been as powerful as those for 20 th  century mortgage lending risk maps - often referred to as redlining. Although extant studies have identified mental health disparities among residents of formerly redlined neighborhoods, the legacies of greenlined or otherwise positively designated neighborhoods are largely unknown. This represents a key gap in the literature, as efforts to illuminate the historical legacies of these maps must also include the ways in which they may have cemented concentrated advantage and prosperity.

METHOD: The current study sought to fill this gap in a population-based sample of 20,222 children and adolescents in 10,111 families, recruited via birth records into the Michigan State University Twin Registry. We fitted a series of multilevel models to illuminate the full legacy of 20 th  century mortgage lending risk maps for youth mental health in the 21 st  century.

RESULTS: Multilevel models indicated that, as expected, youth residing in formerly redlined neighborhoods (those designated as "hazardous") exhibited more symptomatology than youth residing in other types of neighborhoods. However, the most prominent and persistently observed differences were found for youth in formerly greenlined neighborhoods (those designated as "best"), who exhibited substantially better mental health than youth residing in any other type of neighborhood. What's more, the effects of greenlining persisted even when controlling for neighborhood and familial socioeconomic factors, indicating that these variables do not account for the observed effects.

CONCLUSION: Such findings serve to further highlight both the unfair legacies of disadvantage and the entrenched legacies of prosperity wrought by historical mortgage lending risk maps.

title: Efficacy and acceptability of digital safety planning therapy for self-injurious thoughts and behaviors in adolescents with depressive episodes: a randomized controlled trial
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Self-injurious thoughts and behaviors (SITB) represent a significant mental health issue among Chinese adolescents. Research on smartphone-based safety planning as digital therapeutics for SITB in China remains limited. This randomized controlled trial evaluated the efficacy and acceptability of a safety planning mobile application (LIFES) for reducing SITB in adolescents with depressive episodes.

METHODS: Among 189 adolescents with depressive episodes screened, 122 were randomized to either the intervention group (LIFES app plus treatment as usual [TAU], n = 61) or the control group (TAU only, n = 61). Follow-up assessments at 1, 3, and 6 months measured SITB, depression, anxiety, and sleep quality. This trial is registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2300075663; https://www.chictr.org.cn/).

RESULTS: Generalized linear mixed models showed significant time-by-group interaction effects for non-suicidal self-injury frequency (F = 3.39, p = .018), suicide planning seriousness (F = 2.93, p = .034), confidence in suicide completion during preparation (F = 3.10, p = .027), suicide threat/gesture frequency (F = 3.64, p = .013), and total suicidal behavior frequency (F = 3.31, p = .020) after adjusting for depression and anxiety symptom severity, sleep quality, and years of education. The intervention group showed significantly greater reductions in SITB characteristics compared to the control group. User experience surveys indicated good satisfaction with the application.

CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates that safety planning-based digital therapeutics are an effective adjunctive intervention for SITB in adolescents with depressive episodes. Future research should examine the applicability of this intervention to broader populations.

title: The emotion regulation and recognition account of empathy-related processes in autism: a multimodal, multilevel case-control study
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Recent evidence suggests that many autistic individuals exhibit heightened emotional responsiveness to others' affect despite greater difficulty recognizing others' emotions and accurately inferring their perspectives. This study introduces and preliminarily evaluates the Emotion Regulation and Recognition Account (ERRA), a model proposing that susceptibility to emotion dysregulation and challenges with emotion cue interpretation jointly shape empathy-related processing in autism.

METHODS: Children aged 6-13 years (N autistic  = 103; N non-autistic  = 40) participated; groups were matched demographically. Children watched five videos of youth exhibiting strong affect (e.g. sad and angry) and answered questions about their reactions to and understanding of the videos. These responses were coded for empathy-related processes such as emotional contagion and perspective taking. Electrodermal reactivity to and eye gaze towards the videos were also measured. Multilevel models were employed to test hypothesized pathways in the ERRA.

RESULTS: Autistic children experienced greater affective intensity but exhibited less accurate emotion recognition than non-autistic children when observing youth exhibiting strong affect. Greater physiological and affective intensity were associated with greater attention shifting, and more frequent attention shifting among autistic children was associated with less accurate emotion recognition. Less accurate emotion recognition was, in turn, associated with less emotional synchrony and perspective taking, which were linked with less prosocial motivation.

CONCLUSIONS: The findings provide initial support for the ERRA by suggesting that, rather than experiencing indifference, many autistic individuals have strong affective reactions when observing others in distress. These reactions may lead to attention shifting, which can reduce awareness of others' emotional cues, potentially interrupting the unfolding of empathic understanding and responding. Empathy-supporting interventions can build upon the affective responsiveness to others experienced by many autistic individuals.

title: Links of fitbit-derived sleep architecture and fragmentation with ADHD symptoms and externalizing behaviors in adolescents
abstract: Sleep disturbances are linked to adolescent externalizing behaviors and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) symptoms. However, few studies have examined associations between objectively measured sleep architecture and these behavioral outcomes. This study investigated whether specific sleep stages and fragmentation are associated with externalizing behaviors and ADHD symptoms in a large U.S. population-based cohort. Participants were 4,545 adolescents (48.4% female; 73% White) from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study with available Fitbit sleep data and parent-reported behavioral assessments. Sleep predictors included absolute duration and proportional time spent in rapid eye movement (REM), deep, and light sleep, as well as wake after sleep onset (WASO). Outcomes were externalizing behaviors and ADHD symptoms. Models adjusted for annual household income, sex, age, race, and weekend status. Lower REM sleep, both in absolute duration and relative proportion, was significantly associated with higher ADHD symptoms but not with externalizing behaviors after correction for multiple testing. Greater sleep fragmentation, indexed by longer absolute and relative WASO, was associated with elevated ADHD symptoms and, less robustly, externalizing behaviors. Light and deep sleep were not significantly associated with either outcome. REM sleep deficiency was associated with ADHD symptoms, whereas sleep fragmentation was associated with ADHD symptoms and, less robustly, with externalizing behaviors. Associations were cross-sectional; longitudinal and experimental studies are needed to determine whether these sleep characteristics contribute to, or could be targeted to improve, behavioral outcomes in adolescents.

title: The mental health sequelae of mass shootings on affected children, adolescents and young adults - a scoping review
abstract: While the incidence of school shootings is highest in the US worldwide, these events also occur in Europe, such as the recent fatal school shooting in Graz in Austria, highlighting the importance of evidence-based care for the survivors. This study aims to synthesize existing evidence on the short- and long-term effects of mass shootings on the mental health of children, adolescents, and young adults, and to identify risk factors that predispose individuals to psychological sequelae to inform appropriate aftercare recommendations. After conducting a literature search in PubMed, Medline, Scopus and the Cochrane Library, 483 references were identified, which were screened by two independent raters according to inclusion criteria, resulting in 15 eligible studies. Most shootings examined took place in the US, with some focusing on shootings in Finland. All studies examined either adolescents or young adults. No studies examining the effects on children were found. The results showed that directly after such an event, a large proportion of the affected show posttraumatic stress symptomatology (PTSS); in the long-term most recuperate without intervention, however a small percentage remain symptomatic and later develop PTSD. Key risk factors include female sex, younger age, previous traumatic experiences, an avoidant attachment style and a higher grade of exposure. Social support is an important protective factor. Based on the findings, a multitiered approach tailored to the needs of affected individuals is recommended, supported by a coordinated screening process to identify those with relevant risk factors.

title: Hallucinations associated with bilastine in a teenager: case report and disproportionality analysis in VigiBase(®)
abstract: Bilastine is a second-generation H1-antihistamine considered to have minimal central nervous system penetration and low anticholinergic activity. Neuropsychiatric adverse drug reactions (ADRs), including hallucinations, are not expected with bilastine, although such reactions have been reported with other second-generation antihistamines (sgAH). We report the case of a 13-year-old girl who developed visual hallucinations and panic attacks shortly after starting treatment with bilastine, after having experienced a recurrent sensation of presence while taking desloratadine. The patient's symptoms resolved progressively after discontinuation of bilastine, with a Naranjo score of 6 indicating probable causality. VigiBase ®  analysis was also performed and identified a possible association between bilastine and hallucinations. This case, supported by pharmacovigilance data, although predominantly in older adults, suggests a potential pharmacovigilance signal with possible association between bilastine and hallucinations. Furthermore, similar neuropsychiatric ADRs have been reported with other second-generation antihistamines. Clinicians should be aware of this rare but potentially distressing ADR to ensure prompt recognition and discontinuation of treatment.

title: Mental health and urinary incontinence in childhood
abstract: Intermittent and uncontrolled loss of urine is common among children but requires medical attention when it persists beyond age 5 years. Mostly functional in origin, urinary incontinence is caused by a complex inter-relationship of biopsychosocial factors, and evidence shows that mental health problems and adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are common in children and adolescents with urinary incontinence. Mental health problems and ACEs (including abuse, neglect, and household dysfunction) could be both causes and consequences of paediatric urinary incontinence, but research is needed to understand causal pathways. Treatment guidelines increasingly recognise the need to integrate assessment of psychosocial factors and mental health support into clinical care pathways for children affected by urinary incontinence. Parental and societal beliefs, cultural norms, availability of sanitation facilities, economic constraints, and policy-level gaps affect the management of paediatric urinary incontinence. Early assessment and treatment are needed to prevent urinary incontinence from becoming chronic and negatively impacting on children's quality of life, wellbeing, and education.

title: Evaluation of a Commercial Pediatric Sepsis Early Detection Alert in the Emergency Department
abstract:
Key Points Question How well does the pediatric sepsis early detection alert from the largest electronic health record vendor in US hospitals identify children with sepsis? Findings In a multicenter cohort of 166 943 pediatric emergency department (ED) encounters, the alert identified 36% of children with sepsis according to the Phoenix Sepsis Score and alerted prior to diagnosis in 30% of cases. Sensitivity was lower among Black children, those younger than 5 years, and those seen in hospitals that were not pediatric only. Meaning This early detection alert threshold had low sensitivity, which was poorly suited for pediatric sepsis screening; it did not detect most cases of sepsis present in the first 24 hours after ED arrival.

Importance Screening tools have been implemented with the goal of improving early detection of pediatric sepsis, with limited evidence of effectiveness. The Epic Systems Pediatric Sepsis Early Detection Model (PESM) and its associated clinical alert have been widely implemented in emergency departments (EDs) in the US but have not undergone independent evaluation. Objective To evaluate the diagnostic characteristics of the Epic PESM for (1) identifying sepsis and (2) identifying sepsis before patients met Phoenix sepsis criteria. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective multicenter cohort study of pediatric ED encounters was conducted across 8 EDs within a New York health system from January 2024 through June 2025. Children younger than 18 years were included; behavioral health encounters and ED deaths within 1 hour of arrival were excluded. Data were analyzed from August 2025 through July 2026. Exposure Triggering of the PESM alert in the first 24 hours after ED arrival. Main Outcomes and Measures Sepsis was defined as a Phoenix score of 2 or higher. Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) were calculated for the outcome of sepsis within 24 hours of ED arrival. Secondarily, evaluation was restricted to only instances in which the alert triggered before sepsis onset. Sensitivity was evaluated in relevant subgroups, and a subgroup with a sensitivity 10% or more below the overall cohort sensitivity was considered clinically meaningful. Results Among 166 943 pediatric ED encounters, 189 cases of sepsis occurred in the first 24 hours. A total of 76 685 pediatric patients (45.9%) were female, and 79 032 patients (47.3%) were under the age of 5 years. Sensitivity of the PESM for identifying patients with sepsis was 36% (95% CI, 29%-43%); PPV was 3% (95% CI, 2%-4%), and NPV was greater than 99% (95% CI, 99%-99%). The alert triggered before sepsis with a sensitivity of 30% (95% CI, 24%-37%). Subgroup sensitivity was 10% or more below overall cohort sensitivity in Black children (22%; 95% CI, 9%-40%) and among children less than 5 years old (20%; 95% CI, 12%-30%), as well as in EDs outside of tertiary children’s hospitals (25%; 95% CI, 14%-40%). Conclusions and Relevance Per the results of this multicenter cohort study, the PESM alert had low sensitivity for identifying children with sepsis and does not support timely or equitable pediatric sepsis screening. Sensitivity was low in Black children, in children younger than 5 years, and outside of tertiary children’s hospitals.

This multicenter cohort study evaluates the diagnostic characteristics of the Epic Systems Pediatric Sepsis Early Detection Model for identification and early recognition of sepsis using Phoenix sepsis criteria.

title: From discovery to proof: a Translation Evidence Map for precision psychiatry
abstract: Precision psychiatry aims to improve individual-patient decisions by measuring clinically meaningful heterogeneity, not by privileging any one data type, biomarker, or analytical method. This Personal View proposes a Translation Evidence Map that stages claims, from Level 0 (defined use case or discovery-positioning statement) to Level 6 (post-deployment monitoring), linked to measurement reliability, generalisable inference, decision value, safe delivery, and proportionality to risk, clinical need, and inaction. The Map does not replace Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE), biomarker qualification, prediction-model, regulatory, or roadmap frameworks; it identifies the highest defensible claim across components of unequal maturity and the next evidence step for compound precision claims. The Personal View discusses examples spanning inflammatory and circuit-based depression stratification, psychosis relapse monitoring, and suicidality monitoring, illustrating how the Map makes claim maturity, stopping points, stakeholder roles, and trade-offs important to patients explicit.

title: SOS for School Staff Suicide Prevention Program: Perspectives of School Staff
journal: Evid Based Pract Child Adolesc Ment Health
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Schools play an important role in child and adolescent suicide prevention efforts and many states have begun to mandate suicide prevention education for school staff.

OBJECTIVE: This study explored school staff's ( N  = 1509) perceptions of the impact of a brief virtual suicide prevention course titled: SOS for School Staff.

METHOD: This study used an online posttest and three-month follow-up to explore school staff's ( N  = 1509) perceptions via a posttest and follow-up measuring preparation, confidence, and knowledge.

RESULTS: In this study, most school staff agreed that the training increased their preparation (85.4%), confidence (86.2%), and knowledge (89.7%) about responding to a suicide disclosure. Approximately one-third of the respondents used the training content three months after the training, but there was a low response rate for the follow-up.

CONCLUSION: This is a promising suicide prevention training for school staff, who report it improves preparation to identify youth in distress, confidence at engaging youth in caring conversations, and knowledge of how to respond to a student's disclosure of suicidal thoughts and behaviors; however, larger follow-up studies are required.

title: Risk-Stratified Cardiac Monitoring During Antipsychotic Treatment in Adolescents and Young Adults
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Antipsychotic-associated heart rate-corrected QT (QTc) prolongation and sudden cardiac death are uncommon in young people, but risk is concentrated in patients with identifiable clinical vulnerability and during selected drug- or exposure-related situations. We mapped the evidence and developed a risk-stratified framework for clinical monitoring.

METHODS: This structured narrative review searched PubMed in August 2026 using one comprehensive query and 41 targeted subqueries. After PMID-based deduplication, 934 unique records underwent title screening, 382 abstract review, and 158 full-text relevance assessment; 104 database-derived sources met broad relevance criteria. Backward citation checking and author-identified sources added 58 articles. Overall, 162 sources were considered and 100 providing direct, non-redundant support were cited from the original search; three further sources were incorporated during peer review to address reviewer comments, for a final total of 103 cited references. Two authors independently assessed full-text relevance. Youth evidence was prioritized; adult evidence was used for adult-only agents or when youth-specific data were unavailable. Findings were synthesized narratively without formal risk-of-bias or certainty assessment.

RESULTS: Patient-level factors, particularly electrolyte disturbance, bradycardia, restrictive eating disorder or medical instability, thyroid dysfunction, inherited channelopathy, structural disease, and interacting drugs, were more consistently associated with QTc risk than drug identity for many commonly used agents. Ziprasidone and pimozide had the strongest youth-specific drug-related signals. Adult evidence supported heightened caution with sertindole and iloperidone; high-dose phenothiazines and amisulpride in overdose or renal impairment represented exposure- or context-dependent risks. Clozapine required separate myocarditis-focused surveillance. The evidence supports structured baseline risk assessment and targeted ECG and electrolyte testing, with repeat monitoring driven by risk factors, treatment changes, and agent-specific warnings.

CONCLUSION: Monitoring should be tiered rather than uniformly scheduled for all patients. The proposed framework distinguishes core clinical risk assessment from targeted cardiac testing and identifies precautionary intervals that require prospective validation.

title: Associations between perceived stress, sleep quality, and suicidal ideation among Chinese graduating-grade secondary school students: a multi-method study of the moderating role of physical exercise
abstract:
Objective This study aimed to investigate the associations among perceived stress, sleep quality, physical exercise, and suicidal ideation among Chinese graduating-grade secondary school students. Specifically, this study examined whether sleep quality mediated the association between perceived stress and suicidal ideation and whether physical exercise moderated these relationships. In addition, machine-learning prediction models and network analysis were applied to identify important predictors and interconnected symptoms associated with suicidal ideation. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among ninth- and twelfth-grade students from 13 secondary schools in Yunnan Province, China. A total of 4,372 valid questionnaires were collected. Participants completed measures of perceived stress, sleep quality, suicidal ideation, and physical exercise. Mediation and moderated mediation analyses were conducted using PROCESS models after adjusting for demographic covariates. Furthermore, ridge regression and gradient boosting tree models were used to predict suicidal ideation, with Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) applied to evaluate predictor contributions. Network analysis was conducted to explore central and bridge nodes among study variables. Results Perceived stress was positively associated with suicidal ideation, and sleep quality partially mediated this association. Physical exercise significantly moderated the direct association between perceived stress and suicidal ideation as well as the association between sleep quality problems and suicidal ideation. Specifically, higher levels of physical exercise weakened the positive relationships between perceived stress, sleep problems, and suicidal ideation. Machine-learning analyses showed that sleep quality problems, perceived stress, physical exercise, and their interaction terms contributed substantially to the prediction of suicidal ideation, with both models achieving an R 2 of approximately 0.41 in the hold-out test set. Network analysis further identified subjective sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep disturbances, stress-coping burden, and physical exercise frequency as highly connected nodes within the network. Conclusion Among Chinese graduating-grade secondary school students, perceived stress, poor sleep quality, and suicidal ideation were closely interconnected, whereas physical exercise appeared to attenuate these risk associations. Integrating stress management, sleep improvement strategies, and regular physical exercise into school-based mental health programs may provide potential approaches for suicide risk prevention among adolescents.

1 Introduction Suicide is a major global public health concern. The World Health Organization has reported that more than 720,000 people die by suicide each year, making suicide the third leading cause of death among individuals aged 15–29 worldwide ( 1 ). Suicide is conceptualized as a continuum process, in which suicidal ideation represents the initial stage. Suicidal ideation refers to thoughts, desires, or plans to end one’s own life ( 2 , 3 ). Epidemiological evidence indicates that suicidal ideation is relatively prevalent among children and adolescents, and those who experience suicidal ideation are at a substantially higher risk of subsequent suicide-related outcomes ( 4 ). In secondary school students, suicidal ideation is not merely a transient or isolated psychological phenomenon; rather, it may serve as an important risk signal for subsequent mental health problems, suicidal behaviors, and impaired social functioning ( 5 , 6 ). Longitudinal studies have further demonstrated that adolescent suicidal ideation is closely associated with later psychopathology, suicide-related behaviors, and long-term social dysfunction ( 7 ). Therefore, identifying the factors associated with suicidal ideation in secondary school students, as well as elucidating its underlying mechanisms, is of critical importance for school-based mental health education and crisis intervention. Among secondary school students, those in their final year experience multiple academic and developmental stressors, including entrance examinations, academic competition, parental expectations, and uncertainty about future trajectories. Prolonged stress may increase SI by affecting emotional regulation, recovery processes, and daily behaviors. Sleep quality represents a potential pathway linking stress to mental health outcomes, as sleep problems may impair emotional regulation and stress recovery capacity. SI is a complex outcome arising from interactions among stress, sleep problems, health behaviors, and psychological adaptation. Traditional models can examine overall pathways but provide limited information about the relative importance of specific variables. Network analysis and predictive models may therefore provide complementary evidence by identifying key nodes and predictive contributors associated with SI. 1.1 Perceived stress and suicidal ideation Perceived stress refers to an individual’s appraisal of the extent to which situations in life are unpredictable, uncontrollable, and overloading ( 8 ). Compared with objective stressful events, PS emphasizes individuals’ cognitive appraisal of environmental demands and their perceived capacity to cope with those demands ( 9 ). Among final-year secondary school students, multiple stressors—such as entrance examinations, academic competition, performance evaluation, parental expectations, peer comparison, and uncertainty regarding future development—do not exert uniform effects on mental health. Instead, their impact largely depends on whether students perceive these demands as exceeding their coping capacity and controllability ( 10 ). When students persistently appraise stressors as unpredictable, uncontrollable, or unmanageable, their psychological resources may become chronically depleted, leading to heightened tension, anxiety, depressive symptoms, helplessness, and self-devaluation. From a theoretical perspective, PS may represent a key risk factor for SI ( 11 ). According to the stress-vulnerability framework, individuals exposed to sustained high levels of stress, particularly in the absence of sufficient psychological resources, are more likely to develop maladaptive cognitive appraisals and affective dysregulation ( 12 , 13 ). For final-year secondary school students, elevated PS not only intensifies threatening interpretations of examination failure, academic fluctuations, and future uncertainty, but may also undermine problem-solving abilities, emotional regulation capacity, and hopefulness ( 14 , 15 ). When students continuously perceive their current situation as unchangeable and future outcomes as uncontrollable, feelings of hopelessness, perceived failure, and diminished life meaning may emerge, thereby increasing the likelihood of SI ( 16 ). Accordingly, PS is not only a salient indicator of psychological risk in this population but may also serve as a key psychosocial determinant of variability in SI. Based on this rationale, the following hypothesis is proposed: H1 : PS is significantly positively associated with SI. 1.2 The mediating role of sleep quality Sleep quality refers to an individual’s overall evaluation of their sleep experience, typically encompassing subjective sleep perception, sleep onset latency, sleep duration, sleep efficiency, sleep disturbances, and daytime functional status ( 17 ). Among final-year secondary school students, elevated perceived stress is generally associated with a sustained state of tension, worry, and heightened psychological burden. Such persistent stress exposure can disrupt normal sleep processes, leading to difficulties in sleep initiation, impaired sleep maintenance, reduced restorative sleep, and increased daytime fatigue ( 18 ). From the perspective of emotion regulation theory, sleep plays a central role in maintaining functional balance within the prefrontal–limbic system ( 19 ). Sleep deprivation is associated with reduced cognitive reappraisal capacity and impaired inhibitory control, while simultaneously increasing emotional reactivity to negative stimuli. These changes may facilitate the development of maladaptive interpretative biases and helpless cognitions, thereby elevating the risk of suicidal ideation ( 19 ). In addition, from a stress recovery framework, poor sleep quality compromises an individual’s ability to recover from daily stressors, making academic setbacks, interpersonal conflicts, and other stress-related events more likely to accumulate into sustained negative affective experiences ( 20 , 21 ). Within this process, sleep quality may function as a mediating mechanism linking PS to SI, reflecting a statistical pathway through which stress experiences are translated into emotional distress and suicide-related cognitions. Therefore, PSQI may serve as an important bridging mechanism in the association between PS and SI. For final-year students, high-stakes academic demands may lead to repetitive pre-sleep cognitive activity and impaired recovery. Poor sleep may further increase emotional difficulties and reduce coping capacity, suggesting that sleep quality may represent an important statistical pathway linking PS and SI. H2 : PSQI mediates the relationship between PS and SI. 1.3 Physical exercise as a moderator of the association between perceived stress and suicidal ideation Physical exercise is typically defined as a subset of physical activity that is planned, structured, repetitive, and aimed at improving or maintaining physical fitness ( 22 ). More broadly, it represents a form of physical activity characterized by bodily movement produced by skeletal muscles that results in energy expenditure ( 23 ). Regular PE not only enhances physical functioning but also reduces the risk of mental health problems in adolescents through multiple pathways, including neurophysiological regulation, sleep improvement, stress relief, increased positive affect, and enhanced psychological resilience ( 24 , 25 ). For final-year secondary school students, PE may provide an effective outlet for stress release and emotional regulation outside of academic demands. As such, even in the context of elevated perceived stress and sleep-related difficulties, engagement in regular PE may help maintain relatively stable psychological functioning. From a stress-buffering perspective, PE may reduce the adverse effects of stress exposure on psychological outcomes. It may improve mood, enhance self-efficacy, promote social connection, and strengthen emotional regulation capacity, thereby weakening the translation of stress into SI. For students facing intensive academic pressure, maintaining regular PE may provide additional coping resources and reduce vulnerability to negative self-evaluation and suicidal thoughts. Accordingly, PE may serve as a key protective condition that weakens the positive association between PS and SI. Based on this rationale, the following hypothesis is proposed: H3 : PE moderates the relationship between PS and SI. 1.4 Physical exercise as a moderator of the association between sleep quality and suicidal ideation In addition to moderating the relationship between PS and SI, PE may also moderate the association between sleep quality and SI. Specifically, when students experience poor PSQI, their emotional regulation capacity, cognitive control, and stress recovery abilities may be impaired, thereby increasing vulnerability to SI ( 19 ). From a stress-buffering perspective, PE, as an important modifiable behavioral resource, may attenuate the adverse effects of sleep problems on mental health outcomes ( 26 ). On the one hand, regular PE contributes to the improvement of sleep rhythms and sleep restoration processes. On the other hand, it enhances positive affect, self-efficacy, and psychological resilience, thereby weakening the negative impact of poor PSQI on SI ( 27–29 ). Furthermore, from the perspective of Conservation of Resources theory, sleep deprivation leads to continuous depletion of psychological and physiological resources, whereas PE may help replenish such resources by enhancing physical fitness and recovery capacity, thereby buffering the adverse psychological consequences of resource loss ( 30 , 31 ). In addition, from the Interpersonal Theory of Suicide, thwarted belongingness and perceived burdensomeness are key mechanisms underlying SI. PE may reduce SI risk by enhancing social connectedness and promoting more positive self-evaluations, thereby further attenuating the impact of poor PSQI on SI ( 32 , 33 ). For final-year secondary school students, this relationship has important practical implications. Under conditions of intensive exam preparation and prolonged academic stress, sleep problems are highly prevalent. When students also lack regular PE, fatigue, emotional dysregulation, and negative cognitive processing resulting from insufficient or poor-quality sleep may further accumulate, thereby increasing the risk of SI ( 34 ). In contrast, higher levels of PE may provide additional psychophysiological recovery resources, thereby attenuating the positive association between PSQI problems and SI. Based on this rationale, the following hypothesis is proposed: H4 : PE moderates the relationship between PSQI and SI. 1.5 Current study In summary, graduating-grade secondary school students are exposed to a concentrated period of educational transition and academic competition, during which perceived stress, sleep quality, physical exercise, and suicidal ideation may be closely interrelated. Elevated PS may increase the risk of SI, whereas impaired PSQI may represent an important mechanism through which stressful experiences are translated into suicidal thoughts ( 35 ). In parallel, PE, as a modifiable health behavior, may buffer the adverse association between sleep problems and SI ( 36 ). However, most existing studies have focused on single pathways or overall associations among variables. Relatively few have simultaneously examined stress-related risk transmission, the mediating role of PSQI, the moderating effect of PE, the predictive contribution of key variables, and the network structure linking these constructs among graduating-grade secondary school students.
