title: Applying a Behavioral Fit Analysis with Sexual Minority Youth at Risk for Suicide
journal: Evid Based Pract Child Adolesc Ment Health
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Suicide is the second leading cause of death among youth ages 15-24. Sexual minority (SM) youth are at higher risk for suicidal thoughts, behavior, and non-suicidal self- injury than their heterosexual peers. Part of understanding this disparity includes accounting for the role of social drivers of health. The increased risk of suicide and self-harm for SM youth is driven by experiences of minority stress and discrimination that is embedded in society. Recognizing the impact of these factors is essential to inform the delivery of evidence-based interventions for SM youth who are receiving care for suicide prevention.

OBJECTIVE: To describe the process for developing a behavioral fit analysis when working with SM youth who are at risk for suicide, with an emphasis on the role of social drivers of health that may overlap with SM identity as it contributes to suicide risk.

METHOD: A brief review of the literature is provided on the topics of minority stress and existing screening and assessment approaches for suicidal youth. The benefits of a behavioral fit analysis are described and how this supplements existing evidence-based tools. A fictional case example is included to illustrate the direct application of this organizational framework.

RESULTS: A case example of a fictional SM youth is provided with an accompanying fit analysis and treatment plan. Implications for generalization to clinical practice are described, complemented with resources and suggestions for clinicians.

CONCLUSIONS: The use of a behavioral fit analysis balances a nomothetic and idiographic approach to a case conceptualization for SM youth at risk for suicide and incorporates the impact of social drivers of health on the use of evidence-based treatments.

title: Functioning Management & Recovery - Resource Group, a psychoeducational intervention to improve empowerment of people with severe mental illness: a 12-month multicenter randomized control study
abstract:
AIM: Functioning Management and Recovery with the Resource Group (FM&R-GR) is a standardized Psychoeducational Intervention elaborated to improve functioning and empowerment of people with Severe Mental Illness (SMI) living in the community. The aim of this study is to prove its efficacy by the primary and secondary outcomes.

METHODS: 60 patients with SMI were recruited in 5 day-centers (North and South Italy) randomly assigned into 2 groups (Experimental vs Control); patients underwent a multicenter follow-up study with a two time-point evaluation (t0, pre-treatment and t1, 12 months). A highly structured FM&R-GR was used in the Experimental Group (EG), whereas a less structured manual was used in the Control Group (CG). At each time point, Social Functioning, Empowerment and Distress, were assessed as primary outcome; furthermore, Psychopathological Status, Cognitive Functioning, and Cognitive Flexibility were assessed as secondary outcome.

RESULTS: Fifty-nine individuals out of 60 (98.3%) started the study randomly allocated in the EG vs CG. In the EG, 19 people (32.2%) were affected by schizophrenia, 9 (15.2%) by bipolar I disorder with psychotic symptoms and 2 (3.4%) by personality disorders according to DSM-5-TR started the study; in the CG there were respectively 20 (33.9%), 6 (10.2%) and 3 (5.1%). Forty-eight patients, 27 in the EG (56.3%) and 21 in the CG (43.75) completed the study. The total scores of NEL, Distress (p<0.001), and PSPS (p<0.05) showed a statistically significant improvement. The improvement of the other variables in the EG (BPRS, BANS and MFPT) was not statistically significant.

CONCLUSIONS: After 1 year follow-up these results showed improvement in all variables of primary and secondary outcomes, with great statistically significant difference between the two groups for the empowerment, functioning and distress. Furthermore, the pre-post difference in the Experimental Group was statistically significant for all variables with the exception of cognitive flexibility, while in the CG only for the RBANS. Overall, a remarkable impact of this psychoeducational structured intervention was observed on the primary outcome variables.

title: Association between plain-water consumption and suicide attempts among U.S. adolescents: Evidence from the 2017-2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey
abstract:
Background Adolescent suicide attempts remain difficult to predict, in part because research has concentrated on a narrow set of risk factors. We examined whether self-reported plain-water consumption is associated with past-year suicide attempt among U.S. adolescents, whether that association is graded across levels of intake, and whether a zero-intake response adds information beyond established risk factors. Methods We analyzed the 2017, 2019 and 2021 cycles of the U.S. national Youth Risk Behavior Survey (n = 36,779). Missing data, including the plain-water item, were multiply imputed (40 datasets) and pooled by Rubin’s rules, accounting for the survey design. The association was estimated unadjusted, then adjusted for demographics, each of six risk domains, and all domains together. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) models, tuned under two metrics and two penalty rules, provided variable selection and held-out performance; odds ratios come from unpenalized models. Results Reporting no plain water was uncommon (3.6%) and associated with past-year suicide attempt (survey-weighted odds ratio 2.14, 95% CI 1.70–2.71), in each cycle. The association was confined to the zero category: the adjusted odds ratio for none was 2.55 (1.91–3.39) against 3 times/day, whereas among those reporting any plain water there was no gradient (1.01, 0.97–1.06). It remained associated after adjustment for each domain separately (1.45–2.01) but attenuated to 1.34 (0.97–1.85) under simultaneous adjustment. LASSO retained it in every model at the discrimination optimum and, under the one-standard-error rule, in five of six domains but not the full model. Adding it changed held-out discrimination by at most 0.0011. Conclusions Reporting no plain-water consumption in the past seven days was consistently associated with higher odds of a past-year suicide attempt among U.S. adolescents. However, the association was confined to the zero-water category, attenuated after simultaneous adjustment for all risk domains, and did not improve prediction. These findings suggest that the zero-water response may function as a behavioral marker of broader risk rather than as an independent risk factor.

Introduction Adolescent suicide attempts are a critical public health concern in the United States. Data from the Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System (YRBSS) reveal that approximately 9% of adolescents attempted suicide in the past year. This statistic is alarming, given the well-established link between suicide attempts and death by suicide, underscoring the urgent need to better understand the factors associated with these behaviors. Research on risk factors for death by suicide and suicide attempts dates back to 1965 and has increased exponentially throughout the years [ 1 ]. However, despite the amount of research, the ability to accurately predict suicide attempts is limited, barely better than chance, and it is still a challenge [ 1 – 3 ]. A major limitation in the study of suicide attempt risk factors is the ongoing focus on a narrow set of predictors across both empirical and theoretical studies, often replicated across various populations. Empirical research consistently links suicide attempts with prior suicide attempts, schizophrenia, depression, borderline personality disorder, previous psychiatric hospitalizations, and nonsuicidal self-injury [ 1 ]. Popular theoretical models echo this emphasis, with explanations predominantly centered on individual-level factors. For example, the Interpersonal Theory of Suicide (IPTS) [ 4 ], the Three-Step Theory of Suicide [ 5 ], and the Integrated Motivational-Volitional Model [ 6 ] all highlight internal processes like cognition and emotion as key in understanding suicide attempts. According to IPTS, individuals are at the greatest risk when they simultaneously experience thwarted belongingness and perceived burdensomeness [ 4 ]. The Three-Step Theory of Suicide posits that pain, hopelessness, connectedness, and capacity for suicide together contribute to the emergence of both the desire for suicide and eventual suicide attempts [ 5 ]. Similarly, the Integrated Motivational-Volitional Model suggests that defeat, entrapment, acquired capability, and access to lethal means interact to create a high-risk environment for suicide [ 6 ]. More recently, researchers have begun to examine broader socio-environmental and ecological influences on suicide. For instance, studies have investigated the impact of urbanicity, with some reporting significant associations between suicide and factors such as proximity to urban centers, subway access, and residential density [ 7 , 8 ], while others have found no significant relationship [ 9 ]. Although relatively few studies on environmental factors of suicide have focused on youth populations, a systematic review by Ching and colleagues [ 10 ] identified air pollution, drought, and rising temperatures as key environmental stressors linked to increased suicide risk among adolescents. In addition to these physical environmental factors, recent work has highlighted how everyday behaviors such as dietary patterns may shape suicide risk. Studies have found that frequent fast-food consumption, low intake of fruits and vegetables, and higher consumption of caffeinated and sugary beverages are associated with greater likelihood of suicidal ideation, planning, and attempts among adolescents, even after adjusting for known confounders such as age, sex, race, and depressive symptoms [ 11 – 13 ]. Despite growing interest in how diet and environmental exposures shape mental health, one everyday behavior has received comparatively little attention in adolescent suicide research, plain-water consumption. From a developmental science perspective, environmental conditions and everyday exposures are integral to the ecological systems in which youth develop and should be integrated into models of wellbeing [ 14 ]. Evidence at the individual level makes plain-water consumption a plausible candidate for investigation. Experimentally induced mild dehydration degrades mood and increases fatigue, tension, and difficulty concentrating in healthy young adults [ 15 , 16 ]. In a large adult sample, drinking more plain water was associated with lower odds of depression and anxiety [ 17 ]. Among 112,250 Korean adolescents, drinking less than one glass per day was associated with higher odds of depression, suicidal ideation, suicide planning and suicide attempt [ 18 ]. Low plain-water consumption also travels with other markers of adversity: among US high school students it clusters with poor academic grades, physical inactivity, and poor dietary behaviors [ 19 ], and tap water avoidance is closely tied to household food insecurity and to racial and economic disadvantage [ 20 ]. We accordingly treat not drinking plain water as a behavioral indicator rather than a physiological exposure, one that may mark disengagement from routine self-care, symptom burden, or constrained material circumstances, without presuming which of these predominates. A more distant possibility, raised here only as a hypothesis for future work, is that water carries some biological signal, ecological studies link naturally occurring lithium in community water supplies to lower suicide rates in adults [ 21 , 22 ]. Those studies measure lithium concentrations in water systems rather than individual drinking behavior, and they cannot speak to the behavior examined here. What has not been examined is how plain-water consumption behaves when it is placed in direct competition with the risk factors that dominate adolescent suicide research. Prior individual-level studies adjust for a modest set of covariates, which leaves open whether the association is distinct from, or simply absorbed by, the established predictors of adolescent suicide attempts. The present study addresses this gap by testing whether self-reported plain-water consumption is retained as a predictor of suicide attempts when placed in direct competition with established risk factors across multiple domains. Using data from the 2017, 2019 and 2021 cycles of the YRBSS, we fit seven domain-specific Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression models, each organized around a theoretically defined category of suicide risk: substance use, trauma and victimization, dietary habits, physical activity and sleep, suicidal ideation and distress, risk behaviors, and a full model combining all domains. In each model, plain-water consumption is included alongside predictors from that domain, even when it does not conceptually belong to the domain. This cross-domain design functions as a stress test: if plain-water consumption is retained by LASSO even within domains where it is conceptually extraneous, this would be consistent with the indicator carrying information not already captured by those risk factors. Retention under penalization is not on its own evidence of independent or clinical importance, since it depends on the penalty rule, on correlations among predictors, and on coding choices, and we therefore treat it as one piece of evidence rather than as the answer. Alongside this stress test we ask two further questions that bear on how any such signal should be interpreted. The first concerns the shape of the association: whether risk falls steadily as reported consumption rises, or is instead confined to adolescents who report drinking no plain water at all. The second concerns its usefulness: whether the indicator improves out-of-sample prediction of suicide attempts beyond established risk factors. The study is exploratory and cross-sectional throughout, and we frame it as hypothesis-generating. Materials and methods Design and data source We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of the 2017, 2019 and 2021 national Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS), because these are the most recent consecutive cycles that administered every measure this analysis uses. The YRBS is a biennial, school-based survey of students in grades 9–12 attending public and private schools in the United States, using a three-stage cluster sample designed to produce nationally representative estimates. Survey methodology is described in detail elsewhere [ 23 ]. The data are publicly available and de-identified, so the analysis did not constitute human-subjects research requiring review. Respondents missing the suicide-attempt item were excluded, leaving 36,779 in the analytic sample. Missingness on predictors, including the plain-water item, was handled by imputation, so every analysis below uses the same respondents. Measures Suicide attempt. The outcome was derived from the item asking how many times the respondent actually attempted suicide during the past 12 months, dichotomized as any attempt versus none. Plain-water consumption. The YRBS asks, “During the past 7 days, how many times did you drink a bottle or glass of plain water? (Count tap, bottled, and unflavored sparkling water.)” Seven ordered response options run from “I did not drink water during the past 7 days” through “4 or more times per day.” We analyzed this item in two forms. The binary indicator , contrasting “I did not drink water during the past 7 days” against any reported consumption, is the primary exposure and is the form used unless stated otherwise. The ordinal item retains the original seven levels and serves to test whether risk is graded across the consumption distribution. Domain predictors. Forty-seven predictors were organized into six theoretically defined domains. Substance use (11 items): current cigarette, cigar, marijuana, alcohol, vaping and smokeless tobacco use; lifetime heroin, synthetic marijuana, cocaine and methamphetamine use; and being offered drugs at school. Trauma and victimization (9 items): feeling unsafe at school, being threatened at school, physical fighting at school, forced sexual intercourse, sexual violence, sexual abuse by a partner, physical dating violence, bullying, and cyberbullying. Dietary habits (10 items): no intake of fruit juice, fruit, salad, potatoes, carrots, other vegetables, soda, milk, breakfast or sports drinks. Physical activity and sleep (7 items): physical activity, three or more hours of television, three or more hours of video games, physical education attendance, sports team participation, sports-related concussion and eight or more hours of sleep. Suicidal ideation and distress (4 items): suicidal ideation, suicide planning, hopelessness and difficulty concentrating. Risk behaviors (6 items): seatbelt use, riding with a drinking driver, driving after drinking, texting while driving, weapon carrying at school and gun carrying. Demographic covariates. All adjusted models included sex, race/ethnicity, grade, sexual orientation, Hispanic/Latino ethnicity and survey year. Harmonization across cycles. Because question numbering changes between cycles, each variable was located by its description in the cycle-specific codebook rather than by item number. Derived indicators whose definition changed between cycles were rebuilt from the underlying ordinal item, so that every variable carries a single definition throughout. Missing data Missingness on the plain-water item was 19.7% and rose across cycles, from 12.0% in 2017 to 13.6% in 2019 and 29.1% in 2021. It differed by outcome: 25.6% among adolescents reporting an attempt against 19.0% among those not. The 8,895 respondents excluded for a missing outcome (19.5%) were enriched for the exposure: 11.1% reported no plain water against 3.5% of the analytic sample. Differential missingness was not confined to the plain-water item ( S1 and S2 Tables in S1 File ). Multiple imputation by chained equations was performed with the mice package [ 24 ], generating 40 datasets with 20 iterations. The predictor matrix was specified rather than selected by a correlation threshold: every imputation model contained the outcome, the plain-water item, the demographic covariates, survey year and the sampling weight, and was completed with the twenty variables most strongly associated with either the target variable or with its missingness, giving 28–29 predictors per imputed variable. The primary sampling unit and stratum identifiers were held out of the imputation model and reattached afterward for the design-based analyses. The plain-water item was imputed in its seven-level ordinal form by proportional-odds regression; the remaining categorical variables were imputed by polytomous regression and binary variables by logistic regression. All subsequent models were fitted on these imputed datasets. Convergence diagnostics are shown in S1 Fig in S1 File and a comparison of the imputed and observed distributions of the ordinal item in S2 Fig and S3 Table in S1 File . Because missingness on the plain-water item was not independent of the outcome, we did not rest on the missing-at-random assumption alone. A

title: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder and Late-Life Cognitive Impairment
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) affects tens to hundreds of millions of adults worldwide, and preliminary evidence suggests it may be associated with increased risk of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and dementia. However, concerns regarding diagnostic ascertainment and residual confounding remain.

OBJECTIVE: To investigate the association of ADHD with incident cognitive impairment, defined as MCI or dementia, using electronic health record (EHR) diagnoses and genetic liability measured using genome-wide ADHD polygenic risk score (ADHD PRS) in the same individuals.

DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This cohort study used data from the US All of Us Research Program (enrollment May 6, 2018, to October 1, 2023; EHR data from January 4, 1985, to October 1, 2023; mean [SD] follow-up 10.26 [6.75] years). A total of 187 341 participants aged 50 years and older with available EHR and genomic data were included. Data were analyzed from October 2025 to July 2026.

EXPOSURES: ADHD diagnosis and ADHD PRS.

MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Incident MCI or dementia.

RESULTS: Among 187 341 participants (mean [SD] age, 56.41 [7.88] years; 107 266 [57%] female), 3026 (1.6%) had ADHD. Among participants with ADHD, 203 (6.7%) developed cognitive impairment, compared with 6259 (3.4%) among those without ADHD. In adjusted Cox models, ADHD was associated with a more than 4-fold higher hazard of cognitive impairment (hazard ratio [HR], 4.60; 95% CI, 3.99-5.29; P < .001). Adjustments for comorbidities, educational attainment, and health care utilization attenuated but did not eliminate the association. Similarly, ADHD PRS was associated with incident cognitive impairment (highest vs lowest quintile: HR, 1.35; 95% CI, 1.25-1.46; P < .001). Among participants who developed cognitive impairment, comorbid ADHD diagnosis was associated with a nearly 2-fold higher odds of suboptimal mental health (odds ratio [OR], 1.69; 95% CI, 1.18-2.39; P = .01), quality of life (OR, 1.66; 95% CI, 1.14-2.39; P = .02), social satisfaction (OR, 2.39; 95% CI, 1.69-3.37; P < .001), and 20% higher health care utilization (incidence rate ratio, 1.20; 95% CI, 1.09-1.34; P = .003), suggesting greater care burden beyond the elevated incidence risk.

CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this cohort study, convergent clinical and genetic evidence revealed ADHD was associated with a markedly increased risk of late-life cognitive impairment. Among those who develop cognitive impairment, an ADHD diagnosis was associated with worse health outcomes and greater health care utilization, supporting the need for targeted monitoring and integrated care in this population.

title: Characterizing Artificial Intelligence Psychosis in a Large Medical Setting
abstract:
This cohort study estimates the prevalence of AI psychosis, characterizes affected patients, and defines the role of conversational AI in documented psychotic episodes.

Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are increasingly linked to emerging or worsening psychotic symptoms, a phenomenon termed AI psychosis . Existing evidence, however, is limited primarily to case reports, viewpoints, and simulated experiments, with one published analysis of its occurrence in Denmark. While these works offer critical starting points, additional empirical data are needed to elucidate the factors characteristic of those who develop AI psychosis. Thus, we conducted a retrospective electronic health record (EHR) review at a large academic medical center to estimate prevalence, characterize affected patients, and describe the role of conversational AI in psychotic symptoms. Methods This cohort study followed the STROBE reporting guideline and was approved by the Vanderbilt University Medical Center (VUMC) IRB with a waiver of informed consent for secondary analysis of already collected data. Using Epic Clarity, we extracted progress notes dated December 1, 2022, to April 15, 2026, from patients who received behavioral health care and whose records contained AI-related keywords (eFigure 1 in Supplement 1 ). Only patients with a documented psychotic-disorder diagnosis were retained. Two raters (Z.B., S.G.V.) manually screened notes, discarded incidental matches, and classified each patient’s AI interaction into 1 of 3 categories: neutral (eg, using ChatGPT to search for recipes), AI psychosis (psychosis-worsening chatbot use), or AI-related psychotic content (AI incorporated into a delusion without documented chatbot use; included to capture the range of AI-related phenomenology in the EHR while preserving the AI psychosis category for patients with clear use of a conversational AI product). Within the AI psychosis group, Z.B. and M.C.A. assigned interactions to 1 of 4 a priori theoretical categories describing how chatbot use interacts with psychosis : catalyst (precipitates new symptoms in previously healthy individuals), amplifier (worsens preexisting symptoms by validating distorted ideas), coauthor (develops harmful narratives through iterative dialogue), or object (AI becomes the focus of delusional beliefs). Finally, across all patients, medical record review was conducted (Z.B., J.M.S., and M.C.A.) to determine whether the documented AI interaction was part of the patient’s first psychotic episode (index episode), defined as the AI interaction being documented by their treatment team during their first psychiatric presentation for psychotic symptoms. Kruskal-Wallis, χ 2 , and Fisher exact tests were used to compare variables across groups. A 2-sided P < .05 was considered significant. Results Among 578 058 records (215 712 unique patients), 187 encounters from 73 unique patients (25 [34.2%] female and 48 [65.8%] male; median [range] age, 32 [17-81] years) met criteria after algorithmic and manual screening. Twenty-eight patients (0.013% of those receiving mental health care) were classified into the AI psychosis category; 17 were classified as neutral; and 28 were classified into the AI-related psychotic content category. Percent agreement among raters was 86.1%, with J.M.S. serving as tiebreaker. The AI psychosis cohort was primarily male (19 [67.9%]) and White (21 [75.0%]). Unspecified psychosis was the most common diagnosis (8 [28.6%]) ( Table ). ChatGPT was the documented AI product in 15 cases (53.6%), and 24 interactions (85.7%) were documented after the May 2024 release of GPT-4o. Patients with AI psychosis did not significantly differ from those with neutral interactions or AI-related psychotic content on any clinical history variables, such as history of psychiatric hospitalization, psychotropic prescription, or suicide attempts ( Table ). Seventeen patients in the AI psychosis group (60.7%) were experiencing a first psychotic episode, which was significantly more than the neutral (3 [17.6%]; P = .006) or AI-related content (8 [28.5%]; P = .03) groups ( Figure ). Patients with AI psychosis were significantly younger than the AI-related psychotic content group (median [range] age, 27.5 [17.0-66.0] vs 36.5 [18.0-70.0] years; W = 3.931; P = .02) and more likely to have unspecified psychosis than the neutral group (8 [28.6%] vs 0; Holm-adjusted P = .03). Among AI psychosis cases, amplifier was the most common AI psychosis type (18 [64.3%]), followed by object (6 [21.4%]) and catalyst (3 [10.7%]) ( Table ). Percent agreement was 83.3% (J.M.S. as tiebreaker). Discussion In this systematic analysis of AI psychosis, documented in the EHR of a large US medical setting, psychosis-worsening interactions with conversational AI were most common among patients experiencing their first episode of psychosis. Exploratory analysis of theoretical typologies has suggested conversational AI may amplify emerging or pre-existing symptoms. Our findings suggest that the early phase of psychotic illness may confer particular vulnerability to symptom-worsening AI interactions. Our AI psychosis prevalence estimate of 0.013%, which is conditional on a patient receiving a psychosis diagnosis in the EHR, converges with evidence provided by OpenAI, which acknowledged “0.07% of users active in a given week and 0.01% of messages indicate possible signs of mental health emergencies related to psychosis or mania.” The high number of cases after the release of GPT-4o coincides with documented sycophancy in that model, though our design cannot establish causation. Recent simulation studies have identified GPT-4o as performing particularly poorly during extended conversations, and the more recent OpenAI model GPT-5.2 Instant as being more likely to challenge delusional premises. Limitations include ascertainment bias, single-site design, and a rating system that is not clinically validated. Prospective studies incorporating chat logs are needed to clarify mechanisms. Routine assessment of AI use during psychiatric encounters appears warranted.

title: Clinician Recommendations for the Assessment of Preteen Suicide Risk: A Qualitative Study
journal: Evid Based Pract Child Adolesc Ment Health
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To better understand clinician practices for assessing preteen suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STBs) as an initial step to inform the development of a comprehensive suicide risk assessment for this age group.

METHOD: We conducted qualitative interviews with child mental health clinicians ( N  = 31) who routinely assess preteens and clinical researchers with expertise in child and adolescent suicide. We queried about procedures for assessing suicidality (e.g. assessment sources and informants, risk factors to be assessed), developmental considerations (e.g. children's understanding of death), and cultural considerations (e.g. related to race/ethnicity and culture).

RESULTS: Clinicians and researchers provided perspectives on best practices in assessing young children about their STBs, including the importance of rapport building, the use of clinician-administered interviews, tailoring language to the child's developmental level, adopting a multi-informant approach, and taking into consideration how culture impacts expression and perception of STB risk.

CONCLUSION: These qualitative interviews provide valuable insights into understanding how to improve the evaluation of STBs in preteens. This research highlights the need for the development and validation of assessment tools about STBs that are explicitly designed for preteen youth to best identify those at risk.

title: Revisiting the link between childhood adversity and stress-sensitive brain regions in psychosis and bipolar disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract:
Background Brain abnormalities related to childhood adversity (CA) have been reported across clinical presentations in psychotic disorder (PD) and bipolar disorder (BD). This systematic review and meta-analysis examined gray matter volume (GMV) alterations linked to CA in PD and BD. Methods A PRISMA-compliant systematic review was conducted (PROSPERO ID: CRD42022351133). The EMBASE, MEDLINE, and PsycINFO databases were searched from inception to June 2024 for studies investigating CA and structural brain imaging in PD and BD. Study quality was assessed with the Newcastle Ottawa Scale (NOS). Data were extracted and synthesized accounting for sex differences and CA subtypes with brain findings categorized by the presence and direction of associations. Meta-analyses were performed for hippocampal and amygdala volumes. Results In the systematic review ( k = 29), 3056 participants with PD and BD (mean age = 36.6 ± 16.1; 47% female), published between 2011 and 2023, were included. Study quality was fair, with high heterogeneity. Most studies reported significant negative associations between CA and GMV, especially in prefrontal regions, while findings for the hippocampus and amygdala were largely null or inconsistent. Meta-analyses of a study subset identified no significant association between CA and hemisphere-specific and combined volumes of the hippocampus ( k = 5; p ≥ 0.66) or amygdala ( k = 4; p ≥ 0.87). Conclusion CA was not consistently associated with hippocampal or amygdala volume alterations in PD and BD. More consistent evidence emerged for reduced GMV in prefrontal regions, suggesting that neurobiological impact of CA may be more robustly captured at the cortical level.

Introduction Individuals with a psychotic disorder (PD) and bipolar disorder (BD) report higher rates of childhood adversities (CA) than the general population [ 1 , 2 ]. Exposure to CA has consistently been linked to greater illness severity [ 3 , 4 ] and a broad range of cognitive impairments, including reduced cognitive flexibility, lower IQ, poorer attention, emotion recognition, and working memory deficits [ 5 , 6 ]. In parallel, neuroimaging evidence suggests that CA is associated with distinct brain volumetric alterations in subcortical, temporal and frontal regions [ 7 , 8 ] that may underly these cognitive features. Previous meta-analyses have explored the link between CA and brain alterations in healthy adults [ 9 , 10 ]. However, the role of CA in brain abnormalities in individuals with PD and BD remains insufficiently understood. This gap is particularly relevant as increasing evidence conceptualizes PD and BD as part of the same clinical and neurobiological continuum characterized by overlapping genetic, neural, and psychological mechanisms [ 11 ]. Accordingly, examining CA-related brain alterations beyond traditional diagnostic boundaries may be more informative than focusing on disorder-specific effects. In both PD and BD, converging evidence indicates reduction in total gray matter volume (GMV) [ 12 ], as well as volumetric reductions in the hippocampus [ 13 ] and the amygdala [ 14 ], key regions for stress and emotional regulation. Within this transdiagnostic framework, CA may function as a common environmental risk factor that disrupts shared neurodevelopmental trajectories rather than affecting specific diagnostic categories differentially. It has been hypothesized that individuals exposed to trauma and those within PD and BD may share a common mechanism involving dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis [ 15 ]. Exposure to early life stress is thought to induce prolonged activation of this system, leading to elevated glucocorticoid levels that disproportionally affect stress-sensitive brain regions, such as the hippocampus and amygdala. These regions are highly enriched with glucocorticoid receptors, making them particularly vulnerable to neurotoxic effects of chronic stress exposure. Prolonged glucocorticoid activity may result in dendritic atrophy and reduced synaptic plasticity [ 16 ] providing a mechanistic explanation for observed volumetric reductions and suggesting a potential pathway through which CA may induce a transdiagnostic vulnerability. By disrupting neurodevelopmental trajectories common to both PD and BD, CA leads to convergent structural brain abnormalities (i.e., volume reductions), regardless of traditional clinical labels [ 17 , 18 ]. Despite this biological framework, findings regarding CA-related brain alterations remain inconsistent. In the general population, meta-analytic evidence has yielded mixed results. Similar variability has been observed in clinical samples. Earlier structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in psychiatric populations often did not account for trauma history. While earlier structural MRI studies have overlooked the role of trauma, the inclusion of CA measures in clinical samples has expanded substantially in recent studies. This growing body of interest of the literature supports the hypothesis that trauma-related alterations may be involved in the disease etiopathogenesis [ 19 ]. Previous reviews have primarily examined this question within diagnostic categories. Cancel et al. [ 20 ] conducted a systematic review examining the link between CA and neuroimaging data in individuals with schizophrenia and found 15 studies reporting evidence of a negative association between CA and GMV decrease, alterations in white matter integrity, and alterations of functional connectivity. Similarly, Zovetti et al. [ 21 ] reviewed 14 studies focusing on the link between CA and brain alterations in BD and concluded a volume reduction in several brain regions, including the hippocampus, amygdala, thalamus, and frontal cortex. More recently, extending to the broader psychosis spectrum, Bloomfield et al. [ 22 ] conducted a systematic review synthesizing multimodal neuroimaging data reporting that trauma is associated with regional gray matter reductions, altered corticolimbic connectivity, and fronto-temporal dysfunctions. Building on these findings, the current work provides an updated systematic review of the literature. In addition, we conduct a first meta-analysis to quantitatively assess the association between CA and brain volume alterations transdiagnostically across PD and BD. By focusing on published structural MRI studies, we aim to explore the association between CA and GMV, with a focus on the hippocampus and the amygdala, as these regions have been most frequently examined in this context, but we also include studies that identified other GMV alterations. We conduct a meta-analysis of the association between CA and the volume of these GMV structures, examining various important moderators such as sex and neuroimaging methods, variables that have previously been linked to inconsistent findings [ 10 ]. CA subtypes (e.g., abuse and neglect) are discussed descriptively in the systematic review. Within this transdiagnostic framework, we aim to clarify whether CA is associated with (1) reduced hippocampal and/or amygdala volume and (2) broader reductions in GMV across other regions. Methods This systematic review and meta-analysis were pre-registered with PROSPERO International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews. The protocol ID number is CRD42022351133. PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 guidelines were followed to ensure clear reporting of review findings [ 23 ]; see Supplementary Table 1 . Search strategy The primary search was conducted through the following databases: MEDLINE, EMBASE and PsycINFO via the Ovid platform. Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and keywords related to (i) PD and BD; (ii) childhood adversity; and (iii) brain image data (e.g., structural MRI, GMV) were searched using the Boolean operator “OR” and the three categories were combined using “AND”. A manual search across references of papers that had already been found to meet criteria was also conducted, as well as from final included papers and from relevant similar reviews conducted on the same topic as this review [ 20 , 21 ], to identify further studies that may be eligible for inclusion (see Supplementary Table 2 for the full list of search terms used). Eligibility criteria According to the PICO framework [ 24 ], included studies were (1) (P) conducted on adults (aged between 18–80 years) of any gender with a formal diagnosis of a PD or a BD, based on validated diagnostic manuals including current or previous versions of either the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) [ 25 ] or the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) [ 26 ], see Supplementary Table 3 ; (2) (I) reported the presence of CA (see Operationalization of the predictors section below); (3) (C) compared brain GMV of people with and without CA amongst individuals with PD or BD, or examined associations using a non-trauma group as reference (4) (O) quantitatively evaluated changes of brain GMV in relation to CA (see section Operationalization of the outcomes below); (5) included clinical observational studies, cohort studies, or case-control studies; (6) were originally published in English; (7) were published in peer-reviewed journals. To be included in the meta-analysis, only studies that (1) reported volume measurements of the hippocampus and/or amygdala; (2) provided corresponding statistical associations (e.g., correlation coefficients or other effect sizes - see details below) with measures of CA were eligible for inclusion. Operationalization of the predictors (childhood adversities) CA was either defined as general adversity (GA, meaning a composite measure broadly defined) or subtypes - sexual abuse (SA), physical abuse (PA), emotional abuse (EA), physical neglect (PN), and emotional neglect (EN). Exposure was considered present if any of these subtypes was assessed by the study. CA subtypes were analyzed only when independent statistical analyses were conducted and reported in the studies. Operationalisation of the outcome measures (structural brain volumetric changes) The primary outcome of interest is volumetric brain differences of GMV in individuals with PD (including schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder and first-episode psychosis) and BD. Of particular interest are the hippocampus and amygdala volumes, given their established roles in stress response and prior links to CA [ 19 ]. An expanded category labelled “other GMV”, including also GMV measures from additional brain regions (e.g., prefrontal cortex, thalamus, nucleus accumbens), was also considered for the systematic review if they were reported in either whole-brain or ROI studies. Studies employing structural MRI techniques (e.g., voxel-based morphometry, manual or automated tracing) were eligible for inclusion. Studies that used multiple neuroimaging modalities remained eligible, but only structural MRI data were extracted and analyzed. Screening procedure and data extraction All studies found from the initial search were exported into an Excel file and were screened based on title and abstract in duplicate by two authors (DC and AT), with any inconsistencies cross-checked by a third author (MA). Following this, full-text screenings of articles were conducted using the same procedure; any discrepancies were resolved through consensus. The following information was extracted in duplicate from each relevant study: surname of first author, year and country of publication, sample size, mean age, percentage of female participants, study design, clinical diagnoses, CA/subtype, and instrument used to measure CA, technique used to measure volumetric data (manual or automated segmentation), brain region of interest (ROI), brain regions reported to be affected by CA, whether analyses were adjusted and by which confounders, and lastly, the association (effect size, direction with respective test and significance) between the reported CA (predictor) and the reported volumetric structural brain imaging data (outcome). Qualitative data analysis For the systematic review, we appraised the evidence by classifying each association as either significant or not significant, based on a statistical threshold ( p < 0.05 and 95% confidence interval included the null value). Then, among the significant findings, associations were further categorized as either negative (more CA was associated with smaller brain volumes) or positive (more CA was associated with greater brain volumes). The proportions of significant positive and negative associations were then calculated across studies as independent analyses; mixed results were included in both categories. Results from studies examining trauma subtypes or sex differences were included in the overall count of CA findings when they reported associations with brain volume. Some studies that used a whole-brain approach also reported ROI results of the hippocampus and amygdala [ 27 – 29 ] and were therefore included in these counts. When studies used whole-brain analyses without reporting region-specific (hippocampal or amygdala) results, these regions were not classified as non-significant and were excluded from the corresponding ROI-based counts. Quantitative data analysis Statistical analyses were conducted using Comprehensive Meta-Analysis (CMA-version-4) [ 30 ]. Effect sizes reflecting the association between CA and brain volumes were reported as Pearson’s r . In studies where alternative statistics were reported, such as standardized β , Cohen’s d , or F -values, these were converted to Pearson’s r using established methods to ensure comparability as previously described [ 31 ] and used in previous meta-analyses [ 3 ]. The software computed correlation coefficients based on the extracted coefficients. These were first transformed using Fisher’s r -to- z transformation to reduce bias, particularly important when synthesizing data from a limited number of studies, and then converted back to r values for interpretation [ 32 ]. The primary analysis focused on the pooled effect sizes of the association between CA and left and right hippocampal and amygdala volumes given the well-established hemispheric asymmetry [ 33 ] to ensure that lateralized effects were not overlooked. Secondary analyses were performed on combined total hippocampal and amygdala volume, as some studies reported them as such [ 34 , 35 ]. For these secondary analyses, studies that reported separate associations between CA and left and right hemispheric volumes, but not with total, a combined association was computed to obtain a single effect size per region in relation to CA. This was done using inverse-variance-weighted averaging of Fisher’s z -transformed correlation coefficients, which were then back-transformed to Pearson’s r [ 36 ].
