title: Unlocking School Nurses' Capacity for Suicide Risk Screening: Implications for Multitiered System of Supports
abstract:
BACKGROUND: School nurses play an important role in identifying students at risk for suicide, yet their screening methods remain understudied. The purpose of this study was to examine the methods of suicide risk screening used by school nurses, evaluate how district-level integration of school nurses into suicide prevention policies is associated with screening methods, and assess associations between screening methods, self-efficacy, and referral-making.

METHODS: Data were derived from a national cross-sectional, correlational study examining school nurses' roles in youth suicide prevention (N = 578).

RESULTS: School nurses whose responsibilities were explicitly defined in district suicide prevention policies were more likely to use standardized screening questions. In a separate analysis, use of standardized screening questions was indirectly associated with a greater number of referrals to community-based services through higher screening self-efficacy.

IMPLICATIONS FOR SCHOOL HEALTH POLICY, PRACTICE, AND EQUITY: District-level integration of school nurses into suicide prevention policies may strengthen school nurses' capacity to identify and refer students at risk.

CONCLUSIONS: Within a multitiered system of supports (MTSS) framework, integrating school nurses into suicide prevention efforts may strengthen coordinated, equitable approaches to identifying and responding to students at risk for suicide.

title: Psychedelics and disorders of consciousness: a new frontier in neurotherapeutics
abstract: Disorders of consciousness (DoC), including coma, unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (also known as vegetative state), and minimally conscious state, represent profound disruptions in awareness and responsiveness due to severe brain injury, with limited therapeutic options available. Recent advancements in neuroimaging have improved our ability to detect residual brain activity in DoC patients, but effective interventions remain elusive. Psychedelics like psilocybin, lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), and N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT), which modulate brain network dynamics and enhance neural plasticity, have emerged as candidate pharmacological probes and potential therapeutic strategies for DoC. These substances primarily exert their effects through serotonin 2 A (5-HT 2A ) receptor agonism, inducing widespread changes in cortical activity and connectivity, in contrast to the reduced connectivity typically seen in DoC. The entropic brain hypothesis suggests that psychedelics increase neural entropy, potentially fostering more flexible brain states that could facilitate recovery in DoC patients by restoring communication between isolated brain regions. While direct human feasibility evidence has recently emerged from initial pilot and case studies, controlled clinical evidence demonstrating sustained restoration of consciousness remains absent. Consequently, key challenges such as determining optimal dosing, safety, and ethical considerations must be addressed before clinical application. This perspective reviews the neurobiological mechanisms of psychedelics, their potential for treating DoC, and the clinical and methodological hurdles to overcome, emphasizing the need for interdisciplinary research to translate these ideas into effective therapies. Moreover, this exploration contributes to a deeper understanding of consciousness and its modulation through pharmacological means.

title: Mapping the psychosis spectrum - imaging neurosubtypes from multiscale functional network connectivity
abstract: Psychosis exhibits marked neurobiological heterogeneity that is not adequately captured by symptom-based diagnoses. Although prior efforts have identified subgroups, it remains unclear how latent disease variability manifests within the brain's multiscale intrinsic functional organization and whether these patterns can be leveraged to systematically identify biologically driven subtypes of psychosis. Here, we aim to identify Psychosis Imaging Neurosubtypes (PINs)-homogeneous subgroups defined solely from neurobiological features of brain function, independent of clinical or cognitive definitions, and whether these subgroups show meaningful phenotypic differentiation. Resting-state fMRI data from 2103 B-SNIP 1&2 participants were used to compute subject-specific multiscale functional network connectivity (msFNC). We then derived a low-dimensional neurobiological subspace, termed Latent Network Connectivity, which captured system-wide interconnected multiscale information across three components. Projections of probands msFNC onto this subspace revealed three PINs through unsupervised learning that spanned DSM diagnoses (Schizophrenia, Bipolar, Schizoaffective Disorder). Although defined purely from intrinsic neurobiology, PINs exhibited distinct cognitive, clinical, and connectivity profiles. PIN-1, the most cognitively impaired, showed Cerebellar-Subcortical and Visual-Sensorimotor hypoconnectivity, alongside Visual-Subcortical hyperconnectivity. Most cognitively preserved PIN-2 showed Visual-Subcortical, Subcortical-Sensorimotor, and Subcortical-Higher Cognition hypoconnectivity. PIN-3 exhibited intermediate cognition, showing Cerebellar-Subcortical hypoconnectivity alongside Cerebellar-Sensorimotor and Subcortical-Sensorimotor hyperconnectivity. Although covariate-adjusted analyses did not reveal significant clinical differences among PINs, exploratory analyses identified selective differences in YMDR, PANSS, and Age of Onset. Notably, 55% of relatives aligned with the same neurosubtype as their probands, a rate significantly higher than chance and than DSM-based alignment, suggesting potential heritability. Cognitive performance reliably aligns with distinct brain connectivity patterns, which are also evident in relatives, supporting their construct validity. Our PINs partially converged with previously reported BSNIP Biotypes with some correspondence (e.g. PIN1 with Biotype 1) but not with the other Biotypes, which were determined using integrated electrophysiological, cognitive, and oculomotor data, supporting convergent validity, while also indicating that intrinsic rsfMRI derived multiscale connectivity partitions psychosis heterogeneity somewhat differently from multimodal biomarker approaches. These findings underscore the limitations of DSM-based classifications in capturing the biological complexity of psychotic disorders and highlight the potential of imaging-based neurosubtypes to enhance our understanding of the psychosis spectrum.

title: Acetaminophen produces limited molecular and functional effects in human cortical organoids
abstract: Acetaminophen (APAP) is the most widely used analgesic during pregnancy, yet its effects on prenatal human brain development remain incompletely understood. Epidemiological studies have reported inconsistent associations between prenatal APAP exposure and later neurodevelopmental outcomes, underscoring the need for mechanistic evaluation in human-relevant developmental models. Here, we examined how APAP influences early cortical development using induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cortical organoids (COs) generated from six independent lines. Organoids were exposed to physiologically relevant APAP concentrations (25, 50, and 100 μM) for 5 days beginning at day 21 of differentiation, corresponding to late first-trimester cortical development. We assessed organoid growth, apoptosis, differentiation, synaptic maturation, transcriptomic profiles using bulk and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq), and functional network activity using multielectrode array recordings up to 4 months. APAP exposure did not affect organoid size, cytoarchitecture, or viability. Neuronal and progenitor cell proportions, as well as synaptic puncta density were unchanged. Bulk RNA-seq revealed subtle transcriptional changes only at the highest dose (16 differentially expressed genes at 100 μM), enriched for neurodevelopmental pathways. In contrast, snRNA-seq at 3 months revealed no changes in cell type composition or gene expression. Consistent with the limited molecular changes observed, electrophysiological measures including firing rate, burst frequency, and network synchrony, showed no significant differences from controls. Together, these results indicate that direct exposure to parent APAP at the concentrations tested produces minimal molecular perturbations. These findings reflect responses to parent acetaminophen in vitro and do not exclude metabolite-mediated or systemic effects in vivo.

title: The genetic orchestra of autism and its intersections with epilepsy, intellectual disability, and ADHD
abstract: Autism is a complex condition with marked phenotypic variability and a multifactorial etiology orchestrated by diverse genetic and environmental influences. In this review, we dissect what we refer to as autism's "genetic orchestra", spanning from the high-impact "soloists", de novo and ultra-rare variants with large effect sizes, to the "polyphonic background" of common variants which individually exert modest effects but collectively have significant impact. We examine how this orchestra wires neural circuits, with convergent biological pathways modulating synaptic function and chromatin remodeling. Although de novo, rare, and common variants are often studied independently, converging evidence supports a model whereby their influences are largely additive. This genetic orchestra is not condition-specific; autism frequently co-occurs with other neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions, reflecting substantial pleiotropy across both rare and common variant landscapes. Notably, ultra-rare variants tend to associate with co-occurring intellectual disability, ADHD, epilepsy, and psychiatric conditions highlighting their high phenotypic impact. Beyond genetics, layers of environmental and contextual factors further modulate clinical outcomes. In this framework, we also discuss the challenges of identifying genetic variants associated with autism through clinical genetic testing, where yields remain context-dependent, varying by sex and co-occurring conditions. Finally, we address current limitations and future directions in refining our understanding of autism's genetic basis.

title: Maternal immune activation influences social behavior development in a nonhuman primate model
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Women exposed to infection during pregnancy have an increased risk of giving birth to a child who will later be diagnosed with neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) characterized by changes in social development, such as autism and schizophrenia. Preclinical rodent models of maternal immune activation (MIA) have established causal links between elevated maternal cytokines and offspring social deficits indicative of human NDDs.

METHODS: Here, we use a unique nonhuman primate (NHP) MIA model to explore the longitudinal development of social behavior, given their phylogenetic similarity, social complexity, and translational potential for identifying the emergence of NDDs in humans. We explore social behavior (N=28 males) in pairs, social groups, and a dominance assessment.

RESULTS: MIA-exposed and control offspring developed a species-typical repertoire of social behavior and interacted with conspecifics. Yet, consistent with rodent and human studies, we found that MIA-exposed NHP offspring were, overall, less social towards familiar peers. We also found that MIA-exposed offspring were more likely to play with their treatment-matched pair mate during the weaning period, while controls did not exhibit a partner preference. There were also patterns suggesting that MIA exposure led to reduced contact with dams during infancy, greater withdrawals from pair-mates, and reduced positive social interactions with peers.

CONCLUSIONS: These results confirm that NHP models of MIA are consistent with evidence from rodent and human studies indicating that MIA exposure reduces overall sociality. They also suggest that social deficits may be specific to certain behaviors and more subtle or masked during observations in large social groups.

title: BLA kappa opioid receptor inputs to the BNST mediate social stress-induced increases in alcohol drinking
abstract: Aversive social experiences can increase alcohol consumption and precipitate relapse during abstinence. Individuals who drink to alleviate social stress are at a heightened risk for developing an alcohol use disorder (AUD). In rodents, repeated social defeat stress (SDS) enhances motivation to consume alcohol, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the role of dynorphin/kappa opioid receptor (Dyn/KOR) signaling in regulating stress-induced increases in alcohol consumption. We show that repeated SDS increased alcohol intake and preference in both sexes, effects that were attenuated by systemic administration of the KOR antagonist norBNI or local administration of norBNI into the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST). Chemogenetic activation of basolateral amygdala (BLA) KOR-expressing neurons and their projections to the BNST, as well as knockdown of KORs in the BLA, attenuated increased alcohol consumption following SDS. At the molecular level, SDS increased Pdyn mRNA expression and selectively activated BNST-projecting dynorphin neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus. Together, these findings support a working model where Dyn/KOR modulation of the BLA-BNST pathway is critical for increased alcohol drinking induced by social stress, while pointing to the DRN as a candidate upstream source of Dyn. Our results highlight Dyn/KOR systems as a promising therapeutic target for comorbid stress-related pathology and AUD.

title: The claustrum encodes and scales appetitive feeding
abstract: The claustrum regulates reward processing, but its role in feeding remains unknown. We report that palatable food recruits claustral neurons and a claustrum-to-medial prefrontal cortex circuit whose activation reduces high-fat diet intake. These findings identify the claustrum as a key regulator of appetitive feeding, with potential implications for metabopsychiatric disorders.

title: Executive functions as a transdiagnostic endophenotype in developmental psychopathology
abstract: The majority of mental health conditions emerges before adulthood, with prevalence increasing especially during childhood and adolescence. Coupled with high comorbidity between disorders, there is an urgent need to identify transdiagnostic mechanisms that underpin both risk and resilience to developmental psychopathology. Here we propose executive functions (EFs), a set of cognitive processes relevant for goal-directed control of thought and actions, as a promising candidate for such a mechanism. We review evidence that EF development is shaped by both genetic and environmental factors and relies on protracted maturation of neural networks, particularly frontoparietal and cingulo-opercular systems. Disruptions in these systems are associated with elevated risk for internalising and externalising disorders. We therefore propose EFs as a cognitive endophenotype of developmental psychopathology-heritable, measurable, and lying on the pathway from gene to disorder. We review evidence showing that impaired EF is a shared feature across psychiatric conditions and predictive of future symptomatology, supporting its transdiagnostic relevance. We also propose a mechanistic refinement of the EF construct, moving beyond capacity-based interpretations to a model in which EF performance reflects dynamic and contextually informed cost-benefit computations. Disruptions in reward and effort processing-manifesting as anhedonia and apathy-are common across mental health conditions and may compromise EF performance by altering these computations. This integrative perspective helps explain the limited efficacy of traditional EF training interventions on improving mental health symptoms and underscores the importance of motivational and contextual factors. We conclude by outlining a future research agenda focussed on disentangling the specific subprocesses underpinning EFs and their mechanistic links to developmental psychopathology. Recognising EFs as a transdiagnostic cognitive endophenotype governed by rational control processes opens new avenues for precise, developmentally informed, and targeted interventions in youth mental health.

title: Association between polygenic liability to depression and lifetime depression in at-risk adolescents
abstract: Internalising symptoms including depression, anxiety and somatic symptoms in adolescence are common. They can be transient, but they can also persist and progress to major depressive disorder (MDD) Polygenic risk scores for major depression (MD-PGS) may help identify which symptomatic adolescents are at greatest risk of later disorder. In a mega-analysis of two longitudinal population-based cohorts from Brisbane, Australia, we investigated whether polygenic liability to depression improves risk stratification among adolescents with elevated internalising symptoms. Internalising symptoms were assessed at age 14, lifetime MDD was assessed in young adulthood using the Composite International Diagnostic Interview, and MD-PGS were generated using summary statistics from the latest Psychiatric Genomics Consortium major depression genome-wide association study, excluding Australian cohorts. Analyses focused on comparisons between individuals in the top decile of risk and those in the remaining 90% of each cohort. A total of 302 cases with lifetime MDD and 1693 controls were included. Compared with adolescents outside the highest decile of internalising symptoms, those in the top decile at age 14 had a more than two-fold increased odds of lifetime MDD (OR = 2.56, 95% CI 1.92-3.49, p = 5.4 × 10 -10 ). Individuals in the top decile of MD-PGS also showed increased odds of lifetime MDD compared with the remaining 90% (OR = 3.45, 95% CI 2.53-4.71, p = 4.4 × 10 - ¹⁵). Adolescents who were simultaneously in the top decile of both internalising symptoms and MD-PGS had an approximately eight-fold increased odds of lifetime MDD compared with individuals outside the top decile for both risk factors (OR = 8.58, 95% CI 4.04-18.26, p = 1.2 × 10 - ⁵). These findings indicate that polygenic risk scores for depression may have particular clinical utility for stratifying risk among adolescents already presenting with elevated internalising symptoms, identifying a subgroup at very high risk for later major depressive disorder.

title: Prenatal stress reprograms placental signaling and opposes maternal immune activation effects in the fetal brain
abstract: Prenatal psychosocial stress and maternal immune activation (MIA) increase risk for overlapping offspring psychiatric disorders, but whether they influence fetal neurodevelopment through shared or distinct mechanisms is unclear. Positioned at the interface of maternal and fetal physiology, the placenta has a critical role in regulating fetal brain development. Here, we combine mouse placental single-cell RNA sequencing, transcriptomics of matched placentas and fetal brains, maternal cytokine profiling, and human placental RNA-seq to dissect this axis. In mice, chronic stress suppressed interferon signaling across placental immune cells and downregulated oxidative phosphorylation pathway expression in trophoblasts. Stressed dams also mounted a blunted type I interferon response to poly(I:C), resulting in attenuated placental antiviral signaling. Weighted gene co-expression analysis of fetal brains revealed that prenatal stress and MIA regulate overlapping DNA repair, synaptic, and translational networks in opposite directions, with stress promoting signatures of premature maturation and MIA driving replication stress. In human placentas, higher perceived stress was associated with chromatin-regulatory, RNA-metabolic, and extracellular-matrix modules that mirrored the murine stress signature. These findings identify a conserved placental stress-associated transcriptional program and suggest that stress and MIA affect shared neurodevelopmental pathways in opposing directions.

title: Sleep and Drug Use: Neuroimaging Evidence for a Multidimensional Brain Framework
abstract: Sleep plays a critical role in the initiation and maintenance of drug use, as well as recovery among individuals with substance use disorders. Sleep is a multidimensional construct, and a growing body of research has demonstrated the relative independence of various components. Specific sleep characteristics including insomnia (self-reported sleep disturbances), short sleep duration, late sleep timing and sleep irregularity have each been associated with increased risks of drug use. However, it remains unclear whether these sleep components contribute to substance use through shared neurobiological pathways. Conversely, drug use across different drug classes disrupts sleep. The extent to which drug-induced alterations in brain circuits account for shared and drug class-specific sleep disturbances remains poorly understood. In this review, we synthesize evidence from human neuroimaging studies to map sleep components predictive of drug use onto brain regions and large-scale brain networks. The anterior cingulate, insular and orbitofrontal cortices emerge as the brain regions most consistently implicated across sleep dimensions, and these regions play a key role in drug use initiation. We further discuss how chronic use of different drug classes also disrupts these brain regions and broader neural circuits involved in sleep regulation, thereby exacerbating initial sleep disturbances and potentially extending their effects to other sleep dimensions. This review underscores the importance of integrating multimodal sleep and neuroimaging assessments to advance the neurobiological understanding of the bidirectional relationship between sleep, drug use and addiction and highlights directions for future research.

title: Multiple-context extinction strengthens fear suppression through hippocampal dopamine D2R-dependent memory updating
abstract: Extinction learning, which underlies exposure therapy, generates safety memories that are often context-dependent, limiting their persistence and generalization. Although varying contextual cues during extinction has been proposed to strengthen safety learning, the neural mechanisms remain unknown. Here, we compared fear extinction conducted in a single context (SCFE) or multiple contexts (MCFE) in 129S1 and C57BL/6J mice. MCFE enhanced extinction learning and generalized extinction recall in novel contexts at 2-d, with this advantage persisting at 30-d when intervening testing occurred in the trained extinction context. This enhancement required exposure to distinct, but not novel, contexts and did not prevent spontaneous recovery or US-induced reinstatement. Dual Fos-TRAP activity mapping revealed differential recruitment of the fear conditioning-tagged cells following MCFE and identified the hippocampus as a key node supporting MCFE. Consistent with this, chemogenetic silencing of dorsal, but not ventral, hippocampus selectively impaired extinction acquisition during MCFE and abolished its behavioral advantage. Likewise, local blockade of dopamine D2-, but not D1-like, receptors in the dorsal hippocampus eliminated the enhancement in extinction acquisition produced by MCFE. Together, these findings demonstrate that contextual variation strengthens and generalizes extinction learning through dorsal hippocampal dopamine D2-like receptor-dependent memory updating, identifying a neural mechanism through which behavioral modifications of exposure therapy can improve fear suppression.

title: Modulation of the noradrenergic system using transcranial ultrasonic stimulation targeted to the brainstem locus coeruleus in awake mice
abstract: Transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) is a novel neuromodulation technique that can be used to non-invasively target the locus coeruleus (LC). The LC provides the majority of noradrenergic input to the brain and has been implicated in several neurological and psychiatric disorders. Before translation to human studies, establishing a dose-response relationship requires systematic characterization of two distinct effects: (1) the influence of stimulation protocol variations on norepinephrine (NE) release in LC target structures, and (2) the broader brain and bodily effects of LC-targeted TUS. We used fiber photometry to measure TUS-induced activation of LC neurons and release of NE in one of its major projection areas, the hippocampus. To evaluate widespread functional effects, we investigated changes in [ 18 F]FDG uptake in the brain and body in response to LC-targeted TUS using small-animal PET imaging. Five-second trains of TUS resulted in intracellular calcium level increases in the LC, accompanied by a biphasic change in NE levels in the hippocampus and LC, i.e., an initial rise followed by a transient decrease. The same TUS protocol showed a decrease in [ 18 F]FDG uptake across the brain and a strong increase in [ 18 F]FDG uptake in brown adipose tissue. If TUS was prolonged to 30 s the initial biphasic change in hippocampal NE levels was followed by a secondary increase that persisted throughout the remainder of the stimulation period. This study provides the first demonstration that TUS can modulate the LC-NE system in awake mice. Adjusting the stimulation protocol resulted in distinct patterns of hippocampal NE release, highlighting the therapeutic potential of LC-targeted TUS as distinct stimulation protocols may differentially restore disrupted NE levels across disorders. PET imaging further revealed engagement of both central and peripheral systems, emphasizing the broad physiological reach of this approach.

title: ICER-Controlled inhibitory plasticity of amygdala engram neurons regulates fear memory precision
abstract: Fear discrimination-the ability to distinguish threatening stimuli from non-threatening ones-is an essential adaptive behavior, yet the neural mechanisms underlying individual differences in discrimination precision remain unclear. Here, we show that parvalbumin-positive interneuron (PV-IN)-mediated feedforward inhibition to fear engram neurons (ENs) in the lateral amygdala is selectively enhanced following auditory fear conditioning, driven by increased postsynaptic expression of α1 subunit (Gabra1)-containing GABA A  receptors. Disruption of PV-IN activity during fear retrieval-via optogenetic or chemogenetic inhibition-or selective induction of inhibitory long-term depression at PV → EN synapses impaired fear discrimination, increasing freezing to novel tones while sparing responses to the conditioned stimulus. Mechanistically, we identify inducible cAMP early repressor (ICER) as a transcriptional regulator that limits inhibitory plasticity by downregulating Gabra1 expression, thereby promoting fear generalization. These findings establish a previously unrecognized form of inhibitory synaptic plasticity that governs the precision of fear memory and suggest potential therapeutic targets for maladaptive fear overgeneralization in disorders such as post-traumatic stress disorder.

title: Developmental trajectories of internalizing and externalizing behaviors in LGBTQ+ youth in the ABCD Study
abstract: LGBTQ+ youth experience elevated internalizing distress, yet research on externalizing behaviors and their early development remains limited. This study examined trajectories of internalizing and externalizing behaviors from childhood into adolescence using data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study (N = 11,878 at baseline, M age  = 9.80 years, SD = 0.62, 63.3% White, 52.2% male), assessed four times at ages 9/10, 10/11, 11/12, and 12/13. Linear mixed-effects models tested differences between LGBTQ+ and non-LGBTQ+ youth and among disaggregated sexual and gender identity subgroups. In the omnibus comparison, LGBTQ+ youth showed higher internalizing behaviors at age 9/10 (β = 0.18, 95% CI [0.13, 0.22]) and a more rapid increase into adolescence (β = 0.10 [0.08, 0.11]) than non-LGBTQ+ peers, along with higher externalizing behaviors at age 9/10 (β = 0.18 [0.13, 0.23]) and a smaller increase over time (β = 0.03 [0.01, 0.04]; all ps < .001). Trajectories were substantially heterogeneous across subgroups, with the omnibus pattern disproportionately driven by youth holding multiple minoritized identities, who showed the most rapid increases in both domains. Mental health disparities among LGBTQ+ youth thus emerge by late childhood, persist into early adolescence, and are most acute among multiply-minoritized youth.

title: The longitudinal co-development of adverse childhood experiences and child internalizing problems: Examining sociodemographic disparities
abstract: Internalizing problems are prevalent in childhood and are associated with exposure to adverse childhood experiences (ACEs); however, their co-development across childhood remains understudied. Prior research documents sociodemographic disparities (i.e., race/ethnicity, sex, income) in ACE exposure and internalizing problems. The current study examined individual and co-developing trajectories of ACEs and internalizing problems and sociodemographic disparities among 4,655 diverse at-risk youth at ages 3, 5, and 9. Participants were 52.2% boys and racially and ethnically diverse, with 44.7% Black, 22.5% Hispanic, 16.7% Other, and 16.2% White youth. Results showed various trajectories with stable levels of cumulative ACE exposure over time and internalizing problems trajectories that decreased or increased over time. Findings provide some evidence for a dose-response relationship between ACEs and internalizing problems. Youth of Color (φ = 0.26, 0.11, 0.19) and from low-income backgrounds ( ϵ 2  = 0.07-0.09, 0.02, 0.06-0.08) were more likely to be in worse trajectories of ACEs, internalizing problems, and joint trajectories across ages 3, 5, and 9, respectively. Findings underscore the need for culturally responsive trauma-informed interventions and policy-level efforts that target the root cause of inequities.

title: Strength in families: Parental resilience, marital dynamics, and adolescent anxiety and substance use
abstract: Drawing on Luthar's relational framework of resilience, this study examines how parental resilience operates within marital dynamics to shape adolescent adjustment in Mexican-origin families. Using four waves of data from 604 families (M adolage  = 12.41, SD = 0.97; 54.3% girls), we tested a longitudinal cascade linking W1 parental resilience to W4 adolescent anxiety and substance use via W2 marital warmth, W3 marital satisfaction, and W3 adolescents' perceptions of interparental conflict. Actor-partner interdependence models revealed both intrapersonal and interpersonal pathways: wives' resilience predicted own marital warmth, whereas husbands' resilience predicted wives' warmth. Indirect effects indicated that wives' resilience was associated with lower adolescent anxiety and substance use through warmer marital interactions, higher marital satisfaction, and reduced perceived conflict. These findings position resilience as a promotive relational resource enacted within the marital dyad, advancing interparental positivity spillover theory by identifying parental resilience as upstream drivers of family processes that shape adolescent psychopathology.

title: Maternal postnatal depression and sensitive parenting: Considering developmental timing with a causally informative approach
abstract:
Models of intergenerational transmission of depression implicate lower sensitive parenting as a key mechanism linking maternal depressive symptoms and offspring outcomes. A well-developed literature demonstrates consistent, modest, negative associations between maternal depressive symptoms and sensitive parenting. However, this literature relies primarily on methods ill-suited to examine developmental timing or account for confounding with time-varying exposures. To address these limitations, we implemented marginal structural models, an approach developed to test timing effects and address confounding for time-varying exposures. Specifically, we used prospective longitudinal data from a sample of families from low-income, rural U.S. contexts (Family Life Project; N = 1,275; 59% White, 41% Black; 31% living below federal poverty level) to test chronicity and timing effects of maternal depressive symptoms during infancy on sensitive parenting at 35 postnatal months. Unadjusted models suggested that, compared with stable lower postnatal symptoms, chronically higher ( d = −.29, p = .001), early only ( d = −.21, p = .009), and later only ( d = −.26, p = .004) symptoms were all associated with less sensitive parenting, consistent with the existing literature. However, these differences were attenuated ( d s ≤ −.14) and non-significant ( p s ≥ .396) after adjusting for confounding. Results suggest the statistical association between maternal depression and sensitive parenting may be explained by confounding and highlight the importance of considering additional intervention targets that co-occur with maternal depression and may drive reductions in sensitive parenting.

Up to one in five mothers experience elevated depressive symptoms during the postnatal period ( Bauman et al., 2020 ; Field, 2010 ; Hahn-Holbrook et al., 2019; O'Hara, 2009 ), with evidence of even higher rates since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic ( Dagher et al., 2021 ; Iyengar et al., 2021 ). These highly prevalent symptoms have substantial negative impacts at both the individual and societal levels, including maternal emotional suffering, worse physical health, and lost productivity ( Luca et al., 2020 ). Children of mothers with elevated depressive symptoms also exhibit higher likelihood of negative outcomes across various domains ( Gotlib et al., 2023 ). Indeed, more than half of the estimated societal costs of maternal psychopathology operate through negative child outcomes, including more physical and mental health problems and lower levels of academic achievement ( Meaney, 2018 ). Thus, interventions aimed at supporting mothers experiencing depression and their children, particularly interventions targeted toward interrupting intergenerational transmission of risk, have a critical public health relevance. However, current understanding of the pathways through which maternal postnatal depression may impact child outcomes is limited. Maternal parenting behaviors are one potential pathway that has been the focus of considerable research ( Goodman & Gotlib, 1999 ). A well-established body of research has demonstrated a negative association between maternal postnatal depressive symptoms and sensitive parenting (e.g., Bernard et al., 2018 ). In the present study, we extend this existing research by applying a rigorous confounding adjustment approach to examine the causal impact of specific timing patterns of maternal postnatal 1 depressive symptoms on maternal sensitive parenting. Further, we specifically focus here on mothers living in rural poverty, as they are at increased risk of experiencing elevated depressive symptoms due to barriers in care and the additional stressors that come from parenting with limited resources (e.g., Abrams et al., 2009 ; Beeghly et al., 2003 , Dolbier et al., 2013 ; Szurek-Cabanas et al., 2024 ). Maternal Postnatal Depression and Parenting Postnatal depression may compromise the cognitive and emotional resources needed to perceive and respond to often subtle and nuanced infant and toddler cues. Potential reductions in sensitive parenting (i.e., “the ability to perceive and to interpret accurately the signals and communications implicit in [the child’s] behavior, and given this understanding, to respond to them appropriately and promptly” [ Ainsworth, 1969 , p. 2]) are of interest because of the well-documented associations between caregiver sensitivity and child development across important domains, such as self-regulation (Samdan et al., 2020) and mental health ( Goodman et al., 2020 ). A substantial body of research, including multiple meta-analyses, has demonstrated an association between elevated depression and less sensitive parenting ( r s = −.08 to −.16; Bernard et al., 2018 ; Goodman et al., 2020 ; Lovejoy et al., 2000 ). Maternal depression and its potential implications for sensitive parenting and, by extension, offspring outcomes may warrant particular attention during infancy and toddlerhood because of its prevalence in this developmental period (i.e., affecting up to 20% of mother-infant dyads; e.g., Bauman et al., 2020 ). As described in Belsky’s classic model of the determinants of parenting ( Belsky, 1984 ), parenting behaviors are multiply determined, with internal parent characteristics (e.g., depressive symptoms), child characteristics (e.g., temperament), and contextual factors (e.g., family income) all likely interacting to shape parenting behaviors. In line with this model, van Doesum and colleagues (2007) found evidence that the accumulation of multiple risk factors (e.g., maternal depression, lower family income, chronic stress) was related to lower parental sensitivity, and that family income explained additional variance in sensitivity beyond depressive symptoms. Relatedly, in their meta-analysis, Lovejoy and colleagues (2000) found that negative associations between depressive symptoms and positive parenting (which is conceptually similar to sensitive parenting) were stronger among samples of low-income mothers. Thus, clarifying the causal processes linking maternal depression and sensitive parenting—particularly among mothers living in poverty—has important implications for supporting mothers and children. Causality and Developmental Timing Maternal depressive symptoms unfold alongside other contextual (e.g., neighborhood safety), maternal (e.g., physical health problems), and child-level (e.g., temperament) factors that vary over time and jointly shape sensitive parenting. In observational studies, these co-occurring factors may act as confounders (i.e., common causes of both depressive symptoms and sensitive parenting) that bias estimation (e.g., by inducing an association in the absence of a causal effect) of the causal effect of depressive symptoms on sensitive parenting ( Foster, 2010 ). In addition to informing theories of the intergenerational transmission of depression, understanding whether the association between postnatal depression and sensitive parenting is indeed causal has important translational implications for supporting children of mothers experiencing postnatal depression. For example, if postnatal depression does negatively impact sensitive parenting, then, on average, reducing postnatal depression through treatment will increase sensitive parenting. However, in the absence of this causal pathway, additional intervention efforts targeting other factors would be necessary to impact sensitive parenting ( Foster, 2010 ). Randomized controlled trials are considered the gold standard for estimating causal effects because, when randomization is successful, they ensure that the randomized groups differ only on the exposure of interest ( Frach et al., 2023 ). Some randomized controlled intervention studies have examined the impact of interventions aimed at addressing maternal depression on parenting ( Beeber et al., 2010 ; Gureje et al., 2022 ; Hussain et al., 2021 ; Puckering et al., 2010 ; Sheeber et al., 2012 ). A recent meta-analysis of these studies indicated that treating maternal depression positively impacted mother-child interactions ( Cuijpers et al., 2026 ). Notably, the meta-analyzed outcomes included several different parenting/mother-child interaction constructs (e.g., hostility, mother-reported bonding, infant attachment) in addition to those conceptually aligned with maternal sensitivity (e.g., positive parenting, responsivity). Among the studies specifically examining sensitive parenting or a conceptually similar parenting outcome, there was mixed evidence of a causal effect of treatment of depressive symptoms on parenting. For example, two studies found no significant effect of depression treatment on supportive/engaged parenting ( Sheeber et al., 2012 ) or responsive parenting ( Beeber et al., 2010 ), both of which are similar constructs to sensitive parenting. In contrast, three studies did suggest intervention effects of treatment on responsive parenting ( Gureje et al., 2022 ; Hussain et al., 2021 ; Puckering et al., 2010 ). Notably, these kinds of randomized controlled trials are limited in their ability to directly demonstrate a causal effect of depression per se on sensitive parenting. While this design tests a causal effect of depression treatments on parenting behaviors, these treatments likely impact several variables in addition to depressive symptoms, such as work performance or the quality of other relationships. Thus, we cannot assume that any observed changes in parenting are caused by changes in depressive symptoms, rather than other factors. As such, it remains an open question whether the well-documented association between postnatal depressive symptoms and sensitive parenting is causal. Given the substantial developmental changes for mothers ( Orchard et al., 2023 ) as well as infants and toddlers (e.g., Markant & Thomas, 2013 ), across the early postnatal years, it is also important to consider potential timing effects of postnatal depression on sensitive parenting. There is documented variability in the timing and course of postnatal depression, with some mothers experiencing consistently elevated symptoms, and some experiencing more transient symptom elevations (e.g., elevated symptoms in the early postnatal period only, followed by low symptoms; Baron et al., 2017 ). These patterns of maternal symptoms result in different “exposure 2 histories” (i.e., specified temporal patterns of elevated maternal symptoms that differ in timing and chronicity; e.g., chronically higher, early only symptoms). Informed by theories of mother-infant interactions, we expect that effects of postnatal depressive symptoms on sensitive parenting may vary based on exposure history. The Mutual Regulation Model and Feldman’s theory of early mother-infant relationship development both suggest that development during the first postnatal years should be conceptualized as occurring within a dynamic dyadic system comprising a caregiver subsystem, an infant/toddler subsystem, and the interactions between infant/toddler and caregiver ( Beeghly et al., 2016 ; Feldman, 2015 ). Two aspects of these theories are particularly relevant for considering potential timing effects of postnatal depressive symptoms on sensitive parenting. First, the system is especially reliant on caregiver input in the early postnatal months because the infant’s communicative and independent regulatory capacities are limited at this early stage ( Beeghly et al., 2016 ). Second, as the system develops dynamically, later parenting is shaped not only by current conditions, but also by earlier relational processes ( Feldman, 2015 ). These theoretical frameworks suggest that more chronicity and earlier onset of postnatal symptoms may result in stronger negative impacts on sensitive parenting. Typical Approaches to Causal Inference and Developmental Timing in Observational Studies A typical statistical approach for addressing confounding and strengthening causal inference within observational studies in the developmental psychology literature is to treat putative confounders as model covariates in multiple regression or structural equation modeling frameworks. However, the limitations to this approach are well established (e.g., sensitivity to model specification, overcontrol, extrapolation; see Thoemmes & Ong, 2016 ; Vandecandelaere et al., 2016 ). The limitations of regression adjustment are especially pronounced when considering questions of developmental timing, in which both the exposure and confounders vary over time. For example, it is common for researchers to attempt to isolate the effect of an early exposure by “controlling for” (i.e., conditioning on) the effect of a later exposure. However, if part of the effect of the early exposure is mediated by the later exposure, controlling for this later exposure would introduce blocking bias , in which the segment of the early exposure that is transmitted through the later exposure is incorrectly adjusted out of the estimate (see Figure 1 for a simple example). More generally, blocking bias occurs any time one conditions on a post-exposure variable that is part of the causal chain from the exposure to the outcome (i.e., any variable that serves as a mediator of the causal effect; Foster, 2010 ). Blocking bias can become an intractable problem within a regression framework with time-varying exposures. In this case, a variable can serve simultaneously as a mediator of an earlier exposure and a confounder of a later exposure ( Stallworthy, DeJoseph et al., 2026 ). Another less-appreciated type of bias that can emerge when attempting to isolate timing effects within a regression framework is collider (or selection) bias ( Foster, 2010 ). This occurs when one conditions on a variable that opens up an otherwise-closed causal pathway between the exposure and outcome and thus induces a spurious association between exposure and outcome (see Figure 1 for a simple illustration). As can occur with blocking bias, a variable can function as a confounder for one exposure timepoint (and thus induce bias if not conditioned on) and a collider for another (and thus induce bias if conditioned on). In short, attempts to account for confounding with time-varying exposures and confounders within a regression framework can introduce more bias than they alleviate (see Cole et al., 2010 ; Stallworthy, DeJoseph et al., 2026 for additional discussion of the limitations of estimating timing effects within a regression framework). Given these limitations, the existing empirical literature examining timing effects of maternal postnatal depressive symptoms on sensitive parenting may be impacted by several sources of bias. An Alternative Approach: Marginal Structural Modeling To address the complexities introduced above, we implemented a statistical approach from the causal inference literature—marginal structural models (MSMs; Robins et al., 2000 )—developed to address confounding

title: Infant and early childhood mental health professionals' attitudes toward a system of professional endorsement: A quantitative examination of personal factors, professional support, and perceived benefits
abstract: Demand for recognition of the specialized knowledge and skills required of Infant and Early Childhood Mental Health (IECMH) practitioners, researchers, and policymakers resulted in the establishment of standardized professional credentials that document this expertise. However, to date, research on the influences and impacts of an Infant or Early Childhood Mental Health Endorsement on IECMH professionals is scarce. This descriptive, cross-sectional study aims to fill this gap by reporting quantitative findings from a voluntary online survey, the Perceptions of Endorsement Survey (PES), completed by a diverse group of 911 Endorsed professionals across the United States and Australia. The study by a U.S. research team explores how personal factors, professional supports, and perceived benefits influence the likelihood of continuing to participate in the Endorsement system and of recommending it to others (Attitudes towards Endorsement). Regression analyses revealed three factors that were significant predictors of positive Attitudes towards Endorsement: Confidence and Motivation, Endorsement-related Social Influences, and perceived Opportunities. Moreover, the combination of Endorsement-related Social Influences and Opportunities significantly and uniquely predicted positive Attitudes towards Endorsement above what these factors predicted individually. Discussion focuses on how individual-level demographic characteristics, occupational-level factors, social factors, and perceived benefits relate to Attitudes towards Endorsement.

title: The prospective associations between parent and adolescent emotional reactivity and adolescent psychopathology
abstract: This study examined how adolescent and parent emotional reactivity to daily parent-adolescent conflict is associated with adolescent psychopathology over time. A community sample of 237 Taiwanese parent-adolescent dyads (adolescents:  M age  = 14.80,  SD age  = 2.08; 58% female; parents:  M age  = 42.36,  SD age  = 8.57; 68% female) completed 10 days of daily reports on parent-adolescent conflict and emotions, and adolescents reported depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, and externalizing problems at baseline and six-month follow-up. The results showed that greater adolescent negative emotional (NE) reactivity predicted higher depressive ( β  = .17) and anxiety symptoms ( β  = .21), and adolescent positive emotional (PE) reactivity predicted higher depressive symptoms ( β  = .13), anxiety symptoms ( β  = .19), and externalizing problems ( β  = .17). Parent NE reactivity predicted higher adolescent depressive symptoms ( β  = .29) and externalizing problems ( β  = .15). Age moderated the associations between parent reactivity and anxiety symptoms, such that higher parent NE and PE reactivity were associated with greater anxiety only among younger adolescents. Findings highlight that daily emotional reactivity to parent-adolescent conflict is associated with adolescent psychopathology and underscore that parent reactivity represents a distinct risk process, especially consequential for anxiety in early adolescence.

title: Transactional, social causation, or symptoms-driven? Disentangling the longitudinal associations between perceived family, peer, and teacher support and depressive symptoms among multicultural adolescents
abstract: This study examines whether perceived social support from family, peers, and teachers exhibits reciprocal relations with depressive symptoms (transactional model), acts as a protective factor (social causation model), or emerges as a consequence of depressive symptoms (symptoms-driven model) among South Korean multicultural adolescents. A four-wave longitudinal dataset from a nationally representative cohort ( N  = 1,500; 50.67% female;  M age  = 10.98 years,  SD  = 0.37) was analyzed using random intercept cross-lagged panel models. At the between-person level, all three perceived support sources were negatively associated with depressive symptoms across both the joint and bivariate models ( rs  = -0.69 to -0.63,  ps  < .001). At the within-person level, perceived family support predicted subsequent decreases in depressive symptoms in both modeling frameworks ( βs  = -0.07 to -0.05,  ps  < .05), and perceived peer support similarly emerged as a significant prospective predictor when modeled independently ( βs  = -0.07 to -0.06,  ps  < .05). Depressive symptoms did not predict changes in any perceived support source in either framework. The findings support a source-specific social causation model, with perceived family support emerging as the primary within-person protective factor, and highlight the family system as a pivotal intervention target for alleviating depressive symptoms in this vulnerable population.

title: Food neophobia predicts early cognitive development: A longitudinal study
abstract:
Food neophobia, the tendency to reject novel food, has been linked to children's categorization and executive functions in cross-sectional research, but the developmental direction of these relations remains unclear. This longitudinal study examined reciprocal relations between these variables across one school year in French children. Participants were 113 children (50 girls; M age = 48.30 ± 7.20 months at Time 1) recruited from five public preschools in a large metropolitan area. Data were collected between 2023 and 2024 (Time 2). Race and ethnicity data were not collected due to national regulations. Caregivers reported children's food neophobia, and children completed a food categorization task and measures of working memory, inhibition, and cognitive flexibility. Most constructs showed temporal stability across waves. Higher food neophobia at Time 1 predicted lower categorization performance (β = -.263) and lower executive functions (β = -.195), controlling for prior levels. In contrast, categorization performance and executive functions did not predict subsequent changes in food neophobia. These findings suggest that food neophobia prospectively relates to later differences in children's executive functions and their ability to use food-category knowledge under task demands, consistent with the possibility that early avoidance tendencies shape engagement with cognitively informative experiences during development.

Children differ in their willingness to try new foods, a tendency known as food neophobia. Research has linked food neophobia to categorization, the ability to group items, and to executive functions, the skills that support remembering rules, controlling impulses, and adapting to changing situations. This study followed French preschool children over one school year to examine how food neophobia, categorization, and executive functions develop together over time. Children who were more neophobic at the first assessment showed lower categorization and executive-function performance 1 year later, even after accounting for their earlier performance. In contrast, categorization and executive functions did not predict later food neophobia. These findings suggest that food neophobia may be associated with differences in how children engage with everyday experiences that support learning and self-regulation in early childhood.

title: Long-term legacy of parents' secure base script knowledge: Cascading implications for family relationships and children's positive development
abstract:
A large body of research implicates adults’ attachment security, largely formed in their early experiences, as a key factor shaping their future romantic and parenting relationships. Family system theories suggest that the interparental relationship is key for other relationships within the family, including those in individual mother- and father-child dyads. Few studies, however, have elucidated how the legacy of parents’ attachment security unfolds through family relationships to child outcomes. We test a developmental longitudinal cascade, conceptualized as a sequential mediation model, from parents’ attachment security, assessed as their secure base script knowledge when children were infants, to their self-reported interparental relationship quality at toddler age, to their observed relationships with their children at age 3 years, and ultimately, to children’s developmental outcomes at age 4.5 years (self-regulation and moral self). We leverage multi-method data (interviews, reports, observations) from a study of 200 community families in U.S. Midwest (mothers, fathers, and children). We adopt recent perspectives that emphasize positive socialization processes and successful outcomes rather than detrimental pathways conferring risks. In analyses that controlled for the continuity of interparental and parent-child relationships, we supported several mediational paths. Results for mother-child dyads supported the entire hypothesized longitudinal sequence from parents’ attachment security to the parent-child relationship to children’s positive developmental outcomes. For father-child dyads, that key cascade was not supported. However, several shorter alternative indirect paths were found in both dyads. Public significance statement : Adopting a perspective focused on positive factors in development, we highlight how parents’ secure attachment, assessed when children are infants, promotes positive interparental relationships in the second year, then in turn, positive parent-child relationships at age three, and ultimately, children’s positive social-emotional outcomes at kindergarten age.

For the last several decades, following the ascent and increasing prominence of the science of relationships in psychology ( Collins & Laursen, 1999 ; Hinde & Stevenson-Hinde, 1979; Reis & Collins, 2004 ; Vangelisti et al., 2026 ), family relationships have been seen as key contexts in which to understand children’s development. Several distinct but dovetailing perspectives have produced rich literatures elucidating various aspects of origins and interconnected dynamics of family relationships. The blossoming science of relationships provides a rich framework for understanding the continuity of human functioning over the life span, from experiences of early care with one’s parents to forming romantic relationships as adults to becoming parents, providing early care to one’s offspring. Longitudinal studies especially can elucidate mechanisms responsible for the powerful legacy of early experiences. Attachment theory proposed that early relational experiences are key factors in forming individuals’ future enduring attachment orientations that continue to shape and guide their functioning in interpersonal relationships ( Bowlby, 1973 ; Cavallo & Perlman, 2026 ; Dugan et al., 2025 ; Fraley, 2002 ; Haydon et al., 2014 ; Main et al., 1985 ; Simpson & Karantzas, 2019 ; Simpson et al., 2026 ). A large and growing body of research has examined how adults’ early formed attachment orientations guide their relationships with romantic partners (e.g., Dugan et al., 2025 ; Dugan & Fraley, 2022 ; Fraley & Shaver, 2000 ; Feeney & Fitzgerald, 2019 ; Overall et al., 2022 ; Mikulincer et al., 2002 ; Mikulincer & Shaver, 2016 ; River et al., 2022 ; Simpson et al., 2026 ; Simpson & Rholes, 2019 ; Steele et al., 2014 ; T. E. A. Waters et al., 2018 ). In turn, adults in romantic relationships commonly become parents; thus, romantic relationships become critically important upon the transition to parenthood, as highlighted by family system perspectives. A very large body of research has focused on the critical role of the interparental relationship for caregiving, parenting, and the emerging parent-child relationships ( Belsky, 1984 ; Brock & Kochanska, 2016 ; Craft et al., 2021 ; Curran et al., 2026 ; Davies & Cicchetti, 2004 ; Davies & Cummings, 1994 ; Davies et al., 2016 ; Erel & Burman, 1995 ; Jones et al., 2015 ; Overall et al., 2022 ; Rhoades, 2008 ; Stroud et al., 2011 ; Sturge-Apple et al., 2006 ; Taraban & Shaw, 2018 ; Trumbell et al., 2018 ). Finally, parent-child relationships become the uniquely important contexts for children’s development ( Collins & Laursen, 1999 ; Kuczynski & de Mol, 2015 ; Maccoby, 1999 ; Maccoby & Martin, 1983 ). As broadly supported by attachment theory ( Ainsworth et al., 1971 ; Thompson, 2015 ) and socialization theory ( Lansford, 2022 ; Maccoby & Martin, 1983 ), positive relationships, in which the parent is responsive to the child, the child willingly cooperates with and is responsive to the parent, and their interactions are infused with positive affect, have been broadly seen as conducive to children’s adaptive developmental trajectories and promoting a vast array of strengths and competencies ( Coffey, 2021 ; Deater-Deckard & Petrill, 2004 ; S. Kim et al., 2015 ; Kochanska, 1997 ; Kochanska et al., 2008 , 2019 , 2025 ). Our study has four aims, with each seeking to make a novel contribution by addressing a gap in the extant literature. One, as our first aim, we examine longitudinally, over 4 years, the entire developmental cascade from parents’ attachment orientations as they assumed their parenting role when their children were infants to their marital relationships, to their relationships with the child, to child outcomes. Although, as indicated above, studies have robustly supported various elements of that cascade, very few have longitudinally examined the entire chain. Two, most of the above-reviewed research has focused on the transmission of developmental risk ( Belsky, 1984 ; Taraban & Shaw, 2018 ). Researchers have examined parental insecure attachment orientations, dysfunctional interparental and parent-child relationships, and finally, children’s poor developmental outcomes, typically behavioral problems. Although that work is very important, recently researchers have argued for a new agenda complementing – without contradicting – those earlier perspectives by advocating a shift of the emphasis to positive processes and strengths and competencies ( Algoe, 2019 ; Don et al., 2025 ; Han et al., 2023 ; Pluess, 2024 ; Snyder et al., 2021 ). As our second aim, we adopt this new lens in our work, focusing on a cascade from parental security to a positive interparental relationship and its beneficial impact (“positive spillover”) to a positive parent-child relationship ( Davies, Cao, Baker et al., 2025 ; Davies, Cao, Hendrickson et al., 2025 ; Don et al., 2025 ; Kochanska, 1997 ; Kochanska et al., 2008 ) to positive child outcomes, such as strengths and competencies ( Pluess, 2024 ). Our third aim is to heed the call by Reis and Mizrahi (2026) , who advocated for using a combination of robust behavioral observations and self-reports in relationship science and argued that such an approach is key for future progress. To that end, we use rich behavioral assessments of parent-child positive relationships and child outcomes, and we rely on a well-established report measure of the interparental relationship. We employ an innovative methodology to assess parents’ attachment orientations (Attachment Script Assessment, ASA). Adult Attachment Interview (AAI; George et al., 1996 ) has long been seen as the “gold standard” measure because, inspired by Bowlby’s concept of internal working models, it captures the implicit, only partly conscious aspects of representations of relationships. However, AAI is highly labor- and effort-intensive. Newer self-report measures, such as Experiences in Close Relationships (ECR, Fraley et al., 2000 ) and a shorter ECR-RS ( Fraley et al., 2011 ), are easy, valuable, and broadly used alternatives. However, ECR is premised on a person’s explicit reports, and thus it may not fully capture the implicit, not fully conscious components of internal working model of relationships or expectations of the self and others ( Bowlby, 1969/1982 ; Simpson et al., 2026 ). ASA has emerged as a valuable and attractive recent alternative. It captures participants’ secure base script knowledge (SBSK; Groh & Haydon, 2024 ; T. E. A. Waters & Roisman, 2019 ; H. S. Waters & E. Waters, 2006 ; H. S. Waters & T. E. A. Waters, 2021 ), a relatively stable cognitive “script,” or a distilled generalized, abstracted summary of their early experiences of care. SBSK encompasses expectations that others are available and responsive to distress and reliably willing to provide competent and sensitive support, and that seeking support from them is adaptive. ASA utilizes a word-prompt outline method to elicit participants’ brief narratives, and it is easy to administer. Growing evidence has supported its validity ( Dagan et al., 2021 ; Groh & Haydon, 2024 ; H. S. Waters & E. Waters, 2006 ; H. S. Waters & T. E. A. Waters, 2021 ; T. E. A. Waters & Roisman, 2019 ). Our fourth aim is to address a stubborn imbalance in research on family processes by examining parallel data for mother- and father-child dyads. Despite repeated calls for including both parents in research on families ( Cabrera et al., 2014 ; Cabrera et al., 2018 ; Cowan et al., 2019 ; Dugan et al., 2025 ; Schoppe-Sullivan & Fagan, 2020 ), studies still predominantly focus on mothers. Given the growing involvement of fathers in parenting ( Cabrera et al., 2000 ), this is a significant gap. Including fathers in research on longitudinal dynamics of intersecting interparental and parent-child relationships is an especially important target ( Brock et al., 2020 ; Ramsdell et al., 2025 ). Further, although a growing number of studies of parent-child relationships include fathers, only a few have included measures of their SBSK. Psouni (2019) used ASA to assess mothers’ and fathers’ SBSK, but the study did not deploy any measures of parenting. Trumbell et al. (2018) found that for fathers, but not mothers, SBSK served to buffer the impact of marital disengagement on negative parenting. We are not aware of any longitudinal study that has examined longitudinally the entire cascade from parental SBSK to interparental relationship to a positive parent-child relationship to child future development in mother- and father-child dyads. As Jones et al. (2015) argued in their important review, “the prospective links among parental attachment styles, parenting, and child developmental outcomes will require longitudinal research with well-characterized samples of parents and children” (p. 70). Further, they also advocated that “future research should include greater consideration of the role of parents’ romantic relationship quality when studying the links between attachment styles and parenting. The parent–child relationship is just one component of a larger family system that includes (but is not limited to) the parents’ romantic relationship, and it has long been recognized that the marital relationship both influences and is influenced by parent–child relationships (e.g., Belsky, 1981 )”, p. 70. We target both of those programmatic goals in this work. The Current Study In a sequential mediation model, we leverage longitudinal, multi-method data to examine the entire cascade from parents’ attachment security, measured when children were 8 months, to the parents’ subsequent quality of marriage, measured when children were 16 months, to their positive parent-child relationship, measured when children were 3 years, and to children’s key competencies assessed at 4.5 years: self-regulation and moral self. Our choice of measures was grounded in theory and research. We chose ASA as the measure of parental attachment security due to its advantages described above. We selected a well-established self-report of positive interparental relationship, Quality of Marriage Index (QMI, Norton, 1983 ). Although quite simple, it is considered a robust instrument of marital satisfaction, recommended for use in research ( Bradbury et al., 2000 ). Note that we refer interchangeably to marriage quality and interparental relationship quality, as being married was not an eligibility criterion (parents were married in 87% of families). We chose strong, behaviorally based measures of parent-child positive relationships that target their key features, which we had developed and refined in multiple longitudinal studies. We focus on responsiveness and positive affect, with both coded for the parent and the child, defined in age-appropriate terms. Those are classic dimensions in research on parent-child relationships ( Aksan et al., 2006 ; Bornstein et al., 2008 ; De Wolff & van IJzendoorn, 1997 ; Dix, 1991 ; Kochanska, 1997 ; Landry et al., 2006 ; Leerkes et al., 2022 ). Those qualities, reflecting a reciprocal, cooperative orientation within the dyad, infused with positive emotions, have received growing attention since the ascent of attachment-informed perspectives on socialization ( Kochanska, 1997 , 2002 ; Kochanska & Murray, 2000 ; Kochanska et al., 2019 ; Maccoby & Martin, 1983 ). When assessing children’s positive development ( Pluess, 2024 ), we focus on their early self-regulation and moral self, again using behavioral measures we have developed and refined, and tested in multiple studies. Self-regulation is a key skill for a very broad range of developmental outcomes, including school readiness and academic achievement, social and moral development, physical health, and positive relationships with peers and teachers (e.g., Blair & Raver, 2015 ; Eisenberg et al., 2024 ; Moffitt et al., 2011 ; Montroy et al., 2016 ; Robson et al., 2020 ; Rothbart & Bates, 2006 ; Thompson, 2015 ). Children’s early positive moral self or moral self-concept has also been associated with a range of competent and adaptive aspects of functioning later in childhood ( Christner et al., 2020 ; Kochanska et al., 2010 ; Söldner & Paulus, 2025 ; Sticker et al., 2021 ). Extensive literature has supported causal associations between parent-child positive relationships that encompass mutual responsiveness and positive affect, and self-regulation and the moral self. Such relationships have been repeatedly positively associated with multiple aspects of children’s self-regulation ( Bernier et al., 2012 ; Boldt et al., 2020 ; Calkins et al., 1998 ; Eisenberg et al., 2005 ; 2015 ; Feldman et al., 1999 ; Harrist & Waugh, 2002 ; Hertz et al., 2019 ; Hughes & Ensor, 2009 ; J.
