title: The effect of cognitive behavioral therapy for sleep and glycemic outcomes in people with diabetes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sleep disturbances are highly prevalent in individuals with diabetes and are associated with various adverse physiological, psychological, and social consequences. A growing body of research supports the effectiveness of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) in managing sleep problems in diabetes. However, the extent of its positive correlation with sleep quality and glycemic outcomes remains unclear due to the lack of rigorous evidence synthesis.

METHODS: Ten databases (PubMed, Cochrane Library, EMBASE, CINAHL, Web of Science, MEDLINE, APA PsycInfo, China National Knowledge Infrastructure [CNKI], Wanfang Data Knowledge Service Platform, VIP) were searched using keywords related to cognitive behavioral therapy and diabetes, from their inception until June 2026, to identify eligible randomized controlled trials. Researchers independently screened and extracted data from the included studies. The risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool (RoB 2.0). Random-effects meta-analyses were performed using Review Manager software (RevMan) 5.4.1 to estimate overall effects and for prespecified subgroup analyses. Sensitivity analysis, assessment of publication bias, and meta-regression were conducted using STATA 17.0 to explore study-level variables potentially contributing to heterogeneity.

RESULTS: Ten eligible randomized controlled trials involving a total of 2827 participants from 4 countries were included in this synthesis. When comparing CBT to usual care or health education, CBT demonstrated a significant effect size for improving sleep quality (mean difference [MD] = -1.47; 95% confidence interval [CI] = -1.98 to -0.96; P < .00001; I2 = 89%). Significant improvements were also observed for glycemic outcomes (HbA1c: MD = -0.35%; 95% CI = -0.44 to -0.25; P < .00001; I2 = 94%) and insomnia severity (MD = -2.06; 95% CI = -4.24 to 0.12; P = .004; I2 = 88%). However, there was no significant improvement in BMI (MD = -0.12; 95% CI = -0.72 to 0.48; P = .69; I2 = 0%). Exploratory subgroup analyses revealed significant differences based on follow-up time. Through meta-regression, disease type, sample size, and intervention plan were not found to be sources of heterogeneity.

CONCLUSION: Cognitive behavioral therapy significantly improves sleep quality, reduces HbA1c levels, and alleviates insomnia severity in people with diabetes. Future high-quality research is needed to optimize protocols, define target populations, and facilitate wider clinical implementation.

title: Suicidality-Related Emergency Department Visits Among US Children and Adolescents, 2016-2022
abstract:
Objective To examine national trends in suicidality-related (intentional self-harm, self-inflicted injury, and suicide attempt) emergency department (ED) visits among US children and adolescents between 2016 and 2022 and describe demographic and psychiatric correlates across age groups. Method Data were obtained from the 2016 to 2022 Nationwide Emergency Department Sample (NEDS) for patients aged 5 to 19 years with suicidality-related ICD-10-CM codes. Weighted national estimates, demographics, and psychiatric comorbidities were compared across age groups (5-9, 10-14, and 15-19 years). Temporal trends were evaluated using Daniel’s test for trend, with p < .05 considered significant. Results There were an estimated 1,100,785 suicidality-related ED visits (intentional self-harm 61%, self-inflicted injury 39%, suicide attempt 9%). The number of visits increased significantly among age group 10 to 14 for all diagnoses ( p ≤ .01) and among age group 15 to 19 for suicide attempts only ( p = .003). Female patients (74.7%) accounted for most visits. Depression (45.3%) and anxiety (21.6%) were the most common comorbidities. Conclusion Suicidality-related ED visits among US youth remain alarmingly high, especially among young adolescents. The predominance of depression, anxiety, and female patient representation underscores the need for early, community-based mental health interventions and post-ED follow-up care. Clinical guidance • Screen earlier and repeatedly. Incorporate routine suicide risk screening beginning in late elementary school (ages 9–10), especially during well-child visits, school physicals, and emergency department encounters, even when presenting complaints are nonpsychiatric. • Treat self-harm as a high-risk signal. Any self-inflicted injury—regardless of stated intent—should trigger a structured suicide risk assessment, safety planning, and close follow-up, as self-harm often precedes suicide attempts. • Address comorbid depression, anxiety, and trauma aggressively. Early identification and evidence-based treatment (eg, cognitive behavioral therapy, dialectical behavior therapy-informed skills, trauma-focused care) should be prioritized, with coordinated family involvement when developmentally appropriate. • Strengthen transitions of care after emergency department visits. Ensure rapid outpatient follow-up (within 7 days), clear communication with caregivers, and linkage to school- and community-based supports, particularly for preteens and adolescents from low-income households. Diversity & Inclusion Statement One or more of the authors of this paper self-identifies as a member of one or more historically underrepresented racial and/or ethnic groups in science. We actively worked to promote sex and gender balance in our author group. We actively worked to promote inclusion of historically underrepresented racial and/or ethnic groups in science in our author group. The author list of this paper includes contributors from the location and/or community where the research was conducted who participated in the data collection, design, analysis, and/or interpretation of the work.

Plain language summary Using national emergency department (ED) data from 2016 to 2022, the authors found more than 1.1 million suicide-related visits among US youth aged 5 to 19 years. The sharpest increase in emergency department visits occurred in children aged 10 to 14 years, while suicide attempts rose among older adolescents. Depression and anxiety were common diagnoses, and girls were disproportionately affected. These findings highlight the need for early, age-appropriate suicide prevention and post-ED follow-up care.

Suicide, the act of developing and implementing plans to end one’s life, remains a leading cause of death among children in the United States. In 2023, 2,643 children aged 0 to 19 died by suicide. 1 Of these, 481 deaths occurred among children aged 10 to 14, and 2,156 occurred among adolescents aged 15 to 19. 1 Beyond its devastating human toll, pediatric suicidality places a substantial financial burden on the health care system. A recent analysis found that suicide attempts (SAs) among youth 8 to 21 years old generated direct medical costs totaling $869 million in 2021, with prevention of intentional overdoses alone potentially saving $530 million annually. 2 Recent evidence suggests a continued increase in suicide rates among pediatric and adolescent populations. Between 2008 and 2021, suicide rates among children aged 8 to 12 years rose by approximately 8% annually. 3 In 2021, suicide ranked as the third leading cause of death among US high school students aged 14 to 18 years. 4 Importantly, this rise in suicide rates is not confined to adolescents—suicidality has also been increasingly reported among elementary school–aged children. 5 Despite their substantial contribution to our understanding of pediatric and adolescent suicidality, these studies tend to focus on aggregated trends or specific subpopulations, leaving gaps in understanding of temporal changes in SA among children and adolescents. In a more recent comprehensive review, Burstein et al. 6 reported that between 2007 and 2015, suicide-related emergency department (ED) visits doubled among children aged 10 to 18, underscoring the urgent need for enhanced mental health resources and structured postdischarge planning. However, that study excluded children younger than 10 years of age. Importantly, as highlighted in prior literature, studying suicidality at the population level presents important methodological challenges, particularly when relying on administrative datasets. In the absence of direct clinical assessments, researchers must rely on diagnostic coding to approximate suicidality-related behaviors. Within large national datasets such as the Nationwide Emergency Department Sample (NEDS), ICD-10-CM codes provide the most feasible and standardized approach for identifying suicidality-related encounters, including suicidal ideation (SI), self-harm, and SA. Although these codes have limitations due to variability in provider documentation and the lack of universally standardized operational definition, they remain the most widely used and practical method for capturing suicide-related presentations on a scale. Accordingly, ICD-10-CM –based classifications serve as a proxy for suicidality-related behaviors in epidemiological studies of ED utilization. 7 Using this approach, we analyzed NEDS data from 2016 to 2022 to identify recent trends in suicidality-related ED visits among children and adolescents, including children as young as 5 years old. Evaluating these temporal patterns by age group and associated biopsychosocial factors may help guide targeted developmentally informed preventive strategies and resource allocation. Method Data Source We used data from the 2016 to 2022 NEDS, part of the Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project sponsored by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality. 8 NEDS represents the largest all-payer ED database in the United States, encompassing approximately 137 million ED visits annually. 7 The database is de-identified, compliant with Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, and publicly available. This analysis was determined to be not human subjects research by the Creighton University Institutional Review Board (InfoEd Record Number: 2005429). Cohort Identification We included ED visits for patients aged 5 to 19 years. Visits were selected if they contained at least 1 suicidality-related ICD-10-CM diagnosis code (intentional self-harm, self-inflicted injury, or SA). These codes were selected because within the ICD-10-CM system, providers often use these classifications interchangeably when evaluating patients presenting to the ED with suspected SA, and standardized operational definitions for these categories are lacking. 7 However, these diagnostic categories are not mutually exclusive, and individual encounters may include multiple suicidality-related codes. Demographic data extracted included biological sex (male, female), race (White, Black, Hispanic, other), primary payer (Medicaid, Medicare, private, other), income quartile, hospital region (Northeast, Midwest, South, West), hospital location/teaching status (metropolitan/nonteaching, metropolitan/teaching, nonmetropolitan), and psychiatric comorbidities. In addition to psychiatric comorbidities, we also identified history of SI and history of SA. All diagnoses were identified via ICD-10-CM codes 8 ; codes were adapted from Zipursky et al. 9 and are provided in Table S1 , available online. Outcomes The primary outcome was the yearly rate of suicidality-related ED visits per 10,000 US population. Suicidality-related visits were defined as encounters with at least 1 ICD-10-CM diagnosis code for SI, intentional self-harm, self-inflicted injury, or SA. In addition, we examined ED discharge disposition as a secondary outcome. Statistical Analysis Year-over-year trends were assessed using Daniel’s test for trend. 10 Daniel’s test for trend, also known as Spearman rank correlation, is a nonparametric statistical test to detect trend in a time series. Daniel’s test is used when one of the variables is chronological, which in this case was year. To account for yearly population changes, the rate of suicidality-related ED visits was estimated per 10,000 US population. 11 , 12 More specifically, the NEDS-estimated number of yearly suicidality-related ED visits was divided by the yearly US population based on the July 1 estimate provided by the US Census Bureau and multiplied by 10,000. Year-over-year trends in the rate of suicidality-related ED visits were evaluated overall and by age group: children (5-9 years), young adolescents (10-14 years), and adolescents (15-19 years). US Census Bureau nationwide population estimates were used to account for fluctuations in the US population appropriately. Relatedly, age group classifications were informed by the US Census Bureau age ranges. Descriptive characteristics were stratified by age group and compared via χ 2 tests. Two-tailed p < .05 indicated statistical significance. All analyses were conducted using SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc.). Results Between 2016 and 2022, there were an estimated 1,100,785 ED visits among children aged 5 to 19 with a suicidality-related diagnosis (unweighted N = 253,255; 95% CI, 1,046,030-1,155,539). Of those, an estimated 674,446 ED visits were for intentional self-harm (unweighted N = 155,431; 95% CI, 637,144-711,748), 433,951 ED visits were for self-inflicted injury (unweighted N = 99,452; 95% CI, 411,852-456,050), and 95,606 ED visits were for SA (unweighted N = 21,867; 95% CI, 89,895-101,318). Notably, 9.02% (weighted N = 99,242; 95% CI, 94,036-104,463) of ED visits involved patients with more than 1 suicidality-related diagnosis. Demographics Descriptive characteristics by age group are provided in Table 1 . ED visits for intentional self-harm were most frequent in adolescents (63.37%) and young adolescents (57.83%) compared with children (19.12%) ( p < .001). In contrast, ED visits for self-inflicted injury were the most frequent in children (72.90%), followed by young adolescents (42.52%) and adolescents (37.58%) ( p < .001). For young adolescents and adolescents, 8.86% and 8.46%, respectively, of suicidality-related ED visits were for SA, whereas 20.84% of suicidality-related ED visits for children were for SA ( p < .001). Medicaid was the most frequent insurance across age groups (children: 69.86%; young adolescents: 53.74%; adolescents: 45.81%), followed by private insurance (children: 22.58%; young adolescents: 38.64%, adolescents: 43.49%). More than half of suicidality-related ED visits were patients living in a low-income area, according to income quartile by patient zip code (ie, lowest 2 income quartiles) (children: 63.03%; young adolescents: 53.54%; adolescents: 52.72%). Suicidality-related ED visits frequently occurred in the South (children: 38.92%; young adolescents: 35.27%; adolescents: 34.08%) and Midwest (children: 25.31%; young adolescents: 27.78%; adolescents: 28.33%). Most suicidality-related ED visits occurred at metropolitan teaching facilities (children: 68.96%; young adolescents: 67.40%; adolescents: 64.93%). Notably, for adolescents, 21.36% of suicidality-related ED visits were patients with a history of SI, and 13.14% were patients with a history of SA. Similarly, for young adolescents, 23.66% of suicidality-related ED visits were patients with a history of SI, and 12.91% were patients with a history of SA. In suicidality-related ED visits involving children, 12.56% had a history of SI, and 5.45% had a history of SA. Figure S1 , available online, illustrates the year-over-year trend in the rate of all pediatric (5-19 years), young adolescent (10-14 years), and adolescent (15-19 years) suicidality ED visits in which the patient had a history of SA or SI. For all pediatric patients, the year-over-year trend in the rate of suicidality-related ED visits in which the patient had a history of SI was statistically significant ( p trend < .001). This significant trend was also seen specifically in young adolescents ( p trend < .001) and adolescents ( p trend = .014). Interestingly, in adolescents, the yearly trend in the rate of visits with a history of SA was statistically significant ( p trend = .003). However, this trend was not statistically significant in young adolescents ( p trend = .148) or the general pediatric population ( p trend = .052). Psychiatric Comorbidities In general, depression and anxiety disorders were the most frequent comorbidities (45.28% and 21.58%, respectively). Of suicidality-related ED visits involving young adolescents and adolescents, 44.11% and 46.19%, respectively, of patients had a diagnosis of a depressive disorder compared with 14.22% of visits involving children ( p < .001). Likewise, in 19.70% and 22.62% of suicidality-related ED visits involving young adolescents and adolescents, patients had a diagnosis for an anxiety disorder compared with only 8.25% of visits involving children ( p < .001). Other common psychiatric comorbidities that varied in frequency by age group included bipolar disorder; trauma- and stressor-related disorders; schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorders; attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorders; sleep-wake disorders; disruptive, impulse-control, and conduct disorders; autism spectrum disorder; and intellectual disabilities ( Table 1 ). title: Time cost reduces the generalization of fearful avoidance
abstract: Excessive generalization of avoidance behavior is considered a core symptom of anxiety disorders. Avoidance behavior associated with anxiety often involves a certain cost, usually in the form of a reward that is foregone. Avoidance behavior can also be time-consuming, resulting in an additional cost. Little research has examined how time cost influences fearful avoidance generalization. Furthermore, rare studies have investigated how different levels of avoidance costs shape this generalization process. This study therefore focused on how the magnitude of time costs affects the degree to which fearful avoidance is generalized. After the fear conditioning stage, participants were divided into two avoidance time-cost groups. The high-cost group (18-s time delay) spent more time when choosing to avoid danger than the low-cost group (4.5-s time delay). Linear mixed models were employed to investigate the group differences in avoidance generalization. The results revealed a significant effect of time cost on avoidance of the CS+ and the generalization stimuli that were most similar to it, with the high-cost group exhibiting lower avoidance rates than the low-cost group. These findings highlight time cost as an important contextual factor in fearful avoidance behavior and suggest potential implications for interventions development.

title: Systematic review and meta-analysis: the effectiveness of cognitive behavioral therapy and eye movement desensitization and reprocessing in children and adolescents
abstract:
ABSTRACT Background: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is prevalent among children and adolescents, with cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR) widely used treatment options. This study compared the effects of CBT and EMDR in children and adolescents using a meta-analysis approach. Methods: PubMed, EMBASE, CENTRAL, CINAHL, ProQuest Dissertations & Theses, and PsycInfo were searched in March 2025. Randomized controlled trials that compared the effectiveness of CBT and EMDR on PTSD symptoms in children and adolescents aged 6–18 years who had been exposed to traumatic events were included. The Cochrane Risk of Bias version 2 was used to assess the methodological quality of the included studies. A random-effects model was applied to calculate the standardized mean difference (SMD) along with 95% confidence interval (CI), and the I 2 statistic was used to quantify statistical heterogeneity. Results: Five trials (248 participants) were included. There was no statistically significant difference in PTSD symptoms between the CBT and EMDR groups, whether reported by children (SMD: 0.18; 95% CI: –0.07–0.43; I 2 = 0%) or by parents (SMD: 0.23; 95% CI: –0.02–0.48; I 2 = 0%). For anxiety, the pooled estimate did not reach statistical significance (SMD: 0.44; 95% CI: –0.19–1.07; I 2 = 69%). Depression symptoms were higher in the CBT group than in the EMDR group (SMD: 0.44; 95% CI: 0.13–0.76; I 2 = 0%). Conclusion: The comparative effects of CBT and EMDR in reducing PTSD and anxiety symptoms remain inconclusive. Although CBT was associated with higher depression symptoms compared with EMDR, the current evidence is based on a small number of trials, and the pooled estimates should be interpreted with caution.

HIGHLIGHTS This updated meta-analysis clarified the differential effects of cognitive behavioral therapy and eye movement desensitization and reprocessing on post-traumatic stress disorder and comorbid symptoms in children and adolescents. No statistically significant differences between CBT and EMDR were observed for child- or parent-reported PTSD symptoms or for anxiety symptoms. EMDR was associated with lower depression symptoms than CBT in children and adolescents.

List of abbreviations PTSD Post-traumatic stress disorder CBT Cognitive Behavioral Therapy EMDR Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing SMD Standardized mean differences 1. Background A substantial body of research indicates that children exposed to traumatic events are at increased risk of experiencing adverse emotional and psychological outcomes (Downey & Crummy, 2022 ; Tamir et al., 2025 ; Woolgar et al., 2022 ). Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder is highly prevalent among children and adolescents, with rates estimated at 25% and rising from 17% to 28% over the past five years (Tamir et al., 2025 ). Experiencing PTSD at a young age significantly disrupts emotional and cognitive development, often resulting in chronic functional impairment, increased susceptibility to comorbid psychiatric disorders, and a heightened risk of suicide (TT & MB, 2025 ). Psychological interventions are recommended as the first-line treatment for PTSD in children and adolescents (Torrico et al., 2026 ). Several psychological interventions have demonstrated effectiveness in reducing PTSD symptoms in this population. Among these, CBT and EMDR have consistently shown favorable treatment effects and are recommended in clinical practice guidelines (Gillies et al., 2016 ; Syros et al., 2022 ). An earlier meta-analysis found no statistically significant difference between CBT and EMDR in reducing PTSD symptoms (Gillies et al., 2016 ). In contrast, more recent network meta-analyses have suggested that CBT incorporating trauma exposure is among the most effective psychological interventions for reducing PTSD symptoms in children and adolescents (Alkærsig et al., 2026 ; Gkintoni et al., 2024 ; Hoppen et al., 2025 ). However, Alkærsig et al. ( 2026 ) emphasized the need for caution when interpreting these findings because the evidence base for CBT was substantially larger than that for EMDR. Another network meta-analysis comparing CBT and EMDR suggested that EMDR may be associated with greater effectiveness than CBT (Xie et al., 2024 ). In summary, CBT and EMDR are both effective and recommended treatments for PTSD in children and adolescents. However, their comparative effectiveness remains uncertain, underscoring the need for further high-quality studies that directly compare these two interventions. Children exposed to traumatic events frequently experience comorbid anxiety and depression in addition to PTSD. A recent study reported that 40.8% of trauma-exposed children developed PTSD symptoms, of whom 72.6% also experienced anxiety symptoms and 49.6%–74.4% experienced depressive symptoms (Lawrence-Sidebottom et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2022 ). Furthermore, post-traumatic anxiety was associated with an increased risk of subsequent depression (RR = 1 .20, 95% CI: 1.09–1.34) (Lawrence-Sidebottom et al., 2024 ). The presence of comorbid anxiety and depression may complicate clinical management and adversely affect treatment outcomes in children with PTSD symptoms. Psychological interventions for pediatric PTSD aim not only to reduce PTSD symptoms but also to improve common comorbid conditions, particularly anxiety and depression. Previous evidence from conventional meta-analysis suggested that CBT significantly reduced anxiety symptoms but showed no significant effect on depression, whereas EMDR did not demonstrate statistically significant effects on either anxiety or depression (Gillies et al., 2016 ). In contrast, subsequent meta-analyses reported that EMDR was associated with greater reductions in anxiety and depression than CBT in children, adolescents, and adults (Hudays et al., 2022 ; Khan et al., 2018 ). These inconsistent findings indicate that the comparative effects of CBT and EMDR on anxiety and depression remain inconclusive, highlighting the need for further evidence from direct comparative studies. Therefore, this systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to compare the effectiveness of CBT and EMDR for children and adolescents exposed to traumatic events. The primary outcome was PTSD symptom severity, while anxiety and depression were evaluated as secondary outcomes. Since CBT comprises several related treatment protocols used in clinical practice and evaluated in randomized controlled trials, the present review synthesized the available evidence by comparing EMDR with CBT interventions evaluated across eligible studies, rather than restricting the comparison to a single CBT protocol. To account for the clinical heterogeneity of CBT interventions, predefined subgroup analyses were conducted according to CBT therapeutic components. We hypothesized that CBT and EMDR would differ in their effectiveness in reducing PTSD symptoms, anxiety, and depression among children and adolescents exposed to traumatic events. 2. Methods We conducted this systematic review according to the Cochrane Collaboration guidelines for a systematic review of interventions (Higgins et al., 2024 ) and following the PRISMA 2020 statement (Page et al., 2021 ). The protocol of this study was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251013825). 2.1. Search strategies We searched PubMed, EMBASE, CENTRAL, CINAHL, ProQuest Dissertations & Theses, and PsycInfo from the inception of each database to March 2025. There were two main keywords for database searching, i.e. Adolescent . AND cognitive behavioral therapy, post-traumatic stress disorder. A complete list of search terms that were used in each database is presented in Appendix 1. Additionally, we scanned the references of trials that met the inclusion criteria for full-text review. We also conducted citation tracking to screen articles that cited the trials included in our study via Google Scholar. 2.2. Selection criteria Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included if they met the following criteria: (1) studied children or adolescents aged 6–18 years who were exposed to a traumatic event; (2) compared the effect of CBT and EMDR; and (3) reported any of the following outcomes: PTSD, anxiety, or depression symptoms. IM and AK independently screened the titles and abstracts of the search results to determine whether the studies assessed the effects of CBT and EMDR on PTSD symptoms. Full-text articles of potentially eligible studies were subsequently assessed independently by IM and AK. Disagreements were resolved through discussions between IM and AK. If disagreement persisted, TD was consulted to reach a consensus. 2.3. Data extraction IM and AK independently extracted data using a pre-specified data extraction form. Extracted data included study setting; participant characteristics (e.g. age, gender, type of traumatic event, baseline PTSD symptoms); study duration; and intervention details such as the number and duration of sessions. The outcomes of interest were PTSD symptoms (reported by either parents or children), as well as symptoms of anxiety and depression. All extracted data were verified for accuracy by TD. 2.4. Quality assessment IM and AK independently assessed the quality of the included RCTs using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool (Sterne et al., 2019 ). The risk of bias was categorized as high, some concerns, or low. Disagreements were resolved through discussion between IM and AK, with TD acting as the third reviewer to reach consensus. A web-application visualization tool (RobVis 10) was used to generate a traffic light plot summarizing the risk of bias for each RCT (McGuinness & Higgins, 2021 ). 2.5. Analysis We conducted a pairwise meta-analysis to estimate the standardized mean differences (SMD) and corresponding 95% confidence intervals (95% CI). The standardized mean differences were calculated in RevMan 5.4.1, which applies Hedges’ g for small-sample correction. A random-effects model, using the DerSimonian and Laird method, was employed for all analyses (DerSimonian & Laird, 1986 ). Heterogeneity was assessed primarily by considering clinical and methodological diversity across included trials, while the Chi-squared (Q) test and the I 2 value were reported as descriptive information only. Because the number of studies contributing to each comparison was small, both statistics are imprecise and the low I 2 value was not interpreted as evidence of homogeneity (Deeks et al., n.d. ). Time from treatment to outcome measurement, parent involvement in therapy, and components of CBT were used as criteria for subgroup analysis. However, subgroup analysis based on CBT components could only be conducted for one outcome, as intervention characteristics were largely similar across studies for the other outcomes. All analyses were performed using RevMan 5.4. 3. Results 3.1. Search results Out of 2119 articles identified from electronic database searches, six studies were initially selected based on title and abstract screening, with three of these meeting the inclusion criteria. The full list of studies excluded from the review is available in Appendix 2. Additionally, 767 studies were identified through citation tracking, of which two met the inclusion criteria. Consequently, a total of five studies (de Roos et al., 2011 ; de Roos et al., 2017 ; Diehle et al., 2015 ; Jaberghaderi et al., 2004 ; Jaberghaderi et al., 2019 ) were eligible for inclusion in this systematic review ( Figure 1 ), comprising 248 participants. 3.2. Study characteristics and details of interventions All included studies (de Roos et al., 2011 ; de Roos et al., 2017 ; Diehle et al., 2015 ; Jaberghaderi et al., 2004 ; Jaberghaderi et al., 2019 ) were open-label randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Of these, three (de Roos et al., 2011 ; de Roos et al., 2017 ; Diehle et al., 2015 ) were conducted in the Netherlands and two (Jaberghaderi et al., 2004 ; Jaberghaderi et al., 2019 ) in Iran. The duration of the studies ranged from 8 weeks to 3 months, with sample sizes varying from 7 to 43 participants. Across the studies, 26.61% of participants were male, and the mean age ranged from 10.00 to 13.41 years ( Table 1 ). The included studies (de Roos et al., 2011 ; de Roos et al., 2017 ; Diehle et al., 2015 ; Jaberghaderi et al., 2004 ; Jaberghaderi et al., 2019 ) investigated the effects of CBT compared with EMDR for treating PTSD in children and adolescents. CBT typically involved psychoeducation, trauma exposure, cognitive restructuring, and coping strategies. Sessions ranged from 4 to 12, lasting 45–227 minutes. EMDR followed Shapiro's standard protocol with age-appropriate modifications, including bilateral stimulation and positive closure, delivered over 4–12 sessions (45–140 minutes each). Therapists were licensed or EMDR-trained. Parental involvement varied. All interventions aimed to process trauma and reduce symptoms ( Table 2 ). 3.3. Quality of included studies According to Cochrane risk of bias assessment version 2.0, all studies (de Roos et al., 2011 ; de Roos et al., 2017 ; Diehle et al., 2015 ; Jaberghaderi et al., 2004 ; Jaberghaderi et al., 2019 ) were assessed as having some concerns regarding risk of bias ( Figure 2 ). This judgment reflects issues across multiple domains, including potential bias from the randomization process, deviations from the intended intervention, missing outcome data, and selective reporting of the results. 3.4. Effects on PTSD symptoms All five studies (de Roos et al., 2011 ; de Roos et al., 2017 ; Diehle et al., 2015 ; Jaberghaderi et al., 2004 ; Jaberghaderi et al., 2019 ) reported on PTSD symptoms, with assessments primarily conducted using self-report measures. In all studies, children assessed their own PTSD symptoms, while four studies also included parent-reported assessments. Regarding the timing of assessments, all five studies measured PTSD symptoms immediately after treatment; two studies conducted follow-up assessments at 3 months post-treatment, and only one study included a 12-month follow-up ( Figure 3 ). The pooled SMD of PTSD symptoms of CBT compared to EMDR was 0.18 (95%CI: –0.07–0.43), with no observed heterogeneity ( I 2 = 0 .0%) ( Figure 3 A). Similarly, for studies that reported parent-rated PTSD symptoms, the pooled SMD between CBT and EMDR was 0.23 (95% CI: -0.02–0.48), with no observed heterogeneity ( I 2 = 0.0%) ( Figure 3 B). The pooled analyses did not demonstrate a statistically significant difference between CBT and EMDR in reducing PTSD symptoms based on either child- or parent-reported measure. 3.5. title: Efficacy of technology-based psychosocial interventions on quality of life and psychological outcomes in adolescent and young adult survivors of childhood cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
abstract:
PURPOSE: Adolescent and young adult (AYA) survivors of childhood cancer remain at risk of psychological distress and reduced quality of life (QoL). We evaluated the efficacy of technology-based psychosocial interventions on QoL and psychological outcomes in this population.

METHODS: PubMed, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, PsycINFO, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published between 2015 and 2025. Outcomes were QoL, anxiety, depression, distress, and emotional well-being. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2. Standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled with random-effects models (RevMan Web); heterogeneity (I 2 ), subgroup analyses by assessment timing and leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were performed (PROSPERO: CRD420251248328).

RESULTS: Ten RCTs (747 participants) were included. Technology-based interventions were associated with a small but statistically significant improvement in overall QoL (SMD = 0.24, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.39, p = 0.001); the effect was not significant post-intervention but was small-to-moderate at 6-24-month follow-up (SMD = 0.36, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.60, p = 0.004). A small-to-moderate reduction in anxiety was observed (SMD = - 0.35, 95% CI - 0.65 to - 0.05, p = 0.02), whereas effects on depression (SMD = - 0.31), distress (SMD = - 0.04), and emotional well-being (SMD = 0.20) were not statistically significant.

CONCLUSION: Technology-based psychosocial interventions were associated with modest but statistically significant improvements in QoL and anxiety among AYA survivors of childhood cancer, with evidence of sustained benefits over time. Effects on broader psychological domains were more variable; larger, theory-driven trials with standardized outcomes are needed.

title: How Do Mindfulness-Based and Cognitive Behavioral Therapies Help Adults With Opioid-Treated Chronic Low Back Pain? A Qualitative Study
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic low back pain (CLBP) is common and often refractory to existing treatments, necessitating long-term opioid therapy, which has substantial risks. Mindfulness-based (MBT) and cognitive behavioral (CBT) therapies are safe and can be effective for CLBP.

AIMS: To better understand how MBT and CBT may help improve opioid-treated CLBP: METHODS: This qualitative study involved a subgroup of participants with opioid-treated CLBP who completed a 12-month randomized clinical trial comparing the effects of MBT versus CBT. Participants who reported improvements at 12 months, compared to baseline, in main outcomes (assessed with validated "quantitative" questionnaires) and experience with the study intervention, and who attended the intervention sessions were invited to in-depth exit interviews. The interviews achieved thematic saturation. Thematic analysis of transcribed interviews summarized qualitative findings.

RESULTS: Fifty participants (26 MBT, 24 CBT) were interviewed. They were, on average, 58.5 (SD = 10.0) years old. Most were female (60.0%), non-Hispanic (94.0%), and White (82.0%). At baseline, both groups were, on average, moderately-to-severely impacted by CLBP and treated with moderate-to-high daily opioid doses; at 12 months, they quantitatively reported improved pain, function and QoL scores and reduced daily opioid dose. In their qualitative responses, these participants corroborated the quantitative findings, reporting reductions in back pain (98.0% of interviewed participants), functional limitations (100.0%), and opioid dose (98.0%), with the majority attributing these changes to the study intervention they had received (98.0%, 94.0%, and 90.0%, respectively). Participants also reported the interventions helped them cope with emotional challenges and life stressors, and opioid-related adverse effects. Participants did not raise concerns about interventions' safety. Qualitative themes identified intervention-taught techniques participants most frequently used to manage their symptoms.

CONCLUSION: MBT and CBT can improve health and QoL and reduce opioid dose in adults with opioid-treated refractory CLBP, calling for improved access to these safe treatments.

title: Rehabilitative efficacy of cognitive behavioral therapy-based intervention for chronic fatigue syndrome: A systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) has been used for chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS), but previous studies have shown inconsistencies and divergent long-term outcomes. This study aims to assess the effectiveness of CBT in improving fatigue, physical functioning, and psychological health in patients with CFS.

METHODS: We searched PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library from their inception to March 2025. Studies designed as randomized controlled trials, enrolling patients diagnosed with CFS who received CBT as a treatment intervention delivered face-to-face, in groups, or online were included. The primary outcome was the fatigue score, and the secondary outcomes were the physical function score, psychological outcomes, and adverse events. The quality of the included studies was evaluated using the Cochrane Assessment Tool for Risk of Bias Version 2 (RoB 2; The Cochrane Collaboration). Heterogeneity was detected by subgroup analysis and sensitivity analysis.

RESULTS: Fifteen randomized controlled trials with 2270 participants were involved. Meta-analysis demonstrated that CBT yielded significant posttreatment improvements across key outcomes. Fatigue severity was notably reduced, as measured by the Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire (standardized mean difference [SMD] = -0.44, 95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.57--0.32) and the Checklist Individual Strength (SMD = -0.88, 95% CI: -1.16--0.60). Physical functioning (physical function subscale of the Short Form Health Survey-36) subscale also improved significantly (SMD = 0.32, 95% CI: 0.23-0.41). Psychological health benefits were evident through reduced Symptom Checklist 90 (SMD = -0.44, 95% CI: -0.62--0.26) and specific decreases in anxiety (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale-anxiety scale: SMD = -0.28, 95% CI: -0.46--0.10) and depression (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale-depression scale: SMD = -0.27, 95% CI: -0.45--0.09). Follow-up analyses confirmed sustained benefits: short-term (≤ 6 months) showed continued fatigue reduction (Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire: SMD = -0.29, 95% CI: -0.55--0.03) and improved physical function (physical function subscale of the Short Form Health Survey-36: SMD = 0.31, 95% CI: 0.03-0.58); long-term (6-24 months) maintained fatigue relief (SMD = -0.35, 95% CI: -0.50--0.19) and functional gains (SMD = 0.21, 95% CI: 0.06-0.37). Safety analysis showed no statistically significant difference in adverse event rates (odds ratio = 0.61, 95% CI: 0.36-1.01, P = .060).

CONCLUSION: Based on our results, CBT may be an effective option for CFS, but further research is warranted.

title: Do Children Who Develop Faster Go on to Age Faster in Midlife?
abstract: We quantified the association between rate of child development and pace of midlife aging in the Dunedin Study and the Add Health Study. Physical development was quantified in Dunedin participants ( N  = 1,037; age 45) using a composite comprised of (1) birth weight for gestational age, (2) toddler weight gain, (3) timing of behavioral milestones, (4) adiposity-rebound age, (5) timing of adolescent growth spurt, and (6) tempo of adolescent growth spurt. Social development was quantified using the Vineland Social Maturity Scale. Multi-organ-system (cardiovascular, metabolic, renal, immune, dental, pulmonary) longitudinal biological aging was used as the adult outcome. Fast physical development in childhood was associated with faster midlife aging. This was replicated in Add Health ( N  = 1,537; age range = 33-44 years), where girls who menstruated earlier had faster midlife aging. By contrast, faster social development in childhood was associated with slower midlife aging. Findings contribute initial empirical evidence characterizing the link between child-development rate and adult aging in humans.

title: Face-Matching Lineups: A Method to Control Mistaken Identifications in Video Evidence
abstract: When crime is caught on video, suspects can be identified by matching their faces to the perpetrator in the footage. However, errors in face-matching decisions have led to wrongful arrests. We tested face-matching in a nonprofessional student sample from a Canadian university ( N  = 905) with one-to-one comparisons and lineups. On the basis of findings in the eyewitness identification literature, we hypothesized that if face-matching lineups were fair and included known-innocent fillers (i.e., nonsuspects), they would control the error rate on trials with innocent suspects and increase the accuracy of suspect "match" responses. This hypothesis was supported. However, the accuracy of suspect-nonmatch responses was greater for one-to-one comparisons than for lineups. Additionally, we found that applying wisdom-of-crowd approaches to multiple independent decisions could eliminate errors in both match and nonmatch responses. Whether to control face-matching errors with lineups, with the wisdom-of-crowds, or with both depends on practical considerations.

title: Commentary on Alister et al. (2025): Individual Differences or Unsystematic Noise?
abstract: Alister et al. (2025) reported individual differences in the extent to which people find source-dependent and source-independent claims persuasive, but an exploratory analysis showed no discernible relationship between these individual differences and demographic variables such as age, education, politics, and social-media use. Here I show through simulations that the individual-difference patterns Alister et al. identified are largely consistent with random across-trial variation in the absence of underlying differences between individuals. This casts doubt on the strength of their evidence for individual differences and provides one plausible account of why their exploratory analyses did not yield systematic relationships.

title: Neural Representations of Perceptual Reorganization in the Musical Scale Illusion
abstract: The auditory system organizes complex acoustic input into coherent perceptual streams, yet how neural responses relate to physical stimulus structure and reported perception when the two diverge remains unclear. We investigated perceptual reorganization using the scale illusion, in which interleaved tone sequences presented separately to the two ears are typically heard as continuous melodic streams.Thirty participants listened to illusory, zigzag, and continuous sequences during EEG recording and reported whether each sequence sounded continuous or zigzag. Temporal response function models characterized neural encoding and reconstruction of amplitude-envelope (envelope) and pitch-change magnitude features. We tested whether neural responses during illusory listening corresponded more closely to reference patterns associated with the physical zigzag structure or reported continuous organization. Illusory sequences were predominantly categorized as Continuous and elicited longer RTs than non-illusory sequences. Encoding models revealed delayed pitch-change magnitude responses in the illusory condition, whereas envelope latencies remained comparatively stable. For pitch-change magnitude, reconstruction correlations computed over the full sequence exceeded chance levels estimated separately for each reference, with higher correlations for the continuous reference. Envelope correlations exceeded neither chance level, despite a small relative preference for the zigzag reference. These findings show that neural response timing and relative correspondence with the tested reference patterns depend on the modeled feature during the scale illusion. The reconstruction result concerns correlations across complete sequences and does not establish continuous tracking of the perceived melody.

title: Auditory Cues Guide Predictive Gaze Orienting during Navigation in Virtual Reality
abstract: Natural vision is an active, predictive process guided by expectations about when and where information will appear. Yet how gaze is shaped in dynamic, multisensory environments remains poorly understood. Using immersive virtual reality with eye tracking, we examined gaze behavior during naturalistic navigation. Participants cycled through a virtual city while avatar cyclists, first heard overtaking them from behind via spatialized auditory cues, later became visible as they passed. Auditory cues triggered anticipatory gaze shifts to expected locations, indicating that gaze allocation was guided by auditory predictions rather than reactive visual responses. Violations of auditory-spatial expectations elicited longer dwell time. Critically, removing auditory cues impaired predictive gaze orienting, delayed gaze orienting, and increased collisions with obstacles. These findings demonstrate that auditory input fundamentally shapes predictive models guiding visual exploration and adaptive behavior in dynamic environments, underscoring the multisensory basis of active perception in real-world interactions.

title: Flexibility of hierarchical reasoning across age and species
abstract: Hierarchical reasoning underlies complex abilities such as language, mathematics, and tool-use. In this study, we examined how hierarchical reasoning flexibly varies in adults across cultures, children, crows, and monkeys. We also tested hierarchical reasoning across varied task complexities and with stimuli from both visual-perceptual and semantic-conceptual relational domains. We conducted Bayesian modelling analyses with both previously published data (Ferrigno et al., 2020; Liao et al., 2022) and newly collected data. These data were cumulatively from US adults, Tsimane adults from an indigenous community at a field location in Bolivia, 3-to-6-year-old US children, rhesus monkeys, and carrion crows. We found evidence for hierarchical reasoning across age and species, though with much individual and cross-population variation. Adults exhibited the most consistent reliance on hierarchical mechanisms, while children and non-humans showed graded performance influenced by task complexity and stimulus type. In summary, the deployment of hierarchical mechanisms varies across contexts rather than operating as an all-or-none capability. These findings suggest that hierarchical reasoning may be a flexible ability-not necessarily unique to humans, but rather emerging through incremental increases in cognitive capacities across development and evolution.

title: Postural configurations as micro-ecological constraints: How embodied arrangements shape the emergence of bodily-visual communication
abstract: How do embodied configurations shape the emergence of communication? We investigated how bodily-visual communication develops under two interactional arrangements: standing-open and seated-at-table. Seventy dyads (140 participants) created novel speech-free signals for 32 meanings across three rounds of a referential communication task while their movements were recorded using high-resolution motion capture. Across both configurations, dyads showed robust efficiency dynamics: communicative success increased, movement path and volume decreased, articulatory specialisation intensified, and kinematic alignment between interlocutors increased. Configuration effects, however, were expressed most clearly in the movement-based measures rather than in communicative success. Success improved rapidly in both configurations, with only weak and transient evidence for an early standing-open advantage. By contrast, seated-at-table interaction promoted more compact movements and digital specialisation, whereas standing-open interaction involved larger movements and progressive brachiomanual specialisation. The pathways towards similar levels of alignment were also different: participants in the standing-open configuration converged in a linear fashion, whereas seated-at-table dyads converged rapidly by mid-experiment, then relaxed to the level ultimately reached in the standing-open configuration. These findings suggest that embodied arrangements do not primarily determine whether communication becomes successful, but they do shape how communicative efficiency is realised in bodily movement.

title: Cognitive predictors of narrative retelling in early childhood
abstract: This study examined the associations between inhibitory control, working memory, inductive reasoning, awareness, and children's narrative retelling abilities in early childhood. A total of 212 children aged 4-7 years participated in the study. Executive functions were assessed through measures of verbal and visuospatial working memory and inhibitory control, inductive reasoning was assessed using a Raven-like matrix task, and awareness was assessed through perceptual and inferential awareness tasks. Narrative retelling was evaluated using a story retelling task that captured multiple aspects of narrative performance. Correlational analyses indicated moderate associations between inhibitory control, working memory, and several narrative retelling indicators. Narrative retelling performance also increased significantly with age, indicating clear developmental gains from the preschool to the early school years. Structural equation modeling further showed that inhibitory control and verbal working memory were significant predictors of the latent narrative retelling construct, whereas visuospatial working memory and inductive reasoning were not significantly associated with narrative retelling. Awareness showed small but significant associations with certain narrative retelling indicators.

title: Evaluating age-related differences in motor imagery in children aged 5 to 8: feasibility and task-specific modulation
abstract: Motor imagery (MI), the mental simulation of movement without execution, provides a behavioural tool to evaluate sensorimotor representations. However, its characterisation in young children remains debated. This study investigated age-related differences in MI across early primary school years using a multi-task battery. One hundred and eighteen children aged 5-8 years (61 females), spanning the final year of kindergarten (GSM), first grade (CP), second grade (CE1), and third grade (CE2), completed executed and imagined trials of five functional tasks (standing up, typical gait, precision gait, drawing, and cube handling). Psychometric properties of the battery were evaluated. To ensure feasibility, engagement with imagery tasks was verified by comparing executed-imagined consistency in complexity-duration structure (i.e., complex tasks take longer both when executed and when imagined). Age-related differences were evaluated in terms of execution-imagery isochrony and variability across classes. Internal consistency was excellent (α = .91-.98) and test-retest reliability ranged from moderate to excellent (ICC = .68-.92). Engagement increased by age but already exceeded 70 % in the youngest group. Isochrony improved with age for simpler, highly practised tasks (typical gait, standing up), whereas more complex tasks (precision gait, cube handling) showed stable performance across classes. Variability decreased with age, and older children's performance became increasingly influenced by task complexity demands. Findings demonstrate that mental chronometry can reliably capture MI abilities in children as young as five, revealing both developmental gains and task-specific constraints. These results highlight the feasibility of MI assessment in early childhood, warranting the need for longitudinal neuroimaging approaches to clarify mechanistic insights.

title: The Precision Hierarchy Hypothesis: A Unifying Framework to Explain Opposing Serial Effects
abstract: Serial dependence, the phenomenon where current perception is biased toward the previous stimulus, has been interpreted as a mechanism for perceptual stability, smoothing variability in sensory input. However, analyses that include both the previous stimulus and previous response unmasked repulsive effects at the sensory level that were otherwise concealed. Moreover, attractive serial biases fail to scale with environmental correlations, challenging their primary role in maintaining stability. We propose the "precision hierarchy hypothesis," grounded in predictive processing, as a unifying framework for these seemingly contradictory findings. Repulsive effects naturally emerge when priors-shaped by recent trials-are highly precise, making small deviations in incoming input more probable under alternative priors. We further propose that prior precision decreases across hierarchical levels. A higher precision at lower sensory levels leads to repulsive effects, as even small deviations in incoming signal are in conflict with the prior. In contrast, attractive biases emerge at higher, more abstract levels, where deviations are integrated with broader conceptual priors. By dynamically shaping prior precision according to environmental correlations, perception remains adaptive, balancing the need for stability with the sensitivity to detect meaningful changes in the environment. This framework reconciles diverse findings on serial effects and provides testable predictions for future research.

title: Independent regulation of cognitive stability and flexibility in both intra-task and inter-task contexts among children
abstract: Stability and flexibility are essential components of cognitive control, critical for goal-directed behavior and adaptability, particularly in children. However, the relationship between them is debated; traditional unidimensional models suggest a trade-off relationship, while recent studies propose a two-dimensional perspective emphasizing their independence. Previous research mostly focused on adults, overlooking the rapid development of stability and flexibility in children. The current study recruited 38 adults and 73 healthy children aged 9-10 years to investigate the relationship between stability and flexibility in both intra-task (Experiments 1 and 2) and inter-task (Experiment 3) contexts. Experiments 1 and 2 utilized a rule-switching task with stimulus-response consistency manipulation: switch costs measured flexibility, while the consistency effect assessed stability. Both results of Experiments 1 and 2 supported a two-dimensional model for cognitive stability and flexibility in the intra-task context. Experiment 3 employed the color-word Stroop task to measure cognitive stability (congruency effect), and an inter-task correlational analysis was conducted with the switch costs (flexibility indicator) from Experiment 2. The findings revealed no significant correlation between the Stroop congruency effect and rule-switching costs, indicating independence between stability and flexibility in different task contexts, further supporting the two-dimensional model in the inter-task context. In conclusion, this study supports the independence of cognitive stability and flexibility during middle childhood, demonstrating their ability to coexist at high levels based on task demands. These insights deepen our understanding of cognitive control in children and provide a theoretical foundation for offering developmental guidance and developing effective cognitive training programs.

title: Aversive learning retroactively modulates neutral episodic memories structured by prior knowledge of predictive sequences
abstract: Linking memories of temporally separated neutral and threatening experiences can support later recognition of early warning signals. Yet it remains unclear what cognitive processes might allow the seemingly inconsequential neutral events - encoded in safe contexts and thus prone to forgetting - to nevertheless be preserved in memory well enough to inform future threat predictions. Here, we tested whether Pavlovian threat conditioning retroactively strengthens long-term episodic memory for previously encoded neutral events by leveraging prior knowledge of their predictive relations. Young adults first learned to anticipate the order of semantic categories in two deterministic sequences (A → B → C and D → E → F) through repeated presentation of images depicting category exemplars. They then incidentally encoded trial-unique exemplars from each category during sequence viewing. In a next phase, exemplars from the third-position categories were repeated such that one (C) predicted mild electric shocks, whereas the other (F) was never reinforced, creating a category-level threat association through conditioning. After 24 h, recognition memory for exemplars of categories encoded before conditioning depended on sequence and position: when a sequence ended with a shock-predictive category, memory favored the starting category (A) over the following category (B) - an effect absent in the control categories (D and E). These results suggest that aversive learning can retroactively reshape episodic memories of neutral events when they are scaffolded by prior sequence knowledge, bridging temporal gaps and thereby potentially promoting early threat anticipation.

title: When "they" is singular: The interplay between cognitive and social factors predicts pronoun misinterpretations in bilingual English speakers
abstract: Language change is shaped by cognitive biases as well as by sociolinguistic perceptions of linguistic innovation. Although the use of they as a singular pronoun to refer to a generic referent is not new in English (e.g., "An employee can file a complaint if they need to"), a recent innovation extends this usage to refer to known individuals of non-binary gender. This type of socially motivated language change allows speakers to position themselves relative to linguistic innovation. Using the self-paced reading paradigm, we examined the processing of non-binary singular they across unambiguous (one-referent) and temporarily ambiguous (two-referent) contexts. We report on a processing experiment with second-language English speakers from Spain who, by virtue of their bilingual experience, are skilled at language learning and regulating activation of competing representations through cognitive control. We investigate how variability in the adoption of the pronominal innovation is influenced by sociodemographic and cognitive factors. We find that seemingly at-chance group-level performance in resolving temporary ambiguities is the product of bimodal distributions in interpretation within the population. Lingering misinterpretations in some speakers are predicted by a combination of sociodemographic and cognitive factors. Critically, we find that even among participants willing to adopt non-binary language, accurate interpretation of the non-binary singular they is mediated by cognitive resources. The findings bear implications for accounts of language change and the adoption of non-binary pronouns in bilingual communities as a result of individual variability. We outline a proposal for a conceptual Integrated Model of Adaptation to Grammar In Evolution ("IMAGINE").

title: Do smiling faces change children's minds? Testing evaluative conditioning in 3-6‑year‑olds
abstract: This study examined whether preschoolers form preferences for shapes paired with happy or sad faces (evaluative conditioning) and whether the effect varies with age or with the number of different faces paired with each shape. Sixty-one children aged 3-6 years viewed four neutral shapes during a brief conditioning movie. Each shape was assigned to one of four conditions, in which it was paired with a single happy face, a single sad face, five different happy faces, or five different sad faces. Shape preferences were measured before and after the movie, along with memory for the pairings. Children showed clear pre-existing preferences for some shapes, and the pattern differed by age. After accounting for these starting preferences, two additive advantages emerged (for positive over negative faces and for multiple over single faces) and their combination in the shape paired with multiple smiling faces was the only condition to produce a reliable shift from zero. The other three conditions did not produce reliable change, and children's exact age and memory for the pairings did not predict change. These findings suggest that evaluative conditioning in preschoolers is more selective than typically assumed, with the number of different faces paired with a shape emerging as a key factor. The results also highlight the importance of accounting for children's pre-existing preferences when measuring acquired evaluative learning.

title: Disparities in Autism Spectrum Disorder and Perinatal Risk Factors
abstract:
Key Points Question When financial barriers to care are minimal, do disparities in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) diagnosis by socioeconomic and immigration characteristics persist, and do known perinatal risk factors for ASD show similar gradients that may help explain these disparities? Findings In this population-based cohort study of 2.3 million children born in Ontario, Canada, between 2002 and 2020, ASD incidence was highest among children from the most socioeconomically deprived, lowest-income neighborhoods and born to immigrant mothers, and these disparities widened over time. Children in socioeconomically deprived areas were more frequently exposed to maternal diabetes in utero, severe pregnancy complications, and prematurity, with disparities in maternal diabetes worsening over time. Meaning In a universal health care setting, ASD diagnosis was more common among children from disadvantaged and immigrant families, with disparities worsening over time; similar social gradients in perinatal risk factors suggest a potential contribution that warrants direct quantification.

This cohort study examines temporal trends in autism spectrum disorder diagnosis and in perinatal factors associated with risk of autism spectrum disorder across maternal socioeconomic and immigration factors.

Importance In universal health care settings, trends in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) diagnosis remain poorly characterized, yet are critical for identifying inequities that persist despite more equitable health care access. Objective To describe temporal trends in ASD diagnosis and in perinatal risk factors for ASD across maternal socioeconomic and immigration factors. Design, Setting, and Participants This is a population-based retrospective cohort study of children born in Ontario, Canada (2002-2020), linked to maternal health, immigration, and census data. Children were followed up from age 1 year until ASD diagnosis, death, out-migration, or April 2020. Data analysis was performed between August 2024 and March 2026. Exposures Maternal socioeconomic indicators (area-level deprivation, ethnic diversity, income, Ontario Drug Benefit enrollment, and rural vs urban residence) and immigration characteristics (immigration status, category, time since immigration, region of origin, and country income level). Perinatal risk factors included maternal diabetes, maternal age 35 years or older, severe maternal morbidity, and prematurity. Main Outcomes and Measures ASD was identified using a validated administrative algorithm. Incidence rates were calculated per 10 000 person-years and cumulative incidence per 1000 live births at 8 years. Temporal trends were estimated using negative binomial regression with interaction terms between birth year and covariates. Results Of 2 319 302 children (1 188 270 male [51.2%]), 29 374 (1.3%) met ASD criteria, with 80.0% (23 068 children) receiving a diagnosis by age 8 years and 78.5% of cases (23 071 cases) occurring in male children. Diagnosis increased by 10% per birth cohort (95% CI, 10%-11%). Disparities in ASD diagnosis by socioeconomic and immigration characteristics widened across birth cohorts: by the 2012 birth cohort, diagnosis was 2.2-fold (95% CI, 2.0-2.4–fold) higher in the most vs least deprived neighborhoods, 2.0-fold (95% CI, 1.8-2.2–fold) higher in the most vs least ethnically diverse areas, and lower in rural vs urban regions. Diagnosis was 1.4-fold (95% CI, 1.3-1.5–fold) higher among children of immigrant mothers, with the highest rates among mothers from low- and middle-income regions. Diabetes during pregnancy, severe maternal morbidity, and prematurity were more common in marginalized populations, with disparities in maternal diabetes widening over time. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of more than 2.3 million mother-child pairs, ASD diagnoses occurred disproportionately among children from socioeconomically disadvantaged and immigrant families, with disparities widening over time. The higher prevalence of maternal diabetes, obstetric complications, and prematurity in these populations may have contributed to these differences.

Introduction With prevalence increasing globally, autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has become a major public health concern, underscoring the need to understand its risk factors and ensure equitable access to diagnosis and care. 1 Until recently, US surveillance data had consistently found higher ASD prevalence among White and high-income children, 1 , 2 a pattern attributed to underdiagnosis in marginalized groups owing to financial barriers, clinician bias, and limited culturally appropriate screening. 1 , 3 , 4 , 5 However, more recent data show a reversal, with higher prevalence among Black, Hispanic, and Asian or Pacific Islander children than White children. 6 Changes in diagnostic criteria, coding practices, and surveillance methods may contribute to these shifts, illustrating how observed social disparities in ASD prevalence are shaped by evolving patterns of identification and reinforcing the need for ongoing surveillance. 6 Higher ASD incidence among marginalized communities is not unique to the US; European studies of children in the 1990s and early 2000s similarly documented higher rates among immigrant families and those with low socioeconomic status. 7 , 8 , 9 These studies suggested that disadvantaged groups may face disproportionate exposure to prenatal risk factors for ASD. Prenatal conditions, such as maternal diabetes, advanced maternal age, and hypertensive disorders, have been consistently associated with increased ASD risk. 10 , 11 , 12 Despite this, few studies have explicitly assessed whether the distribution of these prenatal exposures aligns with disparities in ASD. Studying ASD disparities within universal health care systems offers an opportunity to assess inequities that emerge independently of access-related barriers, yet contemporary longitudinal data are scarce. Whether the elevated incidence observed in European settings 2 decades ago has persisted or changed remains unclear. In Canada—where health care access is relatively equitable—existing evidence is limited to a few cross-sectional studies and lacks population-based longitudinal assessments of socioeconomic and immigration patterns. 13 , 14 This descriptive study addresses this gap by evaluating 2 decades of ASD diagnoses in Ontario, Canada, across maternal socioeconomic and immigration groups, and by describing trends in key perinatal risk factors for ASD to explore potential mechanisms underlying observed disparities. Methods Data Source and Participants Data for this retrospective birth cohort study were created by linking 10 existing databases at the Institute of Clinical Evaluative Sciences (ICES), a nonprofit organization that compiles data obtained from the routine administration of Ontario’s publicly funded health care system. 15 The cohort comprises records of all in-hospital deliveries in Ontario spanning from 2002 to 2020 linked to corresponding pregnancy, health, immigration, and census records of the mother with 98% completeness (eTable 1 in Supplement 1 ). This study followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology ( STROBE ) reporting guidelines for cohort studies and was approved by the Research Ethics Board at McGill University, which waived the requirement for informed consent because deidentified administrative data were used. Eligible participants included children born in Ontario between 2002 and 2019 with follow-up extending until April 2020. A minimum follow-up period of 1 year was required on the basis of evidence indicating that ASD can only be reliably diagnosed by age 1 year. 16 , 17 , 18 Stillbirths and births less than 21 + 0 weeks’ or more than 43 + 0 weeks’ gestation were excluded. 19 Follow-up ended for all participants in 2020, age 18 years, emigration from Ontario, or death. Outcomes ASD was defined as (1) 3 or more physician billing diagnoses ( International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision [ICD-10] codes F84.0-F84.5) within 3 years or (2) a single diagnosis in hospital discharge, emergency department, or outpatient surgery records. This definition was based on a validation study using the same ICES administrative data, which reported sensitivity of 50% and positive predictive value of 56.6%. 20 We prioritized multiple diagnoses across sources to reduce false-positives and increase specificity. 21 Although this approach underidentifies true cases, broader definitions (eg, a single diagnosis) increase false-positives and may attenuate associations toward the null. 22 Maternal Socioeconomic and Immigration Characteristics The primary exposures were maternal socioeconomic and immigration characteristics. Maternal socioeconomic characteristics included residence (urban vs rural) based on postal code at the time of the child’s birth, enrollment in the Ontario Drug Benefit program (yes or no) since 1992, and neighborhood-level indices of marginalization. The Ontario Drug Benefit is a provincial program that provides coverage for prescription medications for youths younger than 25 years without private insurance, seniors (aged ≥65 years), social assistance recipients, long-term care residents, and individuals with high drug costs relative to income. 23 Neighborhood-level measures were derived from the Ontario Marginalization Index and included material deprivation quintiles (Q1-Q5, with Q5 indicating the highest deprivation), ethnic group concentration quintiles (Q1-Q5, with Q5 indicating the highest concentration of recent immigrants and/or visible minority groups), and income quintiles (Q1-Q5, with Q5 indicating the highest average income). These indices were calculated at the level of dissemination areas (geographic regions of 400-700 people) based on Canadian census data. 24 Immigration characteristics included maternal immigration status (yes or no), based on records from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada for arrivals to Ontario beginning in 1985. Among immigrant mothers, we examined immigration category (economic class, sponsored family class, resettled refugee and protected person, and other), time since immigration at the time of delivery (0-10 years vs >10 years), region of origin, and the income level of the mother’s country of origin based on the 2006 World Bank classification (low-, middle-, and high-income countries). 25 Although some of these variables may also reflect elements of socioeconomic context, they were grouped under immigration characteristics to capture the distinct structural, temporal, and policy-related dimensions of migration. 26 Perinatal Risk Factors for ASD We extracted early-life exposures associated with an increased risk of ASD, including in-utero exposure to maternal diabetes (type 1, type 2, or gestational diabetes), 11 advanced maternal age at birth (≥35 years), 27 severe maternal morbidity, 10 , 28 and prematurity (gestational age <37 weeks). 29 Maternal diabetes was identified using the Ontario Diabetes Database ( International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision code 250; ICD-10 codes E10-E14; look-back to 1991) 30 and gestational diabetes from delivery records ( ICD-10 code O24.4). Severe maternal morbidity includes life-threatening conditions from pregnancy to 6 weeks post partum, identified using the 2018 Canadian Perinatal Surveillance System ICD-10 codes (eTable 2 in Supplement 1 ). 31 These severe maternal complications may impair fetal neurodevelopment via hypoxia and inflammation, may also act as markers of overall maternal health during and shortly after pregnancy, and may be associated with adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes in children. 10 , 28 Statistical Analysis We calculated the number, incidence rate, and cumulative incidence of ASD overall and by maternal socioeconomic and immigration factors. Incidence rates (cases per 10 000 person-years) and corresponding 95% CIs were estimated using the exact Poisson method. 32 Statistical significance was defined as a 95% CI that did not include the null value. Person-years accounted for variation in follow-up time across birth years. Cumulative incidence per 1000 live births was estimated for children with 8 years of follow-up (2002-2012 birth cohorts) using the exact binomial method 32 to provide a more interpretable measure of ASD occurrence. For temporal trends, we estimated the cumulative incidence of ASD by age 8 years for children born between 2002 and 2012, overall and stratified by maternal socioeconomic and immigration characteristics. Each child was followed-up from age 1 year to ASD diagnosis or age 8 years, capturing approximately 80% of cases (eTable 3 in Supplement 1 ). 33 Children born after 2012 were excluded because of administrative data ending in 2020, yielding less than 8 years of follow-up for 2013 to 2020 births. Negative binomial regression was used to estimate ASD incidence by birth cohort across socioeconomic and immigration characteristics, with the log of live births in each birth cohort used as an offset. We fit unadjusted and adjusted models for each maternal characteristic. Unadjusted models included birth year, the covariate of interest, and a birth year–covariate interaction to allow nonparallel log-linear trends. Adjusted models were additionally stratified by maternal age (<35 vs ≥35 years), maternal immigration status (Canadian-born vs migrant; excluded from immigration analyses), and child sex (female vs male). Multivariable analyses were conducted to quantify relative differences by social factors in temporal trends across population subgroups and to provide additional insight into factors potentially contributing to the observed trends. To contextualize findings internationally, we estimated crude prevalence at age 8 years for 2010 to 2020 using negative binomial regression, with projections to 2025. For perinatal factors, we reported the number and proportion of children exposed to perinatal risk factors. We then used binomial regression to estimate the proportion of children exposed to in-utero risk factors per birth cohort (2002-2012), again using an interaction term between birth cohort and covariates to capture nonparallel log-linear trends. Exponentiated model-based proportions were plotted to visualize changes across socioeconomic and immigration strata. Data analyses were performed between August 2024 and March 2026 using R statistical software version 2.0.3 (R Project for Statistical Computing), with the MASS package used to run statistical analyses.
