title: 'Navigating the ride': stakeholder perspectives on public transportation challenges for children with autism in India
abstract:
Abstract Objective To explore the perspectives of primary caregivers, healthcare professionals and transport personnel regarding the challenges associated with public transportation for children with autism spectrum disorder in India. Design This study applied a descriptive phenomenological qualitative design. Setting The study was conducted at a tertiary care teaching centre in South India. Participants 21 participants comprising nine primary caregivers of children with autism spectrum disorder, six healthcare professionals and six transport personnel were recruited using purposive maximum variability sampling. Methods In-depth interviews were conducted with the participants and audio-recorded for transcription. The transcripts were manually coded and analysed using Systematic Text Condensation. Results The results demonstrate that public transport is a complex social ecosystem comprising the child, caregivers, co-passengers and transport personnel. Healthcare professionals and policymakers, while not directly involved in travel, also influence the experience. Three major themes were identified: challenges associated with public transport, facilitators for better travel experiences and stakeholder recommendations for improving travel experiences. Conclusions This study identified key barriers to accessing public transport for children with autism spectrum disorder and their families. Facilitators and potential strategies to address travel-related challenges are also discussed. These findings provide insights into stakeholder perspectives that may inform efforts to improve accessibility and travel experiences on public transport for children.

STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDY This qualitative study included primary caregivers, healthcare professionals and transport personnel, who provided perspectives on different aspects of public transportation for children with autism spectrum disorder. The findings provide insights into barriers to public transportation from individual, familial, societal and healthcare perspectives. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the few qualitative studies from the Global South to explore public transportation for children with autism spectrum disorder and their families. Children with autism spectrum disorder were not interviewed or directly observed; therefore, their experiences of public transportation were represented through adult stakeholder accounts and may not fully reflect their own perspectives. The study did not include government personnel responsible for transport policies, whose perspectives could have provided additional insights into policy-related barriers and potential solutions. Introduction Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is characterised by persistent difficulties in initiating and sustaining reciprocal social interaction and social communication, and by a range of restricted, repetitive, inflexible patterns of behaviour, interests or activities that are clearly atypical or excessive for the individual’s age and sociocultural context. 1 ASD affects 1 in 78 children globally, with a prevalence of 1 in 68 children in India. 2 3 Crucial areas of personal, family, social, educational and occupational functioning are hindered. 1 The increase in the number of individuals identified with ASD signifies a corresponding increase in the necessity to address their unique requirements. Meeting these diverse needs requires a comprehensive understanding of the contextual factors influencing participation and outcomes. Public transportation is a critical component of Indian cities, as it provides mobility for two-thirds of Indian households that do not possess a personal vehicle. 4 Individuals with disabilities who live in rural regions face key challenges related to accessibility, availability and affordability of rehabilitation services. 5 Individuals with disabilities experience various barriers to using public transportation, including physical and social challenges, such as the absence of ramps, long walking distances, extended waiting times, insufficient information at bus stops or stations and negative attitudes from drivers. 6 This might especially be challenging for individuals with ASD who rely on public transport for their mobility needs. 7 Most parents of children with ASD experience difficulties while travelling. 8 Safety and spatial awareness are significant concerns for individuals with ASD and their families when using public transport. 9 Unexpected situations and sensory sensitivities may pose additional challenges during travel, leading to the exhibition of externalising behaviours during travel, which might pose potential danger to self and others. 10 However, the difficulties experienced by children with ASD and their families while using public transportation, such as the public bus systems, have not been extensively examined. 7 India’s Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act (RPWD) (Government of India, 2016) assures accessibility and access to safe transport for persons with disabilities. There are also provisions for travel-related incentives, concessions, assistance for mobility and modifications of vehicles. 11 However, the UNICEF, 2022 Disability Inclusion Policy and Strategy 2022–2030 identifies gaps in services and systemic support for people with disability, which may contribute to social isolation, poverty and affect community participation. 12 These provisions and gaps highlight the importance of understanding how public transportation is experienced in everyday life by children with ASD and their families. In summary, while research on public transportation experiences among children with ASD and their families in India is limited, the available literature indicates challenges across several domains. 7 – 10 Hence, this study aimed to explore the perspectives of primary caregivers, healthcare professionals and transport personnel regarding public transportation for children with ASD and their families in India. Specifically, we aimed to understand the perceived barriers and facilitators to accessing and using public transportation, as well as the strategies and recommendations described by participants to address these challenges. For this study, ‘public transport’ was operationalised as either formal, mass transit networks such as buses, trains or aeroplanes or privately operated para-transit networks like shared auto-rickshaws or taxis. Material and methods Study design We used a qualitative study design based on descriptive phenomenological analysis. The phenomenon of interest was the challenges for children with ASD to access public transport. While direct engagement with children would be the best way to understand their experiences, this would require individualised methodological and ethical adaptations. Hence, it was decided to include caregivers, transport personnel and healthcare professionals, not as distinct stakeholder groups, but as persons who share different aspects of the experience, based on the concept of intersubjectivity. The Systematic Text Condensation (STC) strategy was chosen for analysis as it is highly structured and could be easily used to synthesise data from different stakeholder groups. 13 Its descriptive focus would help present the exact stakeholder experiences, while the condensation phase would facilitate consolidation of the shared experience. Study setting The research was conducted in a tertiary care teaching centre in South India. The data were collected from two outpatient paediatric service settings and one inpatient paediatric service setting at the centre between June 2024 and February 2025. These units follow a family-centred, multidisciplinary care model with child psychiatrists, developmental paediatricians, nurses, occupational therapists, psychologists and speech therapists as the team. Participants This study used purposive, maximum variability sampling to recruit participants. We recruited nine caregivers of children aged 10 years or younger who had been diagnosed with ASD and had used public transportation. We excluded caregivers of children who had difficulties with motor skills. Maximum variability was considered by recruiting participants who varied in gender, age, relationship to child, socioeconomic status, educational status and employment status. Six healthcare professionals involved in the treatment of children with ASD and with at least 2 years of experience working with this population were also interviewed. Variability in sampling was sought by including participants from different healthcare disciplines and with varying years of experience in paediatric care. Additionally, six transport personnel who had been associated with public transport for a minimum of 6 months were interviewed. Heterogeneity was considered by including public transport personnel from mass transit networks as well as para-transit networks across geographical regions of India. Of the 21 participants invited to take part in this study, all agreed to participate and provided written informed consent. Data collection In total, 21 interviews were conducted, including two telephonic interviews, with participants who consented but were unable to attend in person. All the interviews were conducted by the primary author. The interviews were conducted in the participants’ preferred language: Tamil, Hindi, Malayalam or English. The interviews with the caregivers and healthcare professionals were conducted in a therapy room at the study setting with only the interviewer and participant present. The interviews with transport personnel were conducted in a private area next to their workplaces. Separate interview guides were developed for caregivers, transport personnel and healthcare professionals and were translated into the relevant languages ( online supplemental material ). The questions were finalised after discussion with senior colleagues who served as a critical reference group. The interview guides had open-ended questions, with additional probing used where required. The average duration of the interviews was 40 minutes and they were audio-recorded. The interviews were transcribed and translated into English digitally using a Microsoft Word processor by the interviewer. Given the relatively narrow study questions and the specific, direct experience of the stakeholder groups, the authors considered the information power to be sufficient when no new narratives seemed forthcoming. Reflexivity All three authors are occupational therapists based in the psychiatry unit of the tertiary care teaching centre. This unit caters to clients across the life-span, providing both in-patient and out-patient rehabilitative services, following a family-centred, multidisciplinary care model. The first author was a final-year undergraduate at the time of the study. Basic concepts of research methodology and the requirement to do a research study are included as part of the undergraduate occupational therapy curriculum in India. The second and third authors have more than 20 years of clinical and teaching experience and are trained in qualitative research and evidence synthesis. All three authors have hands-on clinical experience with caregivers of children with special needs who reported difficulties accessing healthcare because of transportation-related challenges. These experiences prompted the first author to approach the other authors to develop a study. The first author received constant guidance and supervision from the other authors throughout the duration of the study. To deal with possible bias during data collection and analysis, bracketing was employed through discussing aspects of data that elicited strong emotional reactions. Independent coding was followed by consensus discussions to minimise subjective individual biases. Data analysis Data were analysed using the STC strategy, which prescribes analytic reduction with specified shifts between decontextualisation and recontextualisation of data, involving four steps of (1) total impression, (2) identifying and sorting meaning units, (3) condensation and (4) synthesising. In the first step, the first two authors read the transcripts independently and discussed preliminary themes with the third author (eg, problems faced by caregivers in using public transport). The third author cross-checked the transcripts with the audio files. In the second step, the first two authors independently conducted line-by-line coding to identify text fragments containing meaning units and sorted them into code groups (eg, child-related, systemic, societal barriers faced by caregivers). These codes were discussed with the third author and subsequently, the authors proceeded to condense the data across stakeholder groups. In the final step, the authors synthesised the data to outline the multiple aspects of the children’s experience of public transport. This process was repeated after every few interviews, with the authors engaging in multiple rounds of discussion and constantly comparing the synthesised data with the original transcripts. Quality assurance The quality of the analysis was guided by employing the strategies suggested by Morse et al . 14 Investigator responsiveness was maintained through the authors’ ongoing analysis of data from the initial interviews and inductive use of emerging findings to inform subsequent interviews. Methodological coherence was maintained by aligning the research question, sampling methods, data analysis and interpretation. Ensuring sampling adequacy and appropriateness, and iterative analysis of data were also performed as verification strategies. Patient and public involvement Although children were not directly involved in the study, our participants included the caregivers, who were responsible for supporting their community mobility. Transport personnel involved in providing the commute were also included to provide their perspectives. Results The details of the participants are given in table 1 . The results have been presented as three major themes: challenges associated with public transport, facilitators for better travel experiences and recommendations from stakeholders for better travel experiences. title: Cerebral Lateralization for Language as a Potential Biomarker for the Broad Autism Phenotype: A Functional Transcranial Doppler Ultrasonography Investigation
abstract:
ABSTRACT Introduction Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is associated with language deficits, while growing evidence suggests that atypical cerebral lateralization for language could serve as a potential neural marker for ASD. The present study seeks to investigate cerebral lateralization for language not only in terms of ASD, but also as a potential biomarker for the broad autism phenotype (BAP)—a sum of subclinical traits similar to those of ASD. BAP is often observed in family members of individuals with ASD, and encompasses personality, linguistic, social, communicative, and behavioral challenges that fall short of the diagnostic threshold for ASD. We hypothesize that individuals with ASD will show atypical patterns of cerebral lateralization for language relative to neurotypical controls, with individuals exhibiting BAP characteristics expected to fall between these two groups. Methods To test this hypothesis, neurophysiological and behavioral assessments of cerebral lateralization for language, alongside cerebral lateralization of visuospatial functions—to confirm that the expected differences are specific to language lateralization—will be performed in at least 26 children and adults with high‐functioning ASD, 26 BAP‐positive siblings (BAP group), and 26 neurotypical controls. Behavioral lateralization, namely handedness, will be assessed through neuropsychological tools, while cerebral lateralization will be measured utilizing functional transcranial Doppler ultrasonography (fTCD), a validated and reliable tool specialized for cerebral lateralization assessment. Results This is a Stage‐1 registered report; therefore, no results are available at this time point. Conclusion Findings are expected to inform improved understanding and, potentially, early identification and screening for both ASD and BAP.

1 Introduction Across large‐scale studies, reviews, and meta‐analyses, atypical cerebral lateralization for language processing—that is reduced leftward, and/or rightward language dominance, compared to the general population—has frequently been identified as a structural and functional characteristic of autism spectrum disorder (ASD; Eyler et al. 2012 ; Kleinhans et al. 2008 ; for reviews, see Lindell and Hudry 2013 ; Ocklenburg et al. 2024 ; for meta‐analyses, see Herringshaw et al. 2016 ; Li et al. 2023 ). Indeed, it has been suggested that atypical language lateralization may represent a potential neurophysiological marker of ASD (Herringshaw et al. 2016 ; Jouravlev et al. 2020 ). Yet, these findings have rarely been extended to individuals exhibiting the broad autism phenotype (BAP)—a constellation of subclinical traits that mirror core features of ASD in attenuated form and are often observed in first‐degree relatives of individuals with autism (De Groot and Van Strien 2017 ; Hurley et al. 2007 ; Piven 1999 ). This gap in the literature persists despite substantial evidence that subclinical autistic traits may share underlying neurocognitive mechanisms with clinically diagnosed ASD (Lai et al. 2013 ; Losh et al. 2008 ; Ozonoff et al. 2011 ; for a review see Pisula and Ziętgart‐Sadowska 2015 ). Consequently, systematic investigation of cerebral language lateralization across individuals with ASD, individuals with BAP traits, and the general population is warranted to determine whether meaningful differences exist. Such work is essential for evaluating whether atypical language lateralization may serve as a potential neural marker extending into the broader phenotype. The present study aims to address this question. ASD is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by deficits in social communication and interaction throughout multiple contexts (DSM‐5‐TR; American Psychiatric Association 2022 ). Language deficits are among the most prominent features of ASD, exhibiting high variability and inconsistent patterns both at the population level and within individual linguistic systems (Arutiunian et al. 2024 ; Herbert and Kenet 2007 ; Stefanatos and Baron 2011 ; Waterhouse 2013 ). Epidemiological, genetic, and familial research indicates that ASD is not a discrete condition; rather, its genetic risk factors often manifest in relatives as milder yet qualitatively similar traits—higher rates of language deficits and subclinical ASD‐like characteristics—a phenotype that is known as BAP (Arutiunian et al. 2024 ; De Groot and Van Strien 2017 ; Deisinger 2015 ; Sucksmith et al. 2011 ; Wheelwright et al. 2010 , for a review see, Pisula and Zietgart‐Sadowska 2015 ). BAP encompasses social and communication challenges—most notably rigid and aloof personality traits and pragmatic language difficulties—and displays symptom fluidity ranging from mild to severe presentations, while still falling short of criteria for clinically diagnosable ASD (Bishop et al. 2004 ; De Groot and Van Strien 2017 ; Dovgan and Villanti 2021 ; Sasson et al. 2013 ; Wallace et al. 2016 ). Family studies focusing on first‐ and second‐degree relatives of individuals with ASD further pinpoint elevated rates of developmental language‐related delays, weakened pragmatic language use, and impaired performance on standardized tests of verbal fluency, reading, and social cognition tasks (Eyuboglu et al. 2018 ; Kellerman et al. 2019 ; Losh et al. 2008 ; Ozonoff et al. 2011 ; Ruta et al. 2012 ; Ruzich et al. 2017 ). Although the impairments associated with BAP may appear mild, their negative effects on daily functioning should not be underestimated, as they substantially affect multiple areas of everyday life. Specifically, individuals with BAP may struggle with relationship and social support system building, feelings of loneliness, challenges in professional achievement and practical skills, as well as emotion regulation and coping abilities, compared to individuals categorized as non‐BAP (Jobe and Williams White 2007 ; Lamport and Zlomke 2014 ; Wainer et al. 2013 ). Given that language deficits are a salient feature of ASD, and that language is the most exemplary of lateralized functions, a plethora of studies have investigated language lateralization in ASD, and have overall reached similar conclusions, highlighting patterns of atypical language lateralization (Jouravlev et al. 2020 ; Kleinhans et al. 2008 , Knaus et al. 2010 , Lindell and Hudry 2013 , Peterson et al. 2024 , Rolison et al. 2022 ; for meta‐analyses, see Herringshaw et al. 2016 ; Li et al. 2023 ; for a review, see Pearson and Hodgetts 2020 ). It is generally accepted—based on neurophysiological and behavioral evidence—that language is mainly lateralized toward the left hemisphere in neurotypical individuals, encompassing fundamental language regions (e.g., Broca's area, medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex, and middle and inferior temporal regions; Everts et al. 2009 ; Gaillard et al. 2003 ; Gutierrez‐Sigut et al. 2015 ; Hervé et al. 2013 ). However, this does not seem to be the case for ASD individuals, according to several functional neuroimaging, electrophysiological, and behavioral investigations, often assessing language lateralization via speech, verbal‐fluency, as well as dichotic listening tasks (Gage et al. 2009 ; Lindell et al. 2009 ; Prior and Bradshaw 1979 ; Rolison et al. 2022 ). In addition, there is strong evidence indicating an association between autism and atypical patterns of handedness (i.e., non‐right‐, left‐, and mixed‐handedness; for reviews and meta‐analyses see, Markou et al. 2017 ; Preslar et al. 2014 ; Rysstad and Pedersen 2016 , and Packheiser et al. 2025 ), further supporting the idea that variations in cerebral lateralization may contribute to diversity in the autism phenotype—since handedness posits an indirect index of cerebral lateralization (Carey and Johnstone 2014 ; Knecht et al. 2000 ). Moreover, genetic findings suggest that brain asymmetries, neurodevelopmental disorders, and handedness are partially influenced by the same genes (Ocklenburg et al. 2025 ; Paracchini 2021 ; Sha et al. 2021a , 2021b ). Two studies to date have investigated cerebral language lateralization in BAP. Martínez‐Sanchis et al. ( 2014 ) explored language lateralization in parents of ASD children in a pilot study ( n = 25, 12 fathers, 13 mothers) using a dichotic listening test, which, in most cases, unveils a right‐ear advantage in neurotypical individuals (Hismjatullina 2006 ), and a left‐ear or no preference in ASD individuals (Martínez‐Sanchis et al. 2011 ). Despite results placing the overall sample within average population norms, when analyzed by gender, mothers showed the expected significant negative correlation between data from both ears ( r = −0.61, p < 0.05), indicating typical hemispheric interdependence in verbal auditory processing. In contrast, fathers did not show this relationship ( r = −0.21, p = 0.52), suggesting reduced interhemispheric information integration. These findings may indicate a potential genetic contribution to atypical language lateralization in autism. In an exploratory study, Jouravlev et al. ( 2020 ) examined a large sample of neurotypical individuals ( n = 189) with normal hearing and vision and no ASD or other neurodevelopmental or psychiatric diagnoses. Autism spectrum quotient (AQ; Baron‐Cohen et al. 2001 ) scores were used to quantify autistic traits across participants, showing that only 8 out of 189 participants (4%) presented with clinically significant autistic trait load (AQ ≥ 32). Bivariate and partial correlations were calculated between AQ scores and language lateralization indices derived from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) during a validated language “localization” task (Fedorenko et al. 2010 ; for details on the procedure see, Mahowald and Fedorenko 2016 ). Autistic trait load showed a small but significant negative association with language lateralization, with higher AQ scores corresponding to less lateralized responses ( r (187) = −0.15, p = 0.05, partial r (185) = −0.15, p = 0.04). These findings of more reduced language lateralization in individuals with higher autistic trait load suggest that reduced language lateralization may serve as a potential neural marker associated with ASD liability. Prior studies on cerebral lateralization for language in ASD have primarily relied on neuroimaging methods such as fMRI (Jouravlev et al. 2020 ; Kleinhans et al. 2008 ; Knaus et al. 2010 ; for a meta‐analysis, see Li et al. 2023 ), positron emission tomography (PET; Keeratitanont et al. 2022 ; Muller et al. 1999 ), or magnetoencephalography (MEG; Flagg et al. 2005 ). These methods, however, face practical constraints, including high cost, the requirement for expensive, specialized equipment, and sensitivity to body movements. They also pose challenges for vulnerable participants—such as children and individuals with ASD—who may have difficulty remaining still in a restricted scanning environment for prolonged periods while also staying in a lying position (Satterthwaite et al. 2012 ; Schabdach et al. 2022 ). In contrast, functional transcranial Doppler ultrasonography (fTCD) is not practically limited in terms of the requirement of specific positioning of the participant or body‐movement impact. FTCD is a validated neurophysiological technique that yields results comparable and consistent with those acquired via the gold‐standard method in the field of language lateralization (Knake et al. 2003 ), namely the intra‐carotid amobarbital procedure (Wada test; Wada 1949 ; Knecht et al. 1998a ), as well as fMRI (Chilosi et al. 2019 ; Deppe et al. 2000 ; Somers et al. 2011 ). FTCD is a non‐invasive tool that records fluctuations in blood‐flow velocity within the middle cerebral arteries (MCA). During testing, ultrasound sensors are positioned over the temporal windows on each side of the head to track blood flow velocity in the MCA as individuals perform cognitive tasks (Hage et al. 2021 ). The MCA supplies blood to cortical regions involved in language production—including the inferior frontal gyrus, superior frontal gyrus, middle temporal gyrus, supramarginal gyrus, angular gyrus, primary auditory cortex (Heschl's Gyrus), and basal ganglia structures (putamen, caudate; Gibo et al. 1981 )—and recent work suggests their supply territory is even broader than previously assumed (Kim et al. 2019 ). This makes the MCA a suitable target for assessing language‐related activation. By comparing blood‐flow velocity changes in the left and right MCA, a lateralization index (LI) can be calculated, indicating which hemisphere shows greater engagement during a cognitive task. These velocity alterations reflect the downstream consequences of localized metabolic activity (Iadecola 2017 ). Unlike fMRI and PET—which typically infer hemispheric dominance by contrasting activity levels in left and right brain regions relative to whole‐brain activation—fTCD quantifies lateralization more directly by measuring relative velocity changes between the two MCAs, as mentioned above (Woodhead et al. 2020 , 2026 ). As a result, fTCD provides a straightforward, continuous, and easy‐to‐calculate measure of hemispheric lateralization without relying on threshold‐based decisions (Gutierrez‐Sigut et al. 2015 ; for a discussion, see Johnstone et al. 2020 ). The technique is also highly sensitive, detecting perfusion differences of approximately 1% between paired basal arteries (Deppe et al. 1997 ). Furthermore, fTCD avoids age‐related limitations and can be used across the lifespan: it is completely safe for infants as young as 6 months (Badcock et al. 2018 ), for children as young as 3 years (Bishop et al. 2009 ), and for adults up to 75 years of age (Keage et al. 2015 ). It has also been used with individuals with ASD (Whitehouse and Bishop 2008 ), as described below. FTCD measurements are largely unaffected by body movements (Bishop et al. 2010 ; Woodhead et al. 2020 ). A key limitation of fTCD is its relatively low spatial resolution, as it primarily reflects activity within the basal cerebral artery territories. Compared with fMRI, fTCD offers limited spatial detail because it detects blood flow velocity changes across the distribution of major cerebral arteries rather than within specific cortical regions (Bishop et al. 2021 ). Consequently, fTCD is best suited for assessing hemispheric lateralization, but it cannot determine which specific brain area or neural networks contribute to language processing, nor can it provide information about within‐hemisphere connectivity or microcircuit organization that is accessible with fMRI (Deppe et al. 2000 ). In addition, insonation of the MCA is not feasible in a proportion of individuals due to the absence of an adequate acoustic window (Knecht et al. 1998a ; Somers et al. 2011 ). This limitation predominantly affects adults, whereas failure rates are substantially lower in children (Kohler et al. 2015 ). title: Psychiatric, anesthetic, and procedural characteristics of modified electroconvulsive therapy courses in adolescents treated in a tertiary child and adolescent psychiatry service: a 15-year retrospective cohort study
abstract:
Background Evidence on electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) in adolescents is largely retrospective and rarely reports psychiatric outcomes together with anesthetic and procedural characteristics. We characterized modified ECT courses in a tertiary child and adolescent psychiatry service. Methods This retrospective cohort included adolescents aged 13–18 years treated with modified ECT from 2010 to 2025; the ECT course was the unit of analysis. Illness severity was rated with the Clinical Global Impression-Severity (CGI-S) scale at admission and discharge. The primary outcome was a composite of any documented hemodynamic event, prolonged seizure, or recovery/behavioral event; short or absent seizures were analyzed separately as a technical seizure-adequacy outcome. Logistic models used standard errors clustered by patient. Results Among 156 ECT courses in 150 adolescents (1,465 sessions), diagnoses were schizophrenia spectrum (46.2%), bipolar spectrum (23.1%), neurodevelopmental (18.6%), and depressive disorders (12.2%). Median CGI-S decreased from 5.0 at admission to 3.0 at discharge, with a study-defined decrease of at least 2 points in 152 courses (97.4%) and a discharge CGI-S of 2 or less in 60 (38.5%). The primary composite event occurred in 63 courses (40.4%), involving one event domain in 49 (31.4%) and two or more in 14 (9.0%). Short or absent seizures occurred in 42 courses (26.9%); theophylline use was associated with higher odds of this outcome, most plausibly reflecting confounding by indication. Estimates for age, bipolar spectrum disorder, and succinylcholine dose were imprecise and hypothesis-generating. Conclusions In this severe tertiary cohort, ECT-centered inpatient care was associated with substantial within-course global improvement, and acute course-level events were common but usually confined to a single domain. Acute anesthesia- or procedure-related events and technical seizure adequacy should be reported separately, and exploratory dose or medication associations should not be interpreted causally. Introduction Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is an established intervention for severe, treatment-refractory, or clinically urgent psychiatric disorders and may be life-saving in catatonia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and other conditions requiring rapid symptom relief. Its use in adolescents remains uncommon, reflecting a less extensive evidence base than in adults, variation in clinical practice, and persistent concern and stigma. Recent systematic reviews, registry studies, and retrospective cohorts nevertheless support clinical benefit in carefully selected young people while emphasizing the low certainty of much of the evidence and the inconsistency of procedural and safety reporting [ 1 – 6 ]. A systematic review focused on treatment-resistant mood disorders reported generally favorable outcomes with mainly transient adverse effects [ 2 ]. A European review of 79 publications from 18 countries similarly found improvement across several severe diagnostic presentations but identified substantial variation in practice and major reporting gaps [ 3 ]. More recent cohorts have expanded the available sample sizes and diagnostic breadth [ 1 , 5 , 6 ]. Thus, a central limitation of the literature is not only the predominance of retrospective designs but also the incomplete and inconsistent description of how ECT is delivered and monitored in real-world adolescent settings. Detailed anesthetic and procedural data are another important gap in adolescent ECT research. ECT is a multidisciplinary intervention delivered under general anesthesia with neuromuscular blockade. Anesthetic induction, neuromuscular-blockade strategy, seizure threshold and duration, hemodynamic response, ventilation, and postictal recovery may influence treatment delivery and procedural safety. Although contemporary anesthesia literature indicates that these factors can affect seizure characteristics and ECT outcomes, optimal pediatric strategies remain incompletely defined [ 7 – 9 ]. Neurodevelopmental stage could also influence responses to anesthetic agents, concomitant psychotropic medications, and induced seizures; however, direct pediatric evidence remains limited [ 7 , 9 ]. Accordingly, adolescent ECT has rarely been characterized as an integrated psychiatric, anesthetic, and procedural intervention. Most studies emphasize diagnosis, clinical response, or broadly defined adverse effects while providing limited information on treatment delivery and monitoring across an ECT course. This limits interpretation of procedural events and treatment adequacy and complicates comparisons of real-world adolescent ECT practice across services. Using 15 years of clinical data from a tertiary child and adolescent psychiatry inpatient service, this study characterized the diagnostic distribution, psychiatric indications, global clinical improvement, anesthetic dosing, seizure-related procedural parameters, hemodynamic events, and recovery/behavioral events associated with adolescent ECT courses. Methods Study design, setting, sampling, and ethical considerations This study was designed as a retrospective observational chart review conducted at the Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Clinic of Bakirkoy Prof. Dr. Mazhar Osman Mental Health and Neurological Diseases Training and Research Hospital, a tertiary psychiatric care unit serving as a national referral center for severe and treatment-refractory psychiatric disorders. The study included adolescents aged 13 to 18 years admitted to the inpatient unit who received modified electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) over a 15-year period (December 2010–December 2025). The final analytic cohort comprised 156 distinct ECT courses administered to 150 adolescents; six patients contributed two separate ECT courses. Observations were structured at three hierarchical levels — the patient (150 adolescents), the ECT course (156 courses), and the ECT session (1,465 sessions) — with the ECT course as the unit of analysis. Session-level anesthetic, stimulus, and event parameters were aggregated to the course level: index-session values were used for anesthetic and stimulus parameters, seizure-duration variables were summarized across all sessions within a course, and hemodynamic and recovery events were defined as the presence of at least one such event during the course. Data were collected using a structured data abstraction form developed for this study and completed from written and electronic medical records, physician discharge summaries, pre-anesthetic assessment forms, anesthesia records, and institutional ECT tracking logs. Extracted data were grouped into baseline socio-anthropometric and clinical characteristics, concomitant medication exposure, ECT and anesthetic/procedural parameters, and clinical outcomes and anesthesia- or procedure-related events. The analytic dataset integrated psychiatric, medication, anesthetic, neuromuscular-blockade, seizure-duration, and procedural-event variables within a unified course-level framework. Ethical approval was obtained from the Clinical Research Ethics Committee of Bakirkoy Dr. Sadi Konuk Training and Research Hospital, Istanbul, Türkiye (decision no. 2026-11/25). The Committee waived the need for informed consent for retrospective use of de-identified archival clinical data owing to the retrospective nature of the study. All procedures performed in this study were in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. ECT eligibility and procedure ECT eligibility was determined after comprehensive clinical evaluation by at least two experienced child and adolescent psychiatrists. The indication for ECT, prior treatment response, illness severity, medical condition, and potential risks and benefits were examined in depth. Before treatment, patients underwent multidisciplinary assessments, including pediatric, neurologic, cardiologic, and anesthesiology evaluations when clinically indicated. ECT was initiated only after informed consent had been obtained from the patient’s legal guardian and assent from the adolescent when applicable. All sessions were delivered as modified ECT under an institutional protocol using a Thymatron System IV device (Somatics LLC, Lake Bluff, IL, USA) with conventional bilateral bitemporal electrode placement. Specifically, the center of each stimulus electrode was positioned 2–3 cm above the midpoint of the line connecting the lateral canthus of the eye and the external auditory meatus on the corresponding side of the head. Stimulus dose was recorded as the percentage of the device’s maximum stimulus output, with 100% corresponding to a maximum delivered charge of 504 mC. Anesthesia was induced with propofol (approximately 1.0 mg/kg IV), followed by neuromuscular blockade with succinylcholine (approximately 0.5 mg/kg IV); when succinylcholine was contraindicated or otherwise avoided, rocuronium (0.3 mg/kg IV) was used and reversed with sugammadex. Patients were ventilated with 100% oxygen until spontaneous respiration returned. The initial stimulus dose was individualized through seizure-threshold titration, taking into account factors expected to influence seizure threshold or characteristics, including age, concurrent benzodiazepine or antiepileptic exposure, and other individual clinical characteristics. Stimulus dose was subsequently titrated according to seizure quality, seizure duration, and clinical response. When a seizure was short or absent, management followed institutional practice and could include restimulation at a higher dose, adjustment of anesthetic timing, and, when clinically indicated, adjunctive intravenous theophylline. Prolonged seizures were managed according to institutional ECT anesthesia practice, including continued airway support, hemodynamic monitoring, and pharmacologic termination when clinically indicated; specific termination interventions were not systematically extractable from the retrospective records. Electroencephalographic and motor seizure activity, electrocardiography, and pulse oximetry were monitored continuously, and procedure-related events were documented on a structured institutional monitoring form. ECT was stopped early if no improvement was observed after four to six sessions or if serious complications occurred. Continuation ECT for up to six months and weekly or monthly maintenance ECT were provided when clinically indicated. The number of sessions, stimulus parameters, seizure-duration measures, anesthetic agents, neuromuscular-blocking agents, and procedure-related events were abstracted at the course level. All procedures were performed under the supervision of an anesthesiologist and a psychiatrist experienced in ECT practice. The interval from hospital admission to first ECT was recorded as a service and procedural timing variable. In this tertiary inpatient setting, the interval largely reflected pre-ECT psychiatric stabilization, anesthetic evaluation, medical investigations, consent procedures, scheduling, and procedural preparation rather than a standardized pre-ECT pharmacological treatment phase. Diagnostic classification and catatonia/NMS context Primary psychiatric diagnoses were classified into four mutually exclusive diagnostic categories: schizophrenia spectrum disorders, bipolar spectrum disorders, neurodevelopmental disorders, and depressive disorders. The neurodevelopmental disorders group was diagnostically specific rather than broadly heterogeneous: all courses involved adolescents with autism spectrum disorder and co-occurring intellectual disability. Catatonia and/or neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) was coded separately as a non-mutually exclusive transdiagnostic clinical context, rather than as a primary diagnostic category, because these syndromes may occur across psychotic, affective, neurodevelopmental, and medication-related presentations. Clinical severity and global improvement assessment The Clinical Global Impression-Severity scale (CGI-S) was used as the common severity metric across diagnostic groups. Admission and discharge CGI-S scores were directly documented in the clinical record for 135 of 156 courses (86.5%). For the remaining 21 courses (13.5%) in which an explicit CGI-S rating was not recorded, the investigators retrospectively estimated severity through structured review of the full clinical record—including presenting symptoms, serial progress notes, physician assessments, and available disorder-specific rating-scale data such as the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale and Young Mania Rating Scale—using published scale-linking frameworks to place each course on the CGI-S metric [ 10 , 11 ]. The reconstructions were not independent, blinded re-ratings; therefore, a formal inter-rater reliability coefficient could not be calculated retrospectively. Global clinical improvement was summarized using absolute admission-to-discharge CGI-S change and a study-defined categorical threshold of a CGI-S decrease of at least two points. This threshold was used for descriptive within-course change and is not equivalent to CGI-I response or remission. Discharge CGI-S of 2 or lower was also evaluated as a stringent global severity endpoint. These outcomes were interpreted as global clinical improvement during ECT-centered inpatient care rather than as controlled estimates of ECT-specific efficacy. Medication exposure and data recoding Medication documentation immediately preceding or during the ECT course varied across the retrospective period. The original medication documentation block, including the total number of concurrent psychotropic medications and broad medication-class fields such as benzodiazepine and mood stabilizer/antiepileptic exposure, was available for 123 courses. In addition, several specific binary exposure indicators were verifiable across the full cohort from fields where a blank entry indicated absence, and these entries were recoded according to the verified data-entry protocol. These full-cohort indicators included antipsychotic exposure, clozapine, valproate, antidepressant exposure, and ADHD medication. ECT and anesthetic/procedural variables ECT and anesthesia-related variables included the interval from admission to first ECT, the number of ECT sessions in the course, initial stimulus dose (% of maximum device output), seizure-duration variables, propofol dose, succinylcholine dose, pseudocholinesterase level, theophylline use, maintenance ECT, and anesthesia and neuromuscular-blockade strategy. Weight-adjusted propofol and succinylcholine doses were analyzed in mg/kg and summarized as mean ± standard deviation. title: Exploring the Neural Mechanisms of Acupuncture Stimulation in Autism Spectrum Disorder: Protocol for a Randomized, Sham-Controlled, Multimodal Neuroimaging Trial
abstract: Abstract Background Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by restricted and repetitive behaviors and disturbances in social communication and interaction. Currently, there is no fundamental treatment for ASD, with only a few medications available for use on a limited basis to manage concomitant neuropsychiatric symptoms. The primary therapeutic goal of such treatments is to alleviate symptoms while maximizing the functional independence and quality of life of affected individuals. Many complementary and alternative medicine therapies have been reported to have effects on ASD symptoms; however, evidence is insufficient to confirm their clinical effectiveness. Acupuncture has traditionally been used as a complementary intervention to manage various neurological and neuropsychiatric diseases, including ASD, in East Asia. However, how acupuncture stimulation modulates neural activity at the macroscale level in individuals with ASD remains largely unknown. Objective This study aims to elucidate disease-related brain alterations and explore the acute neural mechanisms underlying acupuncture stimulation in patients with ASD and in typically developing (TD) individuals, using a multimodal neuroimaging approach. Methods This study was designed as a randomized, sham-controlled trial. In this stratified 2×2 design, 70 participants, including individuals with ASD (n=35) and TD controls (n=35), will each be randomly assigned to either the verum or sham acupuncture group, resulting in 4 groups. The verum acupuncture group will receive stimulation at specific acupoints clinically indicated for ASD, eliciting a deqi sensation. The sham acupuncture group will receive superficial needling at nonacupoints unrelated to ASD symptoms. Each group will undergo clinical assessments and multimodal neuroimaging measurements, including functional near-infrared spectroscopy and electroencephalography, before and after acupuncture stimulation. The primary outcome will be differences in resting state network metrics and relative band power in frontal areas by disease status. Secondary outcomes will include differences in these neural markers following acupuncture stimulation between the verum and sham groups, reflecting the group × intervention interaction. Exploratory outcomes will focus on identifying neural markers that correlate with clinical indicators of ASD. Results Recruitment began in April 2025. To date, 23 individuals with ASD and 21 TD individuals have participated in this study. The recruitment process is expected to continue until December 2026. Conclusions ASD presents a significant socioeconomic burden, with no definitive treatment established to date. Although acupuncture is a widely applied intervention for various neurological conditions, including ASD, its large-scale neural mechanisms remain poorly understood. By using multimodal neuroimaging, the present study aims to investigate the immediate neural substrates underlying acupuncture stimulation in patients with ASD. These findings are expected to provide a robust neurobiological foundation for future longitudinal research and the development of evidence-based integrative strategies.

title: Effects of High-Phenolic Extra Virgin Olive Oil on Sensory Processing in Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Pilot Study
abstract:
ABSTRACT No approved treatments currently exist for the core symptoms of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), prompting clinicians and families to seek alternative approaches, including dietary and nutritional interventions. The Mediterranean diet (MeDi), characterized by a high intake of antioxidant and anti‐inflammatory components, is associated with improved health outcomes and reduced risk of chronic diseases. A key element of the MeDi is extra virgin olive oil (EVOO), which is rich in bioactive phenolics, including oleocanthal, oleuropein and hydroxytyrosol. Through its antioxidant and anti‐inflammatory actions, EVOO may contribute to regulating pathological processes in both the central nervous system (CNS) and the gastrointestinal tract, offering a promising avenue for pharmacological and nutritional intervention in children with ASD. This pilot study investigated the effects of a three‐month intervention combining the MeDi with EVOO supplementation on ASD symptoms. Ten children diagnosed with ASD aged 5.00–11.7 years, all boys, were recruited from Northern Greece. The changes in social interaction and communication were evaluated using standardized instruments: the Social Responsiveness Scale (SRS), Word Finding Vocabulary Test (WFVT), Autism Diagnostic Interview‐Revised (ADI‐R) and the Sensory Profile (SP). Paired‐sample t ‐tests revealed significant improvements post‐intervention in SRS ( p = 0.034), ADI‐R A ( p = 0.008), WFVT ( p = 0.020) and ADI‐R B ( p = 0.022) scores. These findings suggest that EVOO supplementation may reduce the severity of social deficits and enhance communication skills in children with ASD.

Following the 3‐month Mediterranean diet and high‐phenolic extra virgin olive oil intervention, significant improvements were observed in social responsiveness, reciprocal social interaction and expressive vocabulary in children with autism spectrum disorder, with the most notable changes occurring in social and communication domains.

1 Introduction Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is defined as a lifelong neurodevelopmental disorder typically identified in early childhood, characterized by deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts as well as restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities (American Psychiatric Association 2013 ; Bjørklund et al. 2020 ; Maenner et al. 2014 ; Thomaidis et al. 2020 ). ASD prevalence was reported as 1 in 44 children in 2021, increasing to 1 in 31 (3.2%) by 2025, with notably higher rates among boys (Maenner 2021 ; Shaw et al. 2022 ). In Greece, a study by Thomaidis et al. ( 2020 ) reported a prevalence of 1.15% among children aged 10–11 years. ASD exhibits substantial phenotypic and biological heterogeneity (Lenroot and Yeung 2013 ; Lombardo et al. 2019 ) and is frequently accompanied by a wide range of comorbid conditions, including anxiety, depression, psychiatric disorders, delayed motor milestones, attention‐deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), epilepsy, gastrointestinal disturbances and sleep disorders (Al‐Beltagi 2021 ; Hawks and Constantino 2020 ; Lord et al. 2000 ; Mannion and Leader 2013 ; Mansour et al. 2017 ; Maski et al. 2011 ; Noland et al. 2020 ; Weir et al. 2020 ). Notably, some studies report comorbidity rates of up to 91% in individuals with ASD (Al‐Beltagi 2021 ; Mannion and Leader 2013 ; Noland et al. 2020 ). The prevalence and presentation of these comorbidities vary widely across studies, reinforcing the view that ASD is not a single condition but rather a spectrum of conditions with distinct pathophysiological profiles (Casanova et al. 2020 ). Evidence suggests that autism may involve subgroups in which one or more bodily systems are selectively affected, and this complexity is further supported by findings indicating that multiple systems can be involved, highlighting their variability (Burns et al. 2017 ; Noland et al. 2020 ). Among the most frequently reported comorbidities in ASD are sensory dysfunctions, with prevalence rates ranging from 45% to 95%. Their consistent presence contributed to the inclusion of Unusual Sensory Behaviours in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM‐5) diagnostic criteria for ASD in 2013 (Grant and Nozyce 2013 ; Maenner et al. 2014 ; Van Etten et al. 2017 ). 1.1 Oxidative Stress, Mitochondrial Dysfunction and Neuroinflammation Given that autism is multidimensional and associated with comorbidities involving diverse physiological systems, including the nervous, immune and gastrointestinal systems, fundamental cellular processes may underlie this condition (Balachandar et al. 2021 ). Oxidative stress is a pathological imbalance between the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and the body's antioxidant defences. ROS are naturally generated in mitochondria during the electron transport chain (ETC) function, where oxygen is converted into energy (ATP). At physiological levels, ROS support signalling pathways involved in growth, repair and immune responses. In excess, however, they damage proteins, lipids and especially mitochondrial DNA, impairing energy production, amplifying ROS generation and perpetuating oxidative stress when antioxidant defences are insufficient (Bhat et al. 2015 ; Bhatti et al. 2017 ; Bjørklund et al. 2020 ; Liu et al. 2022 ; Russell et al. 2002 ; Usui et al. 2023 ; Yenkoyan et al. 2017 ). Multiple lines of evidence support the involvement of oxidative stress in ASD. Elevated levels of nitric oxide, thiobarbituric acid‐reactive substances (TBARS) and xanthine oxidase activity have been detected in the red blood cells of individuals with autism, indicating an increased oxidative load (Essa and Qoronfleh 2020 ). The central nervous system (CNS) is particularly vulnerable to oxidative stress due to its limited antioxidant defences, high energy demands and elevated levels of lipid/ketones and iron (Bjørklund et al. 2020 ). Children are more susceptible, given naturally low glutathione levels from conception through infancy. In ASD, studies have reported reduced mitochondrial glutathione and genetic variations in related pathways, correlating with symptom severity (Liu et al. 2022 ). Notably, low glutathione levels alongside elevated oxidative stress markers have been associated with more severe gastrointestinal symptoms, a common comorbidity in autism (Bjørklund et al. 2020 ; Essa and Qoronfleh 2020 ; Liu et al. 2022 ; Rossignol and Frye 2014 ). Neuropathological studies provide further evidence of chronic neuroinflammation in ASD. Postmortem analyses reveal widespread activation of astroglia and microglia in the cerebral cortex and white matter, confirming an ongoing inflammatory process (Bjørklund et al. 2020 ; Noland et al. 2020 ; Siddiqui et al. 2016 ; Yenkoyan et al. 2017 ). Mitochondrial dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a key mechanism in ASD, potentially contributing to its core pathology. Elevated oxidative stress levels resulting from mitochondrial abnormalities have been consistently documented, particularly in the mitochondrial electron transport system of individuals with ASD (Usui et al. 2023 ). This oxidative stress impacts critical brain regions involved in social behaviour, memory and motor coordination, including the hippocampus, cerebral cortex and cerebellum (Liu et al. 2022 ). 1.2 Sensory Processing Sensory processing constitutes a critical function of the nervous system, as it involves the reception, processing and integration of sensory stimuli, thereby forming the basis for adaptive behaviour and the individual's interaction with the environment (Galiana‐Simal et al. 2020 ). Ayres's sensory integration theory outlines four stages: registration, modulation, discrimination and response. Dysfunction in any stage may result in sensory processing disorder (SPD), characterized by maladaptive behaviours and motor responses (Baker et al. 2007 ). Studies indicate that up to 95% of children with ASD experience some form of sensory dysfunction, which is closely associated with behaviour, social interaction and adaptive capacity (Kirby et al. 2022 ). Individuals with ASD often experience sensory difficulties, ranging from excessive to insufficient responses to sensory stimuli (Maenner et al. 2014 ). Baranek et al. ( 2006 ) identified two primary patterns of sensory dysfunction: hypo‐responsiveness (reduced reaction) and hyper‐responsiveness (exaggerated response). Tools such as Dunn's Sensory Profile (SP) and Ayres' Sensory Integration and Praxis Tests (SIPT) are widely used to diagnose and assess sensory disorders, offering clinically relevant insights into differences between children with and without such conditions (Katsiana 2015b ). Sensory difficulties significantly affect psychosocial functioning, motor development and daily life of individuals with ASD. They are linked to secondary behaviours such as anxiety, aggression, sleep problems and emotion regulation challenges, highlighting the need for deeper investigation into their relationship with core ASD symptoms (Baker et al. 2007 ; Galiana‐Simal et al. 2020 ; Maenner et al. 2014 ). Mitochondrial dysfunction has been linked to increased vulnerability to sensory disorders, especially in individuals with neurodevelopmental conditions, due to the high energy demands of sensory systems. Oxidative stress may further exacerbate these difficulties by disrupting neuronal balance and promoting inflammation (Silva Santos Ribeiro et al. 2022 ; Rossignol and Frye 2014 ). 1.3 Mediterranean Diet (MediDiet)—Extra Virgin Olive Oil (EVOO) Oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction and neuroinflammation are frequently observed in individuals with ASD, with their severity correlating with symptom intensity, suggesting a central role in ASD pathophysiology. Currently, only two FDA‐approved drugs, risperidone and aripiprazole, are available for managing irritability and aggression in individuals with ASD (Baribeau and Anagnostou 2014 ; Goel et al. 2018 ). At the same time, no pharmacological treatments target core symptoms, such as social or communication deficits (Hellings 2023 ). Given the lack of effective pharmacological treatments for core ASD symptoms, interest has grown in alternative approaches such as dietary interventions, particularly the Mediterranean diet, which has long been associated with longevity and the prevention of chronic diseases (Gaforio et al. 2019 ). It is characterized by a high intake of plant‐based foods, fish and seafood; moderate consumption of aged cheese and red wine; limited meat and dairy; and avoidance of processed foods (Guasch‐Ferré and Willett 2021 ; Pollicino et al. 2023 ; Sikalidis et al. 2021 ; Summerhill et al. 2018 ; Vrdoljak et al. 2022 ). Its hallmark is EVOO, the primary fat source (Gaforio et al. 2019 ). EVOO contains monounsaturated fatty acids (e.g., oleic acid) and vitamin E, providing significant antioxidant activity (Salucci et al. 2022 ). Its polyphenols—such as hydroxytyrosol, oleuropein and oleocanthal—have notable anti‐inflammatory, anti‐allergic, antithrombotic, anticancer and antioxidant effects. Hydroxytyrosol protects against oxidative stress, oleuropein reduces inflammation and blood pressure, and oleocanthal acts similarly to ibuprofen (a non‐steroidal anti‐inflammatory drug) (Al Rihani et al. 2019 ; Gorzynik‐Debicka et al. 2018 ; Hrelia et al. 2019 ; Jimenez‐Lopez et al. 2020 ; Presti et al. 2017 ; Yubero‐Serrano et al. 2018 ). These compounds support the neuroprotective role of EVOO (Gonçalves et al. 2024 ). A growing body of literature highlights the protective effects of EVOO in chronic diseases, focusing on its biological and pharmacological–nutritional potential (Gaforio et al. 2019 ; Vrdoljak et al. 2022 ). A study by Pase et al. ( 2015 ) demonstrated that a 20% olive oil–enriched diet (OOED) administered during pregnancy, lactation and post‐weaning in rats significantly reduced oxidative stress markers, such as lipid peroxidation and ROS, while enhancing antioxidant defences (GSH) and upregulating neurotrophic factors (BDNF and FGF‐2) in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus. These findings highlight the neuroprotective potential of EVOO components, particularly hydroxytyrosol and oleuropein, during critical developmental periods (Pase et al. 2015 ). EVOO shows neuroprotective effects in aging and early neurodegeneration through its polyphenols, which modulate inflammation and support neural function (Alkhalifa et al. 2024 ; Chatzikostopoulos et al. 2022 ). In MCI patients, Tsolaki et al. ( 2020 ) found that combining MedDiet with high phenolic early harvest EVOO improved cognition and symptom stability. Gonçalves et al. ( 2024 ) confirmed that oleuropein, hydroxytyrosol and oleocanthal reduce oxidative stress and support neuroprotection in models of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. Beyond neurodegeneration, EVOO's bioactive compounds are also linked to benefits in immuno‐inflammatory diseases, including inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), rheumatoid arthritis (RA), systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and multiple sclerosis (MS), as well as in cancer prevention, Type 2 diabetes management and gut microbiota modulation (Gavahian et al. 2019 ; Trichopoulou et al. 2000 ). Disruptions in the microbiome–gut–brain axis in ASD have spurred interest in dietary interventions (Thoma et al. 2023 ). Rodop et al. ( 2021 ) found that the MediDiet, gluten‐ and casein‐free diets and the ketogenic diet may help reduce inflammation, alleviate gastrointestinal symptoms and improve brain function by regulating short‐chain fatty acids and serotonin levels. The primary goal of the study was to evaluate whether a polyphenol‐rich Mediterranean diet incorporating high‐phenolic EVOO alleviates sensory processing difficulties and related symptoms in children with ASD, potentially mediated by CNS oxidative and inflammatory pathways. 2 Methods 2.1 Study Design This non‐randomized pilot open intervention involved a three‐month Mediterranean diet combined with polyphenol‐rich extra virgin olive oil (EVOO). 2.2 Participants Participants were recruited through personal, email or telephone communication, during which they received detailed study information and were screened for eligibility. Eligible and willing participants provided informed consent in accordance with the GDPR guidelines before scheduling their first visit. The study aimed to evaluate improvement in sensory processing and related domains following the dietary intervention. A total of 37 families were initially approached and received a consent questionnaire along with detailed study information. Of these, 12 families provided written informed consent and completed the preliminary screening materials. However, 27 families ultimately did not participate in the study.
